sens: To experience an intense and prolonged desire for something or someone
To have eagerness, greed to do something
To show impudence, shamelessness
H3700.detail:
1. To experience an intense and prolonged desire: this is the most common meaning of the word. One "languishes" when they ardently wish to be with someone or have something, and they deeply desire it. This is what Jacob does in Genesis 31:30, when Laban says: he languished after his father's house. It is also the image of one who calls and languishes after the work of their hands in Job 14:15: God intensely awaits to see His creatures again.
2. To have eagerness, greed: the word then denotes a strong and carnal desire, often something that devours or consumes. It is the lion "greedy" to tear in Psalms 17:12, who is hungry and waits impatiently for its prey.
3. To show impudence or shame: in Zephaniah 2:1, a nation "without shame" is one that has lost all restraint, all decency. It is almost the absence of the feeling of shame that should hold someone back.
H3700.origine: The Hebrew verb כָּסַף (kasaph) comes from a root that evokes the idea of consuming, of desiring intensely. The word is related to other Hebrew terms expressing ardor and the desire of the heart. Its primary image is that of a thirst or hunger that nothing can quench: one languishes as one slowly consumes away.
H3700.emploi: The verb כָּסַף appears 5 times in the Old Testament. In Genesis 31:30, Jacob languishes after his land and family. In Job 14:15, it expresses God's intense love for His work. In Psalms 17:12 and 84:3, it describes the lion's greed for its prey and the faithful's ardent desire for the courts of God. In Zephaniah 2:1, it takes on a moral sense: the absence of shame. The word thus oscillates between emotional desire (nostalgia, love), carnal ardor (the predator's greed), and a notion of moral restraint.
H3700.portee: This word shows how the Bible speaks of the desires of the heart: do we languish after God and His presence as after what we miss the most? In Job, it reminds us that God Himself "languishes" after us, that He desires us. It is a word of divine tenderness often forgotten. For the faithful, it is a challenge: to direct their ardors toward what is truly worthwhile.

sens: The precious white metal used to make objects or ornaments
Money, that which serves as a means of exchange and payment
Wealth, measurable and possessed goods
The price paid to acquire or redeem something
H3701G.detail:
1. Silver is primarily the metal itself: shiny, malleable, precious. It is worked to make ornaments, vessels, bases for the structure of the sanctuary (Exodus 36:24 speaks of the silver bases of the Tabernacle). It is a valuable material that can be weighed and measured.

2. Then, silver becomes money: the concrete means of buying and selling, paying a debt or service. When Abraham buys a field, he pays in silver (Genesis 23:15-16). It is the universal language of commerce.

3. Silver also represents accumulated wealth, the goods one possesses. Abram was rich "in livestock, in silver and in gold" (Genesis 13:2): three forms of wealth, of which silver is the most portable and useful.

4. Finally, silver can be a price of redemption or compensation. When one bought a slave, a sum of silver was paid (Exodus 21:32); it was the price of their life or service. This meaning carries a moral weight: it is what is exchanged for something or someone.
H3701G.origine: The word הכסף (keseph) comes from a very ancient Semitic root meaning "to peel" or "to scrape," as the precious metal is obtained by scraping the ore or purifying it by fire. The Hebrew word emphasizes the idea of what is refined, purified, separated from the gangue. In Aramaic and Phoenician, a similar word is found. It is a simple, concrete word that speaks of the metal before discussing its function of exchange.
H3701G.emploi: This word appears 331 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the narratives of the patriarchs and in the Law. It designates either the metal (the bases of the Tabernacle in Exodus 36), or the money used to buy or sell (Joseph sold to his masters in Genesis 37:28), or measurable wealth (Genesis 13:2). Over time, silver also becomes the instrument of the most serious transactions: buying a field (Genesis 23), paying a ransom, compensating a victim. In the laws of Leviticus and Exodus, prices are set in silver for redemption, wages, damages. It is a neutral, economic word that leads directly to moral questions of just exchange, greed, and trust in God rather than in wealth.
H3701G.portee: Silver in the Bible is never a simple neutral object. God asks the people to voluntarily offer silver and precious metals for the Tabernacle (Exodus 35:5): it is an act of generosity. Elsewhere, the love of money is denounced as a source of sin. The word invites us to examine our relationship with wealth: is it a gift from God that we manage wisely and justly, or an idol that distances us from Him? Silver in Scripture always reveals what is in the heart.

sens: The market value of something, expressed in money or precious metal
The amount of money required to acquire or redeem something
The numerical estimation of a good or possession
The remuneration or financial compensation
H3701H.detail:
1. The price is primarily the exchangeable value of something — what it is worth in money. When Abraham wants to buy the cave of Machpelah to bury Sarah, he asks that it be given to him "for its value in silver" (Genesis 23:9): the field must be evaluated and a sum fixed.
2. It is also the amount paid to acquire or redeem. If two oxen kill each other, one sells the living ox and "shares the price" of the dead ox between the two owners (Exodus 21:35): each receives a share of the money paid.
3. The price can also be a legal or religious estimation. For a field consecrated to the Lord, "the priest shall evaluate its price according to the number of years remaining until the jubilee" (Leviticus 27:18): one calculates how much this field is worth according to the years.
4. Finally, it is what a person or thing "really costs" — the true price, without haggling. King David refuses a gift: "I want to buy it for its value in silver, for I will not offer to the Lord that which costs me nothing" (1 Chronicles 21:24).
H3701H.origine: This Hebrew word first designates silver or noble metal, then by extension the price or value. It comes from a root expressing the idea of "measuring" or "evaluating": for the price is the measure of value. This word often appears in the laws of the Old Testament concerning buying, selling, redeeming, and sacrifices, where everything must be evaluated according to a just standard.
H3701H.emploi: This word appears about a dozen times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the laws of Leviticus and Numbers, and in narratives of purchase or redemption. In Genesis 23, Abraham pays the "price" of the field of Machpelah to make a tomb. In legal codes, "the price" fixes the compensation due in case of damage (Exodus 21:35), or allows calculating the redemption of a person or a consecrated possession (Leviticus 25:50-51, Numbers 18:16). In 1 Chronicles 21:24, David insists on paying the true price, without saving, because an offering to God must require a real sacrifice. The word thus remains anchored in the economic and legal domain of the ancient world.
H3701H.portee: For the believer, understanding this word reminds us that the value of things is never neutral: it reflects justice and responsibility. When the Bible insists on the just price, it calls for honesty in transactions and respect for the rights of others. David refuses to give to God what costs him nothing (1 Chronicles 21:24): this invites us to reflect on what we truly offer to the Lord, and whether that gift truly engages us.

sens: Precious white and shiny metal, used in jewelry and liturgical objects
Currency, wealth, exchange value
H3702.detail:
1. Silver is a precious, white, and shiny metal, worked by silversmiths to create worship objects, temple utensils, or ornaments. When King Cyrus restores "the gold and silver utensils" of the temple in Jerusalem (Ezra 5:14), these are valuable items that hold worth as a rare and beautiful metal.
2. Silver also functions as currency and a reserve of wealth: it is used to purchase animal offerings ("you shall buy with this silver bulls, rams, and lambs," Ezra 7:17) or to measure royal tributes ("up to one hundred talents of silver," Ezra 7:22). It is a medium of exchange and economic power.
H3702.origine: The Hebrew word כְּסַף (kesaph) designates precious metal since ancient times. Its etymology refers to the idea of something white or shiny. In biblical Hebrew, silver is one of the most precious and commonly used metals in commerce and worship, alongside gold. The word has retained this dual meaning (metal and currency) throughout biblical history.
H3702.emploi: The word silver appears 13 times in the provided usages, primarily in the books of Ezra and Daniel. Ezra 5 and 7 describe the restoration and funding of the temple: silver is a valuable material asset and a means of payment to restore worship. Daniel 2 and 5 use it to describe the composition of statues or treasures, showcasing the wealth of Babylon. In all these contexts, silver represents either an object of liturgical value or a tangible and measurable economic resource.
H3702.portee: This word reminds us that material resources—silver, goods—play a concrete role in God's project. When God commands the reconstruction of the temple through the donations of the king, He shows that even the wealth of nations can serve His purpose. This invites the reader to see their resources not as an end in themselves, but as means to honor God.

sens: Place in Babylon on the route between Babylon and Jerusalem
H3703.detail: Casiphia is a location in Babylon (the ancient empire of Mesopotamia, now Iraq), strategically situated on the route between the capital Babylon and Jerusalem. It is where the leader Iddo and the Nethinim (assistants to the priests of the Temple) resided at the time of the return of the exiles.
H3703.origine: The Hebrew name Casiphia literally means "silvery," probably referring to a characteristic of the place—perhaps mineral resources, a shining watercourse, or a commercial nickname. The exact site in Babylon has not been definitively identified by archaeologists.
H3703.emploi: Casiphia appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:17, during the return of the Jewish exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem in the 5th century BC. Ezra sends messengers to this place to meet Iddo and the Nethinim to recruit qualified servants for the rebuilding Temple. It was thus a center of significant administrative and religious activity among the exiled Jewish community.

sens: Object of amulet, band or tie placed under the arms
False talisman used by false prophetesses to deceive and exploit the people
H3704.detail:
1. The amulet is a band of cloth or an object that was fixed under the arms, that is, under the armpits. It is a concrete physical accessory that the false Israelite prophetesses made and sold to people.
2. These amulets were fraudulent talismans, false magical objects supposed to bring protection or luck. The false prophetesses crafted them to "capture souls" (Ezekiel 13:18), meaning to ensnare, seduce, and dominate credulous people by persuading them that these objects had supernatural power. It was a form of religious exploitation: they sold these lies to keep souls under their control.
H3704.origine: The Hebrew word késet designates a band, a tie, or an accessory wrapped around the body. Its etymology suggests the idea of wrapping or binding. It belongs to the realm of fabric and religious ornament, like the phylacteries or fringes worn by devout Jews, but here it is diverted from its purpose. The word accurately translates what the false prophetesses made: not authentic sacred objects, but counterfeits intended to deceive.
H3704.emploi: The word amulet appears only twice in the Bible, both in Ezekiel 13, where the prophet denounces the false prophetesses of Israel. Ezekiel 13:18 describes the making of these amulets for the armpits and veils for the head, accessories combined in a religious scam. In verse 20, the Lord announces that He will tear these amulets from the hands of the false prophetesses and deliver the souls they sought to capture. The context is one of divine judgment against false prophecy and the exploitation of the weak.
H3704.portee: This text about the amulets exposes how false spirituality exploits the credulity and fear of people, deceiving them with worthless objects presented as magical or protective. For the Christian, it is a warning against false religious promises, talismans, and superstitions: true protection and guidance come from God alone, not from objects or people claiming to hold secret power.

sens: At this present moment
Up to this moment
As a consequence of this
H3705.detail:
1. The word designates the current moment, the instant of speaking. In Ezra 5:17, the governor asks the king to investigate "now" to verify the orders of Cyrus: it is an urgent request at the time of conversation.
2. It also marks the duration extending from the past to the present. In Ezra 5:16, it is said that since the laying of the temple's foundations "until now" the house is being built: this time that endures.
3. It can finally mean "therefore" or "consequently," linking a logical conclusion. In Ezra 4:21, the king orders "therefore" to cease the temple work: this order naturally follows the denunciation of the Samaritans.
H3705.origine: This Aramaic word (the Bible uses here the Aramaic dialect, not classical Hebrew) belongs to the texts of Ezra and Daniel. It is the Aramaic form corresponding to the Hebrew עַתָּה (atta). Its root evokes the sense of "moment," the "then and now." The parallel Hebrew word appears hundreds of times in the Old Testament to denote the present moment or the moment of decision.
H3705.emploi: The word appears 13 times in biblical Aramaic, only in the Aramaic portions of Ezra (chapters 4 to 6) and Daniel (chapters 2 to 7). It is found mainly in official speeches or prayers: King Nebuchadnezzar "now" praises God (Daniel 4:37); King Darius "now" orders the governor of the river (Ezra 6:6); Nebuchadnezzar "now" commands prostration before the statue (Daniel 3:15). The word creates urgency, authority, a moment of immediate action. Sometimes it links two ideas by logical consequence.
H3705.portee: This word invites the reader to grasp the importance of the present moment and immediate decision. In the narratives of Ezra and Daniel, "now" marks a turning point each time: a royal order, a choice of fidelity, a praise of God. It reminds us that every moment when God speaks or when it is appropriate to respond is urgent and decisive.

sens: and other things
and the rest
continuation of a list without exhaustive detail
H3706.detail:
1. The Aramaic word "and so on" (often abbreviated as "etc.") indicates that a list or enumeration continues beyond what has just been explicitly named. It is a shorthand formula: instead of listing everything, one says "and the rest" to imply that there are other items of the same kind. In Ezra 4:10, after naming Osnappar and his actions, the phrase says "and other places on this side of the river, etc." to signify that there are indeed many other locations without listing them all.
2. This expression invites the reader to understand "the continuation of the same sort": when the king writes to Ezra in Ezra 7:12 and ends with "etc.", it means that there would be other titles, other qualities, or other mentions to add, but that we will stick to the essentials. It is an economy of words: showing that the list is open, not closed.
H3706.origine: This Aramaic word is a double form of "now" (כְּעַן, "kean"); it has gradually taken on the meaning of "and likewise," "and so forth." In Aramaic, it marks the continuation of a series whose terms are not all enumerated. It is a practical tool of administrative and official writing, appearing mainly in epistolary texts and royal documents.
H3706.emploi: The word appears four times in the book of Ezra, only in Aramaic passages (Ezra 4:10, 4:11, 4:17, and 7:12). These usages are all in official texts: letters addressed to the king or from the king, administrative correspondence. Each time, it concludes or punctuates a list of elements (peoples, places, titles) by signifying "and so forth." The usage is very administrative and formal, typical of the Persian royal correspondence reported in Ezra.
H3706.portee: This small word reminds us that the Bible does not claim to say everything with exhaustive detail: it mentions what is important for its purpose, then stops. For the reader, it is an invitation not to ask the Bible for complete lists of everything that has happened, but to grasp the essence of the narrative. It is also a mark of authenticity of the documents: royal letters of the time indeed had this concise and administrative style.

sens: to be angry, to be vexed, to be indignant
to provoke someone to anger, to seriously offend them
to cause annoyance, irritation
to sadden, to afflict someone
H3707.detail:
1. The basic meaning is the state of being angry, vexed, or indignant: one experiences a strong and negative reaction to something unjust or unpleasant. It is an anger that rises, as in 1 Samuel 1:6 where Peninnah "provoked" Hannah by belittling her; or in Psalms 112:10 where the wicked is provoked upon seeing the righteous prosper.
2. The word especially expresses the action of provoking someone to anger, of offending them to the point of awakening their fury. This is what the Israelites do when they "provoke" God by their idols and unfaithfulness (Deuteronomy 4:25, 1 Kings 14:9). God finds Himself provoked to anger by the sin of His people.
3. Provocation can also be a simple annoyance or repeated vexation — a wound to one's pride that irritates (like Hannah's annoyance at Peninnah's provocations). It is less intense than fury, but it is persistent.
4. In some cases, the word takes on a more sorrowful nuance: to afflict, to sadden someone to the point of causing moral suffering. Affliction and vexation intersect.
H3707.origine: The verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of tightening, contracting — which happens in the heart when one experiences anger or annoyance. It is a physical and emotional reaction: the heart tightens. The family of the word includes terms related to annoyance and frustration. It is an active verb that implies an agent: someone or something provokes this reaction in someone else.
H3707.emploi: The verb appears 53 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the history of Israel, the accounts of kings, and the prophets. Its subject can be an irritated person (like Hannah) or God irritated by the sin of His people — the latter usage predominates. The Israelites "provoke" God by worshiping other gods, building high places, and refusing to listen to His prophets (Deuteronomy 32:16, 1 Kings 14:9, Jeremiah 25:7). God warns against what will provoke Him (Deuteronomy 4:25, 31:29). Sometimes, it is a rival who provokes another (1 Samuel 1:6-7: Peninnah provokes Hannah). God's irritation is never a mere mood: it is the rightful reaction of the Holy One to the unfaithfulness of His people, and it carries consequences (divine anger, punishment, exile).
H3707.portee: This verb shows how God reacts to the sin of His people. He is not indifferent to unfaithfulness: He is provoked, stirred, hurt in His love. This teaches that God is not a distant and impassive deity, but a Father who feels rejection and unfaithfulness. For the believer, it is a call not to provoke God through sin, but to revere Him and keep His covenant. It is also a comfort for those who unjustly suffer the irritation of others (like Hannah): God sees and hears.

sens: intense anger and irritation
affliction, moral suffering
that which provokes indignation or frustration
H3708A.detail:
1. Grief is primarily intense anger, an irritation that rises within us when we are hurt or annoyed. It is a strong and often brief emotion. In Deuteronomy 32:19, the Lord is indignant — this divine grief — against His sons and daughters who have abandoned Him. In Proverbs 12:16, the fool shows his anger at once, while the wise man knows how to contain it.
2. Grief can also prolong into lasting suffering, pain of heart and body. The psalmist cries in Psalms 6:8: "I am worn out from grief," an image of the exhaustion caused by prolonged affliction. It is this same pain that Hannah feels in 1 Samuel 1:6 when her rival gives her mortifications to irritate her.
3. Sometimes the word designates that which provokes this affliction: a hurtful word, a frustration, a provocation. In Proverbs 17:25, having a foolish son is a source of grief for his parents.
H3708A.origine: The Hebrew word כַּעַס (ka'as) comes from a root that expresses irritation and agitation of the soul. It is related to the idea of being troubled, being shaken by a violent emotion. The root evokes movement, stirring, as if something inside is being stirred in anger or distress. In the Greek Old Testament, this word is often rendered by a term denoting irritation or indignation.
H3708A.emploi: The word is very frequent in the Hebrew Bible, particularly in Psalms and Proverbs, as well as in Ecclesiastes. It designates either the anger of God provoked by the unfaithfulness of the people (Deuteronomy 32:19), or human anger that explodes or is restrained (Proverbs 12:16), or personal affliction that weighs on body and soul (Psalms 6:8, 31:10). In Ecclesiastes, the word takes on a more philosophical hue: wisdom itself causes grief (1:18), for knowing the vanity of the world afflicts the seeker. The context determines whether it is an immediate reaction (anger) or a suffering that settles in.
H3708A.portee: Understanding this word invites us to recognize that anger and affliction are biblical realities, not to deny them. Grief can be just — like God's grief in the face of evil — or unjust — like that harbored by the fool. For the believer, it is a lesson on mastering emotions: the wise does not let sudden grief dominate, but discerns what its true cause is and how to respond. It is also an invitation to entrust our suffering and agitation of heart to the Lord.

sens: sentiment intense de peine ou de souffrance
colère, indignation
vexation, irritation
chagrin profond, affliction
H3708B.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the physical or moral pain felt: acute suffering that affects the body or soul. Job says that his eyes are darkened by pain (Job 17:7), an image of someone whose grief is so great that it even affects their worldview.
2. It also expresses anger and indignation, particularly that of God. Job 10:17 speaks of God's "furies," His repeated anger against Job, seen as a succession of calamities — the pain here is that inflicted on someone, not that which one experiences.
3. The word can also mean vexation or irritation, a kind of annoyance or displeasure. Job 5:2 shows that the fool perishes in his own anger (his vexation), carried away by his feelings.
4. In a broader sense, it refers to deep and prolonged sorrow, the affliction that accompanies illness or distress. Job 6:2 wishes to weigh all his pain and calamities together, so heavy and overwhelming is it.
H3708B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes inner turmoil, the agitation of the soul. It is close to other Hebrew words that denote violent emotional states: anger, irritation, rage. The basic image is that of a strong disturbance, which shakes the person from within.
H3708B.emploi: This word appears four times in the Bible, exclusively in the book of Job. It is used to describe the emotional states of a person in distress: Job himself suffering his afflictions (Job 6:2, Job 17:7) and speaking of his own pain or irritation regarding his situation. The word also applies to God's feelings towards Job (Job 10:17). In all cases, it is a strong and destructive emotion that consumes and paralyzes the one who feels it.
H3708B.portee: This word helps the reader understand the depth of Job's suffering, which is not only physical pain but also a moral and spiritual distress that completely overwhelms him. It shows that anger and pain, when enduring, gnaw at the soul and even cloud our vision. It is a call to seek comfort beyond our wounded emotions.

sens: The palm or the open surface of the hand
The hand as an instrument of action, power, or authority
The sole of the foot
A hollow or curved object
H3709G.detail:
1. The palm is the inner and flat part of the hand. In Exodus 9:33, Moses "raises his hand" toward heaven to stop the hail; in Numbers 5:18, the priest places the offering "on the hands" of the woman.
2. The hand represents the power to act, the ability to do or to withhold. Isaiah 38:6 speaks of the "hand of the king of Assyria" to denote his conquering power. Psalms 24:4 asks: "Who shall ascend the hill of the Lord? He who has clean hands," meaning one who has not committed wrong.
3. The sole is the bottom of the foot, the surface that touches the ground. This is the meaning of kaph when it refers to the foot in Exodus 4:25 or similar contexts.
4. Kaph applies to any hollow or curved object: the hand of a balance (hollow to receive), the hem of a garment (a piece of fabric), a handful of flour (1 Kings 17:12), or the branches of palm trees (naturally curved).
H3709G.origine: Kaph comes from a root that expresses the idea of hollow, concavity. The palm of the hand is naturally hollow, made to grasp and hold. The Hebrew word kaph is the origin of kaf, the eleventh letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which was drawn like an open hand. This idea of hollowness is found in related words: hollow objects (bowls, cups, containers) are also called kaph. In Greek, the word palm (pálmē) translates kaph in the Greek Old Testament.
H3709G.emploi: Kaph appears 133 times in the Old Testament. It is the most common word for "hand" in Hebrew. It is found everywhere: to express innocence (Psalms 24:4, Genesis 20:5), action (Exodus 9:33), power or authority (the hand of the king, the hand of God), and also in ritual gestures (Numbers 5:18). The word also applies to the sole of the foot and to hollow objects: a "handful" of flour (1 Kings 17:12) or the palm branches of palm trees. In many passages, the "hand" is associated with moral strength (innocence or guilt) and the power of action.
H3709G.portee: The hand in the Bible symbolizes much more than the physical organ: it embodies the capacity to act, moral responsibility, and power. To say that one's hands are innocent is to affirm that one's deeds bear no guilt. Understanding that the hand represents authority and power helps to grasp many biblical images: being "in the hand of the Lord" means being under His protection or judgment. It is through our hands that we act, and the Bible reminds us that we are responsible for our actions.

sens: The bottom part of the foot that touches the ground
The hand or palm, particularly the hollow part
The hollow or curved object, like a cup or a container
The power or authority exercised over a territory
H3709H.detail:
1. The sole of the foot is the underside of the foot, the part that touches the ground when walking. It is literally what touches the earth: the dove in Noah's ark found no place to "set the sole of her foot" (Genesis 8:9), for there was only water everywhere.
2. The word also refers to the open hand or its palm. It is the hollow and flat part of the hand that can receive or hold something — the image comes from the shape: a flat surface capable of grasping.
3. By extension, it describes any hollow or curved object: a cup, a vase, or even the hollow of the thigh (Ezekiel 1:7 mentions feet shaped like animals with shining soles).
4. The word also takes on a figurative meaning: the sole of the foot symbolizes grip and domination. When God promises, "Every place that the sole of your foot will tread shall be yours" (Deuteronomy 11:24), it means that the people will possess all the territories they conquer.
H3709H.origine: The Hebrew word kaph literally means "palm" or "flat and hollow surface." It comes from a root that evokes the idea of bending or folding — hence the primary image: the hand closed or open, which naturally curves. The same family gives words for "spoon" and "knife." In Greek, the Psalter translates this word as "foot" or "hand" depending on the context. It is a very concrete word: it depicts what one sees and touches.
H3709H.emploi: The word kaph appears about twenty times in the Old Testament, mostly to describe the foot. It is often found in promises of territory: God assures Israel that every place where the sole of their foot treads will belong to them (Deuteronomy 11:24; Joshua 1:3). It also appears in descriptions of misfortune: God will not give rest to the soles of the feet in exile (Deuteronomy 28:65). Isaiah uses it to show the power of a king who dries up rivers by trampling them (Isaiah 37:25). The word also refers to the paw of an animal (Leviticus 11:27) or the shining feet of celestial beings (Ezekiel 1:7).
H3709H.portee: This word reminds us that it is through simple and physical gestures — walking, placing the foot — that the believer takes possession of God's promises. The land and blessings are not abstract; they are lived out concretely, step by step. Conversely, the absence of rest for the sole of the foot symbolizes loss and exile: without grounding, without land, man is wandering. The word invites us to see that God acts in the real history and geography of the people.

sens: Hollow container, usually made of precious metal, used for drinking or making offerings
Concave or rounded object, particularly a natural cavity of the body
Branch or frond of a palm tree, flat and curved
Capacity, power, authority (figurative sense)
H3709I.detail:
1. The cup is a container intended to hold liquid, often made of gold or silver in the context of worship: Numbers 7:26 describes "a gold cup of ten shekels, full of perfume," offered to the Lord during the consecration of the tabernacle. It is a precious utensil, worthy of religious service.
2. The word also refers to a cavity or anatomical hollow, particularly the joint where one bone fits into another: Genesis 32:25 reports that Jacob "wrestled" and "his hip was dislocated," the Hebrew word indicating the joint cavity of the hip that was dislocated.
3. Kaph can refer to a branch of a palm tree, which naturally has a flat and curved shape: Leviticus 23:40 commands to take "branches of palm trees" for the Feast of Tabernacles, which are waved in celebration.
4. Figuratively, the word expresses power, dominion, or authority, particularly "the palm of the hand" as a symbol of control: 1 Samuel 25:29 speaks of the souls of enemies thrown "from the hollow of the sling," an image of complete mastery.
H3709I.origine: Kaph comes from a very ancient root meaning "to bend" or "to fold." The basic image is that of the palm of the hand, which is naturally hollow and concave. From this primary meaning, all others unfold: hands that hold, bend, shape; hollow or curved objects that recall the shape of the palm's hollow; and figuratively, the hand as a symbol of power and mastery. The word is at the root of the name for the first hand in Hebrew.
H3709I.emploi: Kaph appears 27 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily to designate the cups of the tabernacle and the temple. These cups, always made of gold or silver, are important worship objects, listed in Numbers 7 and mentioned in the descriptions of the temple in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles, notably in 2 Chronicles 4:22 and during the plundering of the temple in 2 Kings 25:14. The word is also used for the hollows of the human body (Genesis 32:25, 32) and for rounded natural elements like palm branches (Leviticus 23:40). It is a concrete word, never purely abstract, rooted in sensory experience.
H3709I.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of detail in worship and adoration: the objects that serve the Lord must be beautiful and precious, worthy of Him. It also invites the reader to see, in the hollow hand, the symbol of receiving and giving — the hand that receives God's blessings, the hand that transmits them. Finally, it roots prayer in the body and in visible creation, far from any abstraction.

sens: large mass of stone that emerges from the ground or dominates a landscape
natural cavity or hollow in the rock serving as a refuge
H3710.detail:
1. The rock is a large rocky formation, a solid outcrop of stone that emerges from the earth. It is an element of the landscape, durable and unshakeable. In Jeremiah 4:29, during a flight from invaders, people "climb on the rocks" to escape danger: the rock is a high place, difficult to access, where one can take refuge.
2. The word also refers to hollows, caves naturally carved in the rock. In Job 30:6, the unfortunate "dwell in the caves of the earth and in the rocks" — the rock then becomes a shelter, a dwelling of refuge for those who have nothing else.
H3710.origine: The Hebrew word keph comes from a root that evokes hardness and mineral solidity. Its basic meaning is "stone" or "rock" in its most massive and visible form. The word has also retained the meaning of "hollow" or "cavity" because the natural rocks of the land are often riddled with caves and hollows — spaces carved by water or the wear of time, which make the rock a refuge.
H3710.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible in Hebrew: in Job 30:6 and Jeremiah 4:29. In both contexts, the rocks are places of refuge — either natural (the caves where the destitute live) or for escape (where people climb to evade an invader). It is a concrete word that paints the landscape of the ancient Near East, rocky and rugged, where stone was a constant element of survival and security.
H3710.portee: The rock in the Bible is often an image of stability and divine protection. These two verses show how the rock can be a refuge for the weak and the fleeing — a lesson that God Himself offers to His people, as He is compared elsewhere to an unshakeable rock that protects those who trust in Him.

sens: Calm someone who is angry or furious
Make gentle and manageable what is violent or hostile
H3711.detail:
1. To appease is to calm anger as one would silence a storm. In Proverbs 21:14, a secret gift "appeases" anger: the present acts as a form of pacification that removes the destructive force of fury. The image is that of anger gradually extinguishing.
2. The verb also evokes the idea of rendering something violent harmless, making it gentle. It is transforming a state of hostility into peace, an aggressive disposition into goodwill.
H3711.origine: The root kaphah in Hebrew means "to cover" or "to smother" — as if one were covering anger to silence it. The verb carries the idea of containing, dominating a force that threatens to escape. The family of this root conveys the action of mastering what is wild or untamed.
H3711.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 21:14. It illustrates a practical wisdom: a well-thought-out gift, offered discreetly, has the power to transform anger into calm. The context is that of human relationships and managing conflicts through thoughtful generosity.
H3711.portee: This verse teaches us that there are simple and gracious ways to resolve tensions: not through confrontation, but through delicate and generous attention. This reflects the patience and wisdom that a Christian can show to restore peace in wounded relationships.

sens: Branch or frond of the palm tree
Vegetative part that greens and produces
Image of vigor and prosperity
Symbol of what can be cut off or destroyed
H3712.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the branch or frond of the palm tree, an emblematic tree of the ancient Near East. It is the green and leafy part that grows at the top of the tree.
2. The branch also represents what is alive and productive: in Job (15:32), the branch that "will no longer green" evokes the cessation of growth, the end of vigor and fertility of life.
3. By extension, the branch becomes an image of the prosperity and strength of a people or nation. In Isaiah (9:13 and 19:15), the "palm branch" and the reed together represent the powerful and the weak of Egypt or Israel.
4. Finally, it is what can be cut off: when the Lord "will uproot" the palm branch, He removes the very symbol of life and prosperity, signifying destruction and humiliation.
H3712.origine: The Hebrew word kippah comes from a root meaning to bend or fold, which evokes the arched shape of the palm fronds. The palm tree itself (tamar) is the characteristic tree of the arid regions of the Near East, a symbol of life in the desert. Palm branches had great cultic and symbolic importance: they were used in religious festivals and marked victories.
H3712.emploi: The word appears three times in the provided biblical usages, always to speak of a prosperity that can be taken away or a power that can be broken. In Job, it refers to the personal withering of a tree that ceases to grow. In Isaiah, it concerns the political powers (Egypt, Israel) whose strength God can crush, represented metaphorically by the palm tree. The context is always one of judgment or decline. The image of the green branch that darkens or is uprooted underscores the fragility of what seems most robust.
H3712.portee: This word reminds the believer that earthly prosperity, even that which seems firmly rooted, remains fragile before the hand of God. It is an invitation not to trust in one's own strength or wealth, but to seek solidity in God's promise. For those going through trial or judgment, the image of the uprooted branch speaks of possible restoration: after the fall, God can make what has been cut off flourish again.

sens: Shallow container, usually made of precious metal, intended to hold liquids or offerings
Cultic vessel or valuable object
H3713A.detail:
1. A cup is a shallow container, distinct from a jar or deeper vase, often shaped from precious metal like gold or silver. It can be used for drinking or presenting offerings at the temple. In 1 Chronicles 28:17, King David receives the model for pure gold and silver cups intended for worship, marking their ceremonial importance.
2. More broadly, a cup refers to a valuable utensil, a treasured object of the temple. In Ezra 1:10 and 8:27, the gold and silver cups are listed among the treasures of the temple in Jerusalem, restored after the exile, highlighting their status as sacred and precious objects.
H3713A.origine: The Hebrew word כְּפוֹר (képhôr) etymologically designates a container of a particular shape, probably related to the image of a cup or shallow vase. It is primarily used for cultic utensils in the temple, notably cups intended for offerings or libations. The word reflects the importance given to material objects of worship in the Israelite tradition.
H3713A.emploi: The word כְּפוֹר appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the context of the temple and worship. In 1 Chronicles 28:17, David establishes the plans for the cups that will adorn the temple, showing that these objects are an integral part of the liturgical service. In Ezra 1:10 and 8:27, during the return from exile, the gold and silver cups are enumerated as major elements of the restored temple treasure. In each usage, the word retains its concrete and cultic meaning, never becoming purely symbolic.
H3713A.portee: The cup reminds the believer that true worship is also expressed through concrete actions and material objects offered to God. These precious cups of the temple symbolize voluntary offering, the concern for beauty in divine service, and the trust that God deserves the best. Their enumeration in Ezra also underscores the faithful restoration of worship after the exile, an image of spiritual renewal.

sens: Fine layer of ice crystals that forms on surfaces exposed to cold air at night
Meteorological phenomenon associated with extreme cold and winter
Biblical image of divine providence and God's creative power
H3713B.detail:
1. White frost is the delicate deposit of ice crystals that appears on the ground and objects when intense cold reigns at night. In the Sinai desert, this fine substance covers the ground like fine grain, so delicate that it disappears at sunrise (Exodus 16:14). This is exactly what happened with the manna: each morning, the people found this white frost, food sent by God.
2. Frost is the poetic term for this icy phenomenon from the sky — the extreme cold that produces these crystals. Job 38:29 mentions it as one of the wonders that only God can accomplish, a power that escapes all human control.
3. In both cases, white frost becomes a biblical image of providence: God who feeds His people (the manna), God who masters the natural elements, God whose power extends to the most subtle phenomena of creation (Psalms 147:16 compares it to wool and ash).
H3713B.origine: The Hebrew word כְּפוֹר comes from a root that evokes the action of forming, of crystallizing. Its basic image is that of crystals formed by intense cold. It is a specific and poetic word that appears infrequently in the Bible, reserved for moments when the Word celebrates the marvelous works of nature — often as a sign of the divine power and wisdom inscribed in creation.
H3713B.emploi: The word כְּפוֹר appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, in very particular contexts. Once, it directly designates the white frost of the morning in the Sinai desert — the natural phenomenon by which God manifested His providence by feeding His people with manna (Exodus 16:14). Twice, it appears in poetic passages where it is called "frost": in God's discourse to Job (38:29), where God claims the ability to "bring forth the frost of the sky," and in the psalm of praise (147:16), where the psalmist celebrates God who "spreads white frost like ash." The word retains everywhere this concrete sense of a manifestation of divine power over nature.
H3713B.portee: This simple word invites the believer to recognize God in minor natural phenomena — not just in great miracles. The white frost of each morning becomes a sign of His constant providence toward His people. Meditating on this word is to learn to see God's hand everywhere, even in the delicate and often unnoticed beauty of creation.

sens: Main structural piece of a building
Structural element that ties and supports a construction
H3714.detail:
1. The word refers to an important piece of wood in the construction of a building, one that ties together the elements of a structure and keeps it standing. It is the wood that forms the main framework, also called a beam or a main piece. In Habakkuk 2:11, God says that if the injustices committed in the construction of a city are blatant, the stones and the wood of its framework will cry out — even the building materials protest against sin.
2. The word can also refer more broadly to the assembly of beams and wood that form the skeleton of a building, ensuring its solidity. Habakkuk speaks of the wood that "ties" the framework, suggesting that it is what holds everything together and gives the edifice its structural integrity.
H3714.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to bind" or "to attach," which reflects its function: it is the wood that binds and holds together the parts of a construction. The root evokes the idea of cohesion and solidarity among the elements. It is a rare word in the Bible, used only once, which makes its exact meaning somewhat uncertain, but the context of building and construction makes it clear.
H3714.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Habakkuk 2:11. It is found in a prophetic oracle where the prophet denounces dishonesty and injustice: a city or house built by sin is destined to cry out against those who built it. The framework and the stones become silent witnesses to the crime. It is a technical and concrete word, used to evoke the very structure of the building as silent and undeniable evidence of the evil committed.
H3714.portee: This passage shows that even inanimate things — stone, wood — bear the weight of sin and crime; creation itself rises as a witness against injustice. It reminds us that iniquity cannot remain hidden: it leaves traces in everything it touches, visible to God and, in the prophet's vision, even inscribed in matter. It is an invitation to righteousness in our actions, for everything we do has consequences inscribed in the world.

sens: A young lion, weaker and less experienced than the adult
A lion in general, regardless of age (broad usage)
Strength and power, especially that of a leader or ruler
Cruelty, threatening violence
Pride and boldness
H3715A.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a young or juvenile lion, not yet fully mature. Samson encounters a "roaring cub" charging at him in the vineyards of Timnah (Judges 14:5): it is a young animal but already dangerously aggressive.

2. By extension, it is used for "lion" without particular nuance of age. The psalmists speak of the "cubs" of their enemies as a general threat (Psalms 35:17), not always distinguishing between young and adult.

3. In royal and prophetic imagery, the cub symbolizes sovereign power: the king inspires a terror similar to the roar of the lion (Proverbs 20:2), and God presents Himself as a cub that tears apart His enemies (Hosea 5:14).

4. The word also carries the idea of ferocity and rapacity: the cubs ravage the land and devastate cities mercilessly (Jeremiah 2:15).

5. In prophetic visions (notably in Ezekiel), the cub represents the pride, arrogance, and boldness of an earthly power that believes itself invincible (Ezekiel 19).
H3715A.origine: The Hebrew word כְּפִיר (kephir) comes from the root קפר or an etymon that refers to the idea of youth or smallness ("leaper," from קפז "to leap"). It specifically designates the young lion, one that leaps and jumps vigorously. The family also includes other young or vigorous animals. In ancient Egypt and the Levant, the lion was a prestigious and feared animal, a symbol of royal strength, which explains its frequent use in biblical prophetic and poetic literature.
H3715A.emploi: The word appears 31 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the poetic (Psalms, Proverbs, Job) and prophetic (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea) books. In historical narratives (Judges, 1 Samuel), it refers to a real animal encountered: the cub of Samson (Judges 14:5) is a concrete creature that attacks him. In poetry and prophecy, the image becomes metaphorical: the psalmists compare the wicked to cubs that threaten them (Psalms 35:17), the prophets describe kings and empires as greedy cubs (Ezekiel 19), and God Himself is portrayed as a cub to express His terrible judgment (Hosea 5:14). The meaning fluctuates between the real animal and its use as a symbol of power, danger, or divine majesty.
H3715A.portee: The cub reminds the biblical reader that power and aggression do not always triumph: Samson defeats the cub that attacks him, showing that the animal's strength matters less than the strength given by God. When the prophets compare empires and kings to cubs, they warn that these powers can be fierce, but they ultimately remain under God's control, who can break them like one breaks prey. For the Christian, it is an invitation not to fear hostile forces, however formidable they may be.

sens: small cluster of houses, less significant than a town
H3715B.detail: 1. A village is a small grouping of rural dwellings, less fortified and less populated than a town. Here, it refers to the villages located in the valley of Ono, where Sanballat and Geshem propose a meeting to Nehemiah (Nehemiah 6:2).
H3715B.origine: The Hebrew word כְּפִירִים (kephirim) is the plural of כְּפִיר, which comes from the root meaning "village" or "small rural locality." In biblical Hebrew, this word distinguishes small habitats (villages) from large fortified cities (עִיר, ir). The context of Nehemiah evokes these small centers in the region of Ono, in the coastal valley near Jerusalem.
H3715B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible in this form: in Nehemiah 6:2. It designates the villages in the valley of Ono where Nehemiah's adversaries attempt to lure him to trap him. This context shows how Sanballat and Geshem, governors of neighboring regions, propose an apparently innocuous meeting in small localities, far from the vigilance of Jerusalem, to better implement their hostile plan.
H3715B.portee: This word reminds us that the threat against God's plans can come from proposals that seem ordinary and from places that appear safe. Nehemiah discerns the trap beneath this banal invitation to a village: this encourages the believer to remain vigilant and not to be led away from his mission by deceptive suggestions.

sens: City of Canaan, formerly of the Gibeonites
Assigned to the tribe of Benjamin during the division of the land
Place of residence for the Israelites after the exile
H3716.detail:
1. Kephira was a Canaanite city that belonged to the group of Gibeonites. Its name means "lioness" in Hebrew, which may evoke the strength or pride of the place. It appears at the conclusion of the covenant with the Gibeonites (Joshua 9:17), listed among the four main Gibeonite cities.
2. During the division of the Promised Land, Kephira was assigned to the tribe of Benjamin as a Levitical city (Joshua 18:26). It thus became part of the territory of Benjamin and served as an administrative or religious center.
3. After the Babylonian exile, descendants of the inhabitants of Kephira returned to settle in the city (Ezra 2:25 and Nehemiah 7:29). These passages show the continuity of the Israelite presence in the same place, where 743 people are counted upon returning from exile.
H3716.origine: The Hebrew name כְּפִירָה (Kephira) comes from the root meaning "lioness." In Hebrew, כְּפִיר refers to a young lion or lion in general, and the feminine form Kephira may evoke a lioness or, more figuratively, a strong and imposing place. This type of geographical name, borrowed from the animal kingdom, was common in Canaan to designate places of refuge or strength.
H3716.emploi: Kephira is mentioned four times in the Bible, always as a defined and identifiable place. It first appears during the truce concluded between Israel and the Gibeonites (Joshua 9:17), where it is named among the four cities of the Gibeonite territory. Then, in the details of the territorial division (Joshua 18:26), it is attached to Benjamin. Finally, it reappears in the lists of return from exile (Ezra 2:25 and Nehemiah 7:29), where the number of its returned inhabitants is specified. This consistency of the name suggests a stability of the locality and its administrative importance.

sens: Fold a fabric or cloth upon itself to make it thicker or more durable
Multiply by two, repeat an action twice
Strike with repeated blows
H3717.detail:
1. Fold a fabric or cloth upon itself to make it thicker or more durable — this is the idea of folding something in two. In the tabernacle, the sixth curtain was folded at the front of the tent (Exodus 26:9), or the breastplate of the high priest was made in two layers for added strength (Exodus 28:16, Exodus 39:9).
2. Multiply by two, repeat an action twice — this gives new strength through repetition. When one "doubles" a rug, one increases its thickness; when one "doubles" sword strikes, one strikes with more intensity and frequency (Ezekiel 21:19).
3. Strike with repeated blows — this is the consequence of doubling an action: doubled and tripled sword strikes signify a rapid and overwhelming succession of wounds.
H3717.origine: The Hebrew verb כָּפַל comes from a root that evokes the idea of folding, doubling, putting in two. It is related to significant words "double," "twice," "duality." The starting image is very concrete: that of two superimposed layers, of something folded in two to become stronger or more visible.
H3717.emploi: This verb appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, all in the context of the construction of the tabernacle and worship. The first three uses (Exodus 26:9 and Exodus 28:16, 39:9) describe the work of the weavers: doubling the curtains and the breastplate to increase their strength and value. The last use (Ezekiel 21:19) employs the word in a more metaphorical way: the blows of the sword are "doubled," which emphasizes not the physical structure of an object, but the intensity and repetition of a destructive action.
H3717.portee: This word reminds us that in the worship of the tabernacle, every detail was carefully considered: doubling the fabrics made them stronger and more worthy of the holy place. For the believer, this evokes the importance of solidity and quality in serving God. The doubling in Ezekiel also emphasizes that divine justice is not hesitant: it strikes with force and determination.

sens: What is repeated twice, what counts for two
The intensity, the multiplied extent
What penetrates deeply, that sinks in
H3718.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is that of double, of what is repeated or multiplied by two: Jerusalem received from the hand of the Lord "double for all her sins" (Isaiah 40:2), meaning a double measure, a proportion that counts for two times the fault.
2. The word extends to the idea of extent and intensity: God's wisdom is described as "immense" (literally "double"), as it surpasses all that can be conceived (Job 11:6). This is a way of saying that something is considerable, doubled in strength or extent.
3. In a different context, the word can evoke the action of penetrating or sinking deeply: "Who can penetrate between its jaws?" (Job 41:4) uses this image of something going double, sinking further in.
H3718.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to fold" or "to double." The basic image is that of two layers, of what is folded upon itself or multiplied. This root appears in other forms of Hebrew to express everything related to duplication or intensification.
H3718.emploi: This word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. It first denotes a double quantity (Isaiah 40:2, where Jerusalem receives a double compensation), then it takes on a sense of extent and greatness that exceeds any ordinary measure (Job 11:6, where divine wisdom is limitless). Its use in Job 41:4 shows a possible nuance toward the idea of penetration or depth. The context of each passage influences the translation: depending on whether one emphasizes multiplication, excess, or depth, one can translate as "double," "immense," or "penetrate."
H3718.portee: This word reminds us that God often acts with a generosity or power that exceeds simple equity: He gives a double, He possesses immense wisdom. For the believer, this invites reflection on the excess of divine grace and not to reduce God to the limits of our ordinary categories.

sens: Intense and passionate desire
Ardent thirst for something
Tendency to eagerly turn towards something
H3719.detail:
1. The word expresses an intense and passionate desire, like a burning hunger — not just the lack of food, but a yearning for something with an almost irresistible force. In Ezekiel 17:7, the vine "eagerly spread its roots": it turns towards the eagle with a kind of thirst, as if it ardently seeks to be watered.
2. It is a movement of the heart or the whole being towards what one covets. The vine "directed its branches towards him": this is not a passive gesture, but a surge, an extension of oneself to reach the object of desire.
3. The image also suggests a natural tendency to lean towards what attracts us, like a thirsty creature turning towards its source of water. The word paints a state where one cannot help but seek what one is hungry for.
H3719.origine: The Hebrew verb קָפַן (kâphan) originates from a root expressing hunger and intense desire. In its simplest form, it describes the physical need for food, but it quickly enriches itself with a moral and passionate nuance: it is the greed of the heart that ardently desires, the covetousness that drives one to act. The word belongs to the family of biblical terms describing inner impulses.
H3719.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 17:7. The context is a political allegory: a planted vine (the kingdom of Judah) eagerly turns towards a second eagle (the king of Egypt), in the absence of the first eagle (the king of Babylon). The word here has a tone of reproach: the vine blindly throws itself, with all its heart, towards what seems to offer the help it desires, but which turns out to be a temptation or a political error. Greed is presented as a passion that blinds and misleads.
H3719.portee: This word reminds us that greed, intense and uncontrolled desire, is a dangerous spiritual force. It pushes us to turn towards false sources of life and satisfaction, instead of clinging to God alone. In Ezekiel, the vine misled by its greed becomes the image of Israel forgetting its true Lord to court the powers of the world — a timeless warning against covetousness that diverts from true good.

sens: Lack of food, state of one who needs to eat
Physical suffering caused by prolonged absence of food
Extreme distress due to deprivation
Calamity, disaster striking a region or people
H3720.detail:
1. Hunger is primarily the concrete lack of food: the body demands to eat. In Job 30:3, miserable and hungry men are forced to flee to barren and desolate lands to survive, an expression of destitution itself.
2. It also denotes the intense suffering caused by this deprivation — not only discomfort, but the pain of hunger that torments the body and mind. The Hebrew word carried the image of this piercing pain.
3. More broadly, hunger represents a calamity, a plague that can strike an entire region and threaten the life of the people. In Job 5:22, the context mentions hunger among other disasters (devastation, wild beasts) that the righteous should not fear.
4. Metaphorically, hunger illustrates any form of extreme distress and abandonment in the face of forces that escape control.
H3720.origine: The Hebrew word כָּפָן (kaphan) expresses the idea of hunger and deprivation. It belongs to a family of Semitic roots that evoke weakness, exhaustion, and lack. The notion of hunger is not limited to simple appetite: it includes suffering and the weakening of the body and soul in the absence of what nourishes and sustains.
H3720.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in Job. In Job 5:22, it is part of a promise that those who fear God will not fear devastation or famine — an assurance of divine protection in the face of great misfortunes. In Job 30:3, it describes the pitiful condition of men reduced to misery and hunger, forced to seek refuge in the desert. These uses show that hunger is viewed as a serious plague, a calamity capable of reducing human beings to extreme distress.
H3720.portee: Hunger reminds the reader that material security is never guaranteed and often depends on a protection that surpasses us. For those who suffer, it invites them to cry out to God; for those who enjoy abundance, it is a call to compassion towards the poor and hungry. It makes us aware of our dependence and the human misery in the absence of grace.

sens: To bend the body forward, lower the head or torso
To be in a bent posture, stooped
To humble oneself, submit respectfully before God
H3721.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to physically bend one's body or a part of it downwards. It is the action of leaning or lowering: when the psalmist's soul "bent" (Psalms 57:7), he expresses an attitude of lowering, like someone collapsing under a weight of distress.
2. The word also describes a prolonged state: to be bent, to remain stooped. The Lord "upholds all who are bent" (Psalms 145:14 and 146:8): these are people whom misfortune or age has caused to bend, and God raises them up. The image is of a person whose back has become hunched, who can no longer stand upright.
3. Finally, the verb takes on a spiritual meaning: to bend before God is to humble oneself, to recognize one's smallness. When one asks, "With what shall I come before the Lord, and bow myself before the Most High God?" (Micah 6:6), to bend means to adopt a posture of submission and reverence.
H3721.origine: The Hebrew verb כפף comes from a root that evokes the movement of bending, of flexing. The family of the word includes derivatives that all retain this idea of flexion. The starting image is physical: the body that bends, like a branch that is curved. This notion of flexion naturally extends to the attitude of the soul or spirit that submits.
H3721.emploi: The verb appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Psalms and the prophets. It is first used to describe a physical or moral distress (the soul that bends), and then to evoke the protective action of God who upholds those who are bent. The sense of humiliation before God in worship appears in the prophet Micah. The word remains always concrete: it paints a bodily image, even when it speaks of the soul or spirit.
H3721.portee: This word reminds the reader that the posture of the body expresses the state of the heart. To bend before God is to acknowledge that He is the sole Master and that we are fragile. But the Bible assures that God upholds those who are bent: it is a promise of restoration and regained dignity for those who humble themselves before Him.

sens: Covering, erasing a sin or a defilement through a ritual act
Performing a sacrifice or rite to obtain forgiveness
Appeasing someone, reconciling them with oneself
Purifying a person or place from what ritually defiles them
H3722A.detail:
1. To make atonement primarily means "to cover" in the literal sense: in the Israelite ritual, the priest performs specific actions (laying on of hands, pouring out blood) that "cover" the sin of the one who committed it, as if to hide it, erase it before God. Leviticus constantly returns to this idea: "the priest shall make atonement for him" (Leviticus 5:16), meaning he will perform the act that reconciles the sinner with God.
2. This verb also refers to the act of sacrifice itself, the complete rite that purifies. When the Bible says one "makes atonement" (Numbers 25:13), it speaks of everything that unfolds around the sacrifice: the choice of the victim, the offering, the priest's intercession. It is an official act, performed before the Lord.
3. To make atonement can also mean "to appease" an offended person: Jacob promises Esau: "I will appease him with this present that goes before me" (Genesis 32:20). Here, the idea is to calm anger, to restore peace through an offering or a gesture of reconciliation.
4. The word also encompasses ritual purification after a legal defilement (illness, contact with a corpse, etc.). The priest "makes atonement" not for a moral sin, but to restore cultic purity, allowing the person to reintegrate into the community.
H3722A.origine: The Hebrew verb כִּפֶּר comes from a root that evokes the idea of "covering" or "overlaying." The image is that of a covering that hides, that masks. The word is closely related to the noun כִּפּוּר (Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement), which marks the great moment of the Israelite religious calendar. In the Septuagint (the Old Testament translated into Greek), this verb is rendered by words like "hilaskesthai," which emphasize appeasement and reconciliation with the deity. This root expresses a repeated and regular action: it is the foundational gesture of Israelite worship.
H3722A.emploi: The verb "to make atonement" is one of the most important in Leviticus: it appears more than 93 times in the Old Testament, especially in the books of worship (Leviticus, Numbers, Exodus). It structures the entire sacrificial system: atonement is made for sin (Leviticus 4:20), for guilt (Leviticus 5:16), for purification after a defilement (Leviticus 12:7), and also to consecrate the sanctuary (Exodus 29:36). The great Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur (Leviticus 16:32 and 34), concentrates this rite: the high priest "makes atonement" for all Israel. There is also a relational dimension: in Psalms 78:38, the Lord "forgives" iniquity (the same verb), showing that atonement is never magical, but rests on divine grace. The term unites visible sacrifice and invisible forgiveness.
H3722A.portee: This word reveals that the relationship with God, in the Old Testament, passes through specific acts, rituals that embody repentance and trust. Atonement is not a vague feeling, but a gesture, an offering, a concrete step. For the Christian discovering the Gospel, this word prepares to understand that Jesus himself fulfills what the entire sacrificial system foreshadows: he is the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). The death of Jesus on the cross is the definitive atonement, the total and final covering of sin, making the repetition of sacrifices unnecessary.

sens: Covering a surface with a protective substance, such as pitch
Waterproofing an object by covering it with an adhesive material
H3722B.detail:
1. To coat means to apply a protective layer on something. In the context of Noah's ark, God commands Noah to coat the ark "with pitch inside and out" (Genesis 6:14): it involves covering it with a sticky, waterproof substance to protect it from water. The word evokes the concrete image of spreading, smearing a viscous material over a surface.
2. By extension, to coat can mean to waterproof or insulate by applying a protective layer. This practical act of covering transforms the ark into a watertight vessel capable of floating and preserving life inside during the flood.
H3722B.origine: The Hebrew verb כָּפַר comes from a root that fundamentally means "to cover" or "to overlay." This same root gives rise to the noun copha (pitch or bitumen), the very material in question in the account of the ark. The primary meaning of the word in the Bible focuses on the idea of protecting a surface by covering it with a waterproof substance, from which its religious and metaphorical use is derived.
H3722B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Segond in Genesis 6:14, where God asks Noah to coat the ark with pitch. The context is clearly practical and material: it is a concrete action aimed at making the vessel watertight before the flood. This literal sense, which describes a physical coating, remains the only one attested in the provided usages, without any apparent metaphorical extension.
H3722B.portee: This verse reminds the reader that God gives precise and concrete instructions for survival and deliverance. The act of coating the ark with pitch shows how practical and meticulous obedience to God's commandments becomes the instrument of his protection. For the believer, this detail reveals that God cares for every aspect of our salvation.

sens: small grouping of dwellings, smaller than a city
rural settlement in a given area
H3723G.detail:
1. A village is a small grouping of houses and people, less significant than a fortified city. It is a common administrative and geographical term in Israel to designate rural localities and hamlets. In Joshua 18:24, the village of Chephar is listed among the cities and villages assigned to the tribe of Benjamin: it is an ordinary territorial possession of God's people.
2. The term also refers to a set of dwellings established within a defined space of a region, with its inhabitants and boundaries, distinct from a large city.
H3723G.origine: The Hebrew word כָּפָר (kafar) comes from a root that expresses the idea of covering or surrounding. The village is the place where people gather and "cover" together — it is a closed, known, defined space. This word is very common in the Old Testament to name the small localities of the territory of Israel, in contrast to the large fortified cities (like Jerusalem).
H3723G.emploi: The word כָּפָר appears only once in the provided usages, in Joshua 18:24, where it is included in the list of territories distributed to the tribes after the conquest of Canaan. It simply designates a minor locality, without particular connotation — it is an element of the administrative and geographical division of the land. Elsewhere in the Bible, this word is regularly used to enumerate territorial possessions and distinguish small population centers from large cities.
H3723G.portee: This word reminds us that God divided the promised land not only into prestigious large cities but also into humble villages where ordinary families lived — each place, big or small, had its place in God's plan for his people.

sens: small human settlement, less important than a city
rural community with its houses and inhabitants
simple and pastoral living place
H3723H.detail: 1. The village is a small human settlement, distinct from the fortified city or capital: it is a more modest agglomeration. In 1 Chronicles 27:25, villages are mentioned alongside fields and towers, showing that they form the rural fabric of the kingdom, providing its agricultural and pastoral resources. 2. The village also refers to the community of people living there, characterized by its simple and pastoral nature. In the Song of Solomon 7:12, "to dwell in the villages" evokes peaceful and intimate rural life, away from urban tumult, in proximity to nature and one another.
H3723H.origine: The Hebrew word כָּפָר (kaphar) literally means a small grouping or rural establishment. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of covering or protecting, as if the village were a place where people gather and protect each other. The word is related to כֹּפֶר (kophar), another form also designating the village, and evokes the image of a small, gathered, and sheltered community.
H3723H.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible translated by Segond. In 1 Chronicles 27:25, it describes the administrative organization of David's kingdom: the villages were part of the king's economic system, alongside fields and towers, providing for royal provisions and treasures. In the Song of Solomon 7:12, it takes on a more poetic and intimate hue, evoking peaceful rural life and love away from the city. In both cases, the village is an element of the landscape and daily life in Israel, clearly distinguished from the fortified "cities."
H3723H.portee: The village reminds us that biblical life largely took place in a rural setting, where people lived close to the land and to one another. For the believer, the contrast between the city (place of power and administration) and the village (place of simple living) invites meditation on the value of humble and communal life, and on the beauty of creation in its pastoral setting.

sens: Price demanded to free someone from a critical situation or death
Financial compensation to repair a harm or fault
Sum of money offered to obtain a favor or divert someone from their duty
Substitute, that which replaces someone or takes the place of another
H3724A.detail:
1. The ransom is primarily the price of life: when someone has caused the death of another, a sum can be imposed on them to escape the avenger of blood (Exodus 21:30), but never to redeem the life of a murderer who deserves death (Numbers 35:31).
2. It can also be compensation for damage: one who damages another's property must pay compensation to repair the harm done.
3. The word also designates a bribe or present slipped to someone to make them turn a blind eye or abandon their principles (1 Samuel 12:3): Samuel refuses this ransom of corruption.
4. Figuratively, the ransom becomes what replaces someone: the wicked serves as a ransom for the just, meaning they substitute for them in punishment (Proverbs 21:18).
H3724A.origine: The Hebrew word כֹּפֶר (kopher) comes from a root meaning to cover or erase. Originally, the ransom covers the crime, erasing guilt by compensating it with money. It is a price that "covers" the offense and restores balance. The same word is also used for tar or pitch, which covers and protects surfaces.
H3724A.emploi: This word appears thirteen times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of law and wisdom. It first appears in legal prescriptions (Exodus, Numbers) to address cases of accidental death and murder: the law clearly distinguishes between one who can be compensated and one who cannot be redeemed (Numbers 35:31-32). In Proverbs, it takes on a broader meaning: the ransom represents what is offered to corrupt someone (1 Samuel 12:3, Amos 5:12), or what replaces a man in punishment (Proverbs 21:18). Job uses it in a context of divine wisdom: there is a ransom that God accepts to save the just.
H3724A.portee: This word opens to the reader the entire biblical logic of redemption and substitution: something or someone can take the place of another, paying the price in their stead. It is a strong image of what the New Testament calls redemption in Jesus Christ: He alone is the definitive ransom, the ultimate price paid to free humanity from sin and death. Understanding this word helps to grasp how the Bible envisions salvation: not as a free and magical outpouring of grace, but as a price truly paid, a substitution truly accepted.

sens: black, sticky substance obtained from the distillation of tar
waterproof material used to coat and protect a surface
H3724B.detail:
1. Pitch is a black, thick, and sticky substance obtained by cooking or distilling tar. It is a natural product known since antiquity. It has remarkable viscosity and remains sticky when heated.
2. Its main use is to seal, waterproof, and protect porous surfaces. Noah must coat the ark with pitch "inside and out" to make it waterproof and thus preserve the wood from rot (Genesis 6:14). Pitch perfectly fulfills this function: it creates a protective barrier between the wood and moisture.
H3724B.origine: The Hebrew word kopher designates a substance based on tar or bitumen. The same word is also used to speak of "ransom" or "expiation" (kaphor, a derived form), as at its core it conveys the idea of covering, of recapping. This common root emphasizes that pitch "covers" the wood just as an expiation "covers" sin — the image is of something that covers to protect.
H3724B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 6:14, during the construction of Noah's ark. God commands Noah to coat the ark with pitch to make it watertight. This is a purely practical and technical use: the aim is to protect the wood from water. This concrete vocabulary underscores the material reality of the Flood narrative and Noah's faithfulness to the detailed divine instructions.
H3724B.portee: The mention of pitch reminds us that the salvation of Noah and his family also depended on concrete material means: a solid construction, appropriate materials, faithful execution of God's plans. It speaks to us of foresight and practical obedience, not only in faith but in action.

sens: Shrub or small plant that produces fragrant flowers
Valuable plant used in perfumery and cosmetics
H3724C.detail:
1. The privet is a shrub or small plant cultivated for its very fragrant white flowers. It is a valuable plant, appreciated for its pleasant aroma. In the Song of Songs, the lover compares his beloved to a "cluster of privet" (Song of Songs 1:14), evoking beauty and delicate fragrance.
2. This plant was also used in cosmetics and perfumery in antiquity. It is among the most precious essences of the garden of love described in Song of Songs 4:13, alongside pomegranates and spikenard, indicating that it was highly valued for its fragrant and ornamental qualities.
H3724C.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of covering or transforming: the privet was reputed for its coloring properties and its use in care. Plants of the same lexical family exist in Arabic with the meaning of "henna." This name specifically designates a Mediterranean plant with very fragrant white flowers, prized in ancient Middle Eastern cultures.
H3724C.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the Song of Songs, the Psalmist's love poem. In chapter 1, verse 14, the beloved compares his friend to a cluster of privet from the vineyards of En-Gedi, a region famous for its gardens. In chapter 4, verse 13, he lists the precious plants of the garden, including privet among the most excellent fruits and fragrances. These two occurrences show that privet symbolizes beauty, aroma, and value in the poetic context of love.
H3724C.portee: For the reader of the Song of Songs, privet evokes natural beauty, fragrance, and purity that characterize human love according to the Bible. This fragrant shrub reminds us that the senses — smell, sight — are gifts from God that enrich our experience of life and love. The choice of this specific plant, among all those available in the Holy Land, emphasizes that the beauty and fragrance of the one we love are authentic and natural.

sens: Small rural settlement, without walls or fortifications
Locality dependent on a larger city
H3724D.detail: 1. The word designates a small rural settlement, without fortifications or walls — unlike the fortified cities of the Philistines. In 1 Samuel 6:18, "fortified cities" are explicitly contrasted with "villages without walls": villages are inhabited places but open, less significant than cities. 2. These villages often form an administrative or territorial unit linked to a main city. They depend on or revolve around it, forming a sort of district with it.
H3724D.origine: The Hebrew word כֹּפֶר (kopher) is a spelling variant of כָּפָר (kaphar, H3723). It comes from a root that evokes the idea of "covering" or "surrounding," which fits well with a village as a grouping of closely-knit houses. It is a common word in the Old Testament to designate rural life.
H3724D.emploi: The word appears once in the Bible in 1 Samuel 6:18, in the account of the return of the Ark of the Covenant among the Philistines. In this context, it refers to the small villages of the Philistine territory. The passage clearly contrasts villages and fortified cities, showing that villages are more modest and vulnerable habitats. This word reflects the geographical and administrative organization of the biblical world: fortified cities dominate, while villages complement them.
H3724D.portee: This word reminds us of the concrete life of the biblical world: the majority of people lived in villages, not in large cities. Understanding this reality helps to better visualize how biblical narratives unfold in real places familiar to the first readers.

sens: Act of repairing a fault, reconciling with God through a sacrifice
Victim sacrificed to obtain forgiveness
Action of redeeming or averting divine wrath
H3725.detail:
1. Expiation is primarily the ritual act by which one repairs an offense against God. It is a gesture of reconciliation: when the people of Israel have committed a fault, a sacrifice is offered to restore peace with the Lord. The high priest Aaron, for example, makes "expiations on the horns of the altar" once a year with the blood of the victim, to cleanse the sanctuary of all impurity (Exodus 30:10).

2. Expiation can also refer to the animal or offering itself that serves to repair the wrong. It is the thing offered, not just the action: "You shall offer a bull daily as a sin offering for expiation" (Exodus 29:36).
