3. By extension, the word can mean redemption or ransom: the money paid to redeem oneself from a fault or to substitute for a penalty. When the Israelites give "the money of redemption," they pay for their souls to be covered, protected (Exodus 30:16).
H3725.origine: The Hebrew word כִּפֻּרִים (kippourim) comes from the root כפר (kafar), which literally means "to cover" or "to erase." The initial image is that of a covering that hides, that covers the fault or wrong. In biblical Hebrew, this root is also used for "bitumen" which waterproofs and protects. Expiation is thus the act of covering, putting a veil over sin so that God no longer sees it, or diverting it, erasing it. The same root produces related words: כפר (kofer), the price of redemption, and כהן (kohen), the priest, the one who performs this act of covering.
H3725.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the context of Levitical worship and expiation rituals. The most solemn day is the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), the tenth day of the seventh month, when "expiation is made for you before the Lord" (Leviticus 23:27-28). On that day, no work is to be done, as the act is grave and sacred. Expiation concerns both the sanctuary and the people: the altar is purified with the blood of a victim (Exodus 30:10), a personal ransom is paid for "the redemption of your persons" (Exodus 30:16). The meaning of the word oscillates between the rite of expiation (the collective act), the expiatory victim (the object), and the price or ransom (the material equivalent). Each use reinforces the idea that the fault can be erased, covered, or diverted by an external means — animal, sacrifice, or payment — rather than by mere repentance.
H3725.portee: For the Christian, this word illuminates the essence of Christ's sacrifice. Jesus is presented in the New Testament as the ultimate "expiation" for all sins, the Lamb who, once for all, "covers" and diverts God's wrath. Understanding its Hebrew meaning helps to grasp that the Gospel does not eliminate expiation; it fulfills it: instead of a thousand victims, one definitive sacrifice. The Day of Atonement, this moment of sacred terror, takes on its full meaning when viewed as a shadow of the cross.

sens: village of the tribe of Benjamin
locality mentioned in the division of the promised lands
H3726.detail: 1. Képhar-Ammonaï is a small village located in the territory of Benjamin, whose name means "village of the Ammonites." It is one of the twelve cities listed during the division of the territory of Benjamin among the tribes of Israel (Joshua 18:24).
H3726.origine: The name is composed of two elements: "Képhar" (כָּפָר), which means "village" or "hamlet" in Hebrew, and "Ammonites," referring to a group or population. This geographical name follows the common pattern of Palestinian localities that bore the name of their inhabitants or the peoples who inhabited them before the conquest.
H3726.emploi: Képhar-Ammonaï appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 18:24, during the description of the territory assigned to the tribe of Benjamin after the conquest of Canaan. It is listed among twelve cities with their villages, indicating that it was a modest but significant establishment in the administrative organization of the tribe.

sens: the solid gold lid of the ark of the covenant
the place where God forgives the sins of His people
the throne of God above the earth
the symbol of forgiveness and reconciliation between God and man
H3727.detail:
1. The mercy seat is the pure gold lid placed on the ark of the covenant at the heart of the temple: a rectangular plate measuring two and a half cubits long by one and a half cubits wide, on which rested two golden cherubim with wings outstretched toward each other (Exodus 25:17-20).
2. It is the place where the high priest sprinkled the blood once a year, on the Day of Atonement, to obtain forgiveness for the sins of Israel: on this lid, he sprinkled the blood of the sacrifice seven times to reconcile God with His people (Leviticus 16:14-15).
3. It is from there that God spoke to His people: between the two cherubim, above the mercy seat, the divine presence was manifested (Numbers 7:89).
4. The mercy seat represents the forgiveness offered by God — not a judgment, but a covering of mercy over the sins of the people.
H3727.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root "kafar" which means "to cover" or "to atone." The mercy seat is therefore what "covers" sins, what "makes atonement": it embodies the idea that God "covers" the guilt of His people rather than punishing it. The two cherubim that adorn its top symbolize the royal and holy presence of God above the people.
H3727.emploi: The word appears 22 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the books of the Pentateuch and the ancient history of Israel. It is first encountered in the instructions for making the ark (Exodus 25, 35, 37), then in the accounts of its inauguration and installation (Exodus 40, Leviticus 16). Its main role is to mark the place of forgiveness: on the Day of Atonement, the mercy seat is the focal point of the reconciliation rite (Leviticus 16). God speaks to Moses there (Numbers 7:89). The word fades after the period of the monarchy, as the mercy seat loses its importance when the Temple is destroyed and Israel loses the instituted worship.
H3727.portee: The mercy seat teaches believers that divine forgiveness is not a distant or abstract act: it has a concrete place, a price paid (the blood), and a face-to-face encounter between God and man. For the Christian, this image of the atonement cover illuminates the meaning of the cross: Jesus Christ, through His sacrifice, becomes the ultimate mercy seat, the eternal place where God meets the sinful man and forgives. It is a reminder that divine mercy has solidity, a visible form, and is offered freely to those who seek it.

sens: to crush or trample underfoot
to bend or bow down
to completely cover with fine dust
H3728.detail: 1. The word primarily evokes the action of crushing or trampling something underfoot, as one crushes ashes or dust while walking: it is an image of brute and degrading domination. 2. It also means to bend, to bow something or someone down under a weight or violence — the image is one of pressure that crushes dignity. 3. Figuratively, in Lamentations 3:16, "to cover with ashes" expresses complete humiliation: the prophet, after having his teeth broken, finds himself entirely covered with gray dust, which dehumanizes him and makes him unrecognizable, a symbol of extreme mourning and dishonor.
H3728.origine: The Hebrew verb קָפַשׁ (kaphash) fundamentally expresses the action of pressing, bending, or bowing. Its root suggests an action of compression or crushing. The meaning of "to cover" naturally follows: what is crushed turns into powder that covers everything. In biblical Hebrew, it is a dark image associated with humiliation and mourning.
H3728.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Lamentations 3:16. In this passage from the cry of pain of the prophet Jeremiah over the destruction of Jerusalem, the verb in the Hiphil form ("to make cover") reinforces the idea that God has reduced the dignity of the people to nothing: not only are their teeth broken (total destruction), but they are also covered with ashes (complete abjection). It is a language of extreme distress and humiliation.
H3728.portee: This word reminds the reader how Scripture expresses the depths of mourning and suffering. The image of ashes covering everything serves to show not only physical pain but also inner annihilation, the experience of being reduced to nothing. For the believer going through distress, this validates the intensity of their cry: the Bible itself uses such raw and desperate language.

sens: to tie someone with ropes or chains
to immobilize someone to render them defenseless
H3729.detail:
1. To tie someone with ropes or chains: this is the most concrete and frequent meaning in the provided usages. In Daniel 3:20-24, King Nebuchadnezzar orders his soldiers to "bind" Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego with ropes before throwing them into the fiery furnace. The text even specifies that they are bound with their clothes, which shows that the bindings completely encircle them.
2. To immobilize someone to render them defenseless: the verb "to bind" not only describes a physical action but also the intention that guides it. To bind someone is to deprive them of their freedom of movement, to put them in a position where they cannot flee or defend themselves. This is why the king can throw the three men "bound" into the fire without fear that they will escape.
H3729.origine: The Hebrew verb כָּפַת (kapat) comes from a root that evokes the idea of tightening or compressing. In biblical Aramaic (Daniel is written in Aramaic), the word כְּפַת (ke.phat) retains this sense of encirclement and immobilization. The family of this verb includes other forms that reinforce the idea of constraint and limitation of freedom.
H3729.emploi: The verb "to bind" appears four times in the book of Daniel, all in the account of the three young men in Daniel 3:20-24. This account tells how King Nebuchadnezzar, angered by Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego's refusal to bow down before a golden statue, orders them to be bound and thrown into a fiery furnace. The text's insistence that they are "bound" (repeated four times in four verses) emphasizes their apparent vulnerability before the king's power. Yet, the miracle that follows shows that these bindings cannot prevent God from protecting them.
H3729.portee: This word teaches us something profound about freedom and the power of God. Even when bound, defenseless, thrown into the flames, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego do not fear: for no human binding can hinder the hand of God. For the Christian reader, this account serves as a reminder that the most oppressive circumstances are never stronger than the faithfulness of the Lord toward those who seek Him.

sens: Ornament in the shape of a bulb or rounded swelling that adorns an object
Capital or architectural crown at the top of a column
H3730.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a decoration in the shape of a ball or swelling, like a small carved apple. On the sanctuary lampstand described in Exodus 25:31-36, the "apples" are rounded ornaments placed at the base of certain branches, between the flowers and almond-shaped cups. These ornamental elements, made from a single piece with the lampstand, give a delicate and finished shape to the object.
2. The word is also used to designate the capital, that is, the architectural part that crowns the top of a column or vertical structure. In Amos 9:1, the prophet speaks of the "capitals" of the altars, the upper part on which the rest of the structure rests. This capital is struck, leading to the collapse of the entire construction.
H3730.origine: The Hebrew word kaph.tor likely comes from a root that evokes swelling or protrusion. Its basic image is that of a rounded, bulging shape, like an apple. The word may also have referred to a button or a nail in architectural constructions. In the Septuagint (Greek translation), it corresponds to Greek words describing ornaments and crowning structures.
H3730.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the Bible, primarily in Exodus 25 and 37 to describe the ornaments of the seven-branched lampstand constructed according to divine instructions. These references precisely enumerate the arrangement of ornamental apples along the stem and branches. It also appears in Amos 9:1 to describe the capital of the idolatrous altars that the Lord commands to be destroyed, and in Zephaniah 2:14 in a context of desolation. The word thus oscillates between two uses: the light and beautiful ornament of legitimate worship, and the structure that must be overturned when it serves a corrupted religion.
H3730.portee: This word invites us to notice that God, in giving instructions for the sanctuary, pays attention to the details and beauty of what glorifies Him. The ornamental apples of the lampstand are not superfluous: they are part of the harmonious whole that God demands. Conversely, the overturning of the capitals of the altars in Amos shows that this beauty does not save an idolatrous worship from divine condemnation. The Bible thus teaches that the beauty of our offerings pleases God, but it must reside in an obedient heart and life.

sens: Island or coastal region, original home of the Philistines
Territory from which the Philistines migrated to Canaan
H3731.detail:
1. Caphtor is the name of an island or coastal region, probably located in Crete or Asia Minor, which is presented in the Bible as the original home of the Philistines before their settlement in Canaan. Amos 9:7 establishes a parallel: just as God brought Israel out of Egypt, He brought the Philistines out of Caphtor, showing that this people, like Israel, experienced a divine migration.
2. Caphtor also designates the starting point of the Philistine migration. In Deuteronomy 2:23, the Caphtorim (inhabitants of Caphtor) come out of this island to settle in Gaza, replacing the Avvites. Jeremiah 47:4 speaks of the "remnants of the island of Caphtor" to refer to the survivors of the Philistines, emphasizing that this people, although dispersed in Canaan, retains its original geographical identity.
H3731.origine: The name Caphtor could mean "crown" in Hebrew, perhaps alluding to its status as a distinguished region or its insular shape. The word appears only in these three biblical occurrences in reference to this island or coastal region. The exact etymology remains debated, but the biblical context clearly identifies it as the cradle of the Philistines, a maritime civilization that played a major role in the history of Israel.
H3731.emploi: Caphtor is mentioned three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to identify the geographical origin of the Philistines. In Deuteronomy 2:23, it marks the starting point of their migration to Canaan. In Amos 9:7, this name illustrates how the Lord guided the peoples in their movements, establishing that the God of Israel also commands the destinies of nations. In Jeremiah 47:4, it is mentioned to remind of the identity of the Philistines at the time of their prophesied destruction, showing that even in judgment, their original identity remains recognized. These uses place Caphtor at the heart of the Old Testament theology of nations.
H3731.portee: Caphtor reminds biblical readers that all nations have a history and an origin known to God, and that the Lord controls the migrations and destinies of peoples, not just that of Israel. This name invites recognition of divine sovereignty over the course of universal history and shows that even foreign nations, like the Philistines, are under the control of the God of Israel.

sens: People originating from Caphtor (Crete)
Inhabitants of the island of Caphtor
Ancestors of the Philistines according to biblical tradition
H3732.detail: 1. The Caphtorim are an ancient people originating from Caphtor, an island identified with Crete. They appear in the genealogical lists of Genesis as descendants of Egypt (Genesis 10:14). 2. This people is presented as conquerors: in Deuteronomy 2:23, we learn that the Caphtorim destroyed the Avvites who lived in villages near Gaza and settled in their place. 3. According to the Bible, the Caphtorim are linked to the origin of the Philistines, who would become a major people in Canaan and formidable enemies of Israel.
H3732.origine: The name "Caphtorim" derives from Caphtor, a toponym meaning "crown" in Hebrew. This name designates the historical island of Crete, from which this maritime and trading people came. The form of the word follows the usual Hebrew pattern for designating the inhabitants of a region (group or ethnic formation).
H3732.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible: in Genesis 10:14, in Deuteronomy 2:23, and in 1 Chronicles 1:12 (where it repeats Genesis 10:14). All three occurrences are part of genealogical or historical passages. In Genesis 10, the Caphtorim are listed among the peoples descended from Egypt, suggesting their arrival or control from Egypt. In Deuteronomy 2, the text reports a particular event: the invasion of Canaan by the Caphtorim and their establishment at the expense of the previous people, the Avvites. No distinction is made between different groups of Caphtorim: the word always designates the same people.

sens: A type of palanquin or closed cage fixed on the back of a camel to seat a traveler
A structure of equipment allowing a person to be transported sitting high on an animal
A place where objects can be hidden, sheltered by its framework
H3733A.detail:
1. The saddle is a type of closed palanquin, a cage or cabin carried on the back of a camel, which allows a traveler to sit comfortably and securely. It is an elevated structure that protects the rider from the elements and prying eyes. In Genesis 31:34, Rachel takes advantage of it to hide under her father Laban's camel's saddle.
2. The saddle serves as travel equipment: it is a practical setup for long journeys on camelback in the desert. It allows for sitting while traveling rather than riding directly on the camel.
3. The saddle, thanks to its closed framework and compartments, offers a place to conceal things. Rachel hid the teraphim (household idols) under the saddle, showing that it has hollow space and an effective shelter for hiding objects from view.
H3733A.origine: The Hebrew word כָּר (kar) refers to a transport equipment characteristic of the desert regions of the ancient Near East. Its exact etymology is uncertain, but the word specifically denotes this type of palanquin or closed cage that is fixed on a camel. It is a specialized term for a well-defined object in the culture of nomads and Eastern travelers.
H3733A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 31:34, in the story of Jacob and Laban. Rachel, who leaves her father's house with her husband Jacob, steals the teraphim (small household idols) that her family worshiped. When Laban pursues her and searches her belongings, she hides sitting under the camel's saddle, pretending to be unwell. Laban searches everywhere but does not find the idols. This passage shows the saddle as a daily travel equipment in the desert, known and accepted by all.
H3733A.portee: This account reveals how Rachel prefers to take her family's gods with her rather than leave them with Laban. Her cleverness—hiding under the saddle—highlights how she uses the customs and ordinary objects of travel to protect what is important to her. For the reader, this raises questions: should one keep false gods? Will God allow Jacob to live happily with a woman who hides idols? This bizarre scene prepares the reader for the spiritual purification that Jacob will undertake later.

sens: Grassy land where herds graze
Abundant and rich grass that feeds livestock
Image of fertility and divine blessing
Image of fragility and vanity of the wicked
H3733B.detail:
1. The pasture is primarily a field covered with grass where sheep and livestock come to feed. It is a grassy space, natural or prepared, essential to pastoral life in Israel: in Isaiah 30:23, the happy future announced by the prophet includes that "your herds will graze in vast pastures."
2. The word also refers to the grass itself in its richness and nourishing greenness. In Psalms 65:14, the psalmist celebrates that "the pastures are covered with flocks," an image of fertile land blessed by God that produces abundantly.
3. The pasture becomes a biblical image of blessing and prosperity: fertile lands ensure the life of the flock and the wealth of the shepherd, symbolizing God's generous action toward His people.
4. In Psalms 37:20, the psalmist contrasts the fate of the wicked with that of the righteous: the enemies of the Lord "vanish, they vanish like smoke" as do the "most beautiful pastures"—a striking image of fragility: no matter how lush it is, the pasture burns up and disappears.
H3733B.origine: The Hebrew word kar comes from a root that evokes the idea of an enclosure or a defined space. It is related to words denoting a circle or an enclosure. The pasture is concretely this grassy space, defined or not, where grass grows naturally or is cultivated for the herds. It is a concrete and vivid term from the nomadic and pastoral life of the ancient Near East.
H3733B.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the Psalms or the Prophets. In Psalms 65:14, it celebrates the fertility of creation filled with grazing flocks. In Isaiah 30:23, it announces to the restored people days of fertility and material abundance. In Psalms 37:20, it serves an inverse comparison: the beautiful pastures vanish like smoke, just as the wicked will disappear. It is thus a poetic and prophetic word, laden with images of prosperity or vanity depending on the context.
H3733B.portee: The pasture reminds the reader that the provision of each day comes from the hand of God: everything that nourishes and sustains life—both material and spiritual—is a divine gift. This image also invites meditation on the vanity of earthly things: even the most beautiful pastures do not last. For the believer, the pasture evokes trust in divine provision and humility in the face of the temporal nature of all that is not eternal.

sens: young male sheep
adult male sheep, ram
fat animal fattened for food
war ram, siege engine
H3733C.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the young male sheep, the lamb in the strict sense: an animal still in the early stage of its life, as seen in 1 Samuel 15:9 where the "fat lambs" are listed among the spoils of war, choice beasts.
2. It also applies to the adult male sheep, the ram: in 2 Kings 3:4, Mesha paid tribute with "one hundred thousand lambs and one hundred thousand rams with their wool," showing that the word encompasses the entire life of the male sheep.
3. In a context of wealth or food, the word emphasizes the fattened animal, savory: in Isaiah 34:6, it speaks of "the fat of the kidneys of rams," highlighting the meaty quality, suitable for sacrifice or feast.
4. In a war context, the word shifts to the ram used as a weapon: it is the siege engine called "ram" in French, which breaks down walls (Ezekiel 4:2 and 21:27 clearly mention this technical sense).
H3733C.origine: The Hebrew word kar comes from a root that evokes the idea of roundness and thickness: a sheep with a thick, massive body. The same family of words in Hebrew designates other robust animals. In Aramaic and Arabic, similar terms are found. The word has retained this connection with bodily fullness, hence the natural transition from young sheep to massive ram, then to the siege engine which also has the round and massive shape of the ancient ram.
H3733C.emploi: The word kar appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in lists of livestock (Deuteronomy, 1 Samuel, 2 Kings), in prophecies (Isaiah, Jeremiah), and in descriptions of sieges (Ezekiel). In Deuteronomy 32:14, it is among the riches that God refuses to His ungrateful people. In 1 Samuel 15:9, the people spare the "fat lambs" instead of devoting them to divine ban, marking their disobedience. In Isaiah 16:1, the lambs are offered as tribute to the sovereign. The sense of "siege ram" clearly appears in Ezekiel 4:2 and 21:27 where the war instrument bears the name of the animal that inspired it. Amos 6:4 mentions the lambs of the flock in a context of debauched luxury.
H3733C.portee: The word lamb/ram in the Bible evokes pastoral wealth, the well-being of the people, and also their sin when they refuse to obey God (1 Samuel 15:9). It also recalls the theme of sacrifice: the lamb is the classic animal offered to the Lord. The siege ram, on the other hand, symbolizes military power and threat. These images work together to show how God judges, through war and judgment, a people that prefers wealth to obedience.

sens: Measure of capacity for grains and liquids
Large quantity of provisions or tribute
H3734A.detail:
1. The cor is a volume measure used in Israel to assess grains (wheat, barley, flour) and liquids (oil, wine). It is a standardized unit that allows for counting harvests and tributes: thus Solomon consumed thirty cors of fine flour each day (1 Kings 4:22), and Hiram received twenty thousand cors of wheat annually (1 Kings 5:11).
2. The cor also signifies abundance and generosity in commercial transactions or tributes: when King Jotham defeats the Ammonites, they deliver to him ten thousand cors of wheat and as much barley as tribute (2 Chronicles 27:5). The word then carries the idea of a massive quantity, a testament to the wealth and power of a king or a nation.
H3734A.origine: The Hebrew word kor denotes an ancient measure of capacity, likely borrowed from a neighboring language. Its Aramaic equivalent kor (כּוֹר) is attested in later texts. The cor represents ten ephah (for grains) or ten bath (for liquids), making it a large unit of measure. This system of measurements was common in the ancient Near East for quantifying tributes, in-kind wages, and royal provisions.
H3734A.emploi: The cor appears five times in the Bible, exclusively in the historical and prophetic books. It regularly measures the tributes paid to the kings of Israel (Solomon in 1 Kings 4:22 and 5:11, Jotham in 2 Chronicles 27:5) and compensations between nations (the tribute of the Ammonites). The prophet Ezekiel also uses the cor to explain the relationship between liquid measurement units (45:14). The context is always that of administration, royal economy, and commercial or tributary transactions.
H3734A.portee: The cor reminds us that the wealth and power of the kings of Israel were measured in concrete resources — food, oil, tributes — necessary to sustain the royal household and the army. These enormous figures (thirty cors per day for Solomon, twenty thousand cors of tribute) illustrate the abundance promised by God to faithful kings, but also the material burden represented by maintaining a court and administration. For the reader, these concrete measures make tangible the cost of power and the economic stability that God granted to His people.

sens: Unit of measure of capacity for dry materials (notably grain)
Unit of measure of capacity for liquids (notably wine and oil)
Large quantity, expressed by this measure
H3734B.detail:
1. The cor is an ancient unit for measuring grains and other dry materials: a single biblical occurrence shows it associated with wheat (Ezra 7:22), where the cor represents an important measure capable of holding about 220 liters.
2. The same cor is also used to measure liquids, notably wine and oil: Ezra 7:22 mentions "baths" (the liquid equivalent), showing that these two measurement systems coexist and correspond (10 ephah of grain = 10 baths of liquid = 1 cor).
3. In the context of Ezra 7:22, the cor becomes a counting unit to express abundance: one hundred cors of wheat illustrate a massive, royal provision, marking the generosity of King Artaxerxes towards the temple in Jerusalem.
H3734B.origine: The Hebrew word kor comes from a root meaning "to dig" or "to sink," evoking the idea of a hollow container used for measuring. It belongs to an ancient metrological system of the Near East, where the cor was a standardized unit, equivalent to 10 ephah (a smaller unit). This measurement system was common in Assyria and Babylon, from where it spread to neighboring regions, including Israel.
H3734B.emploi: The word cor appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in Ezra 7:22. In this passage from the fifth century B.C., the Persian king Artaxerxes allows Ezra to take large deposits from the royal treasury for the temple in Jerusalem. The "one hundred cors of wheat" are among the massive provisions granted: it is an official, administrative measure, testifying to the importance of the metrological system in use in the Persian empire. The unique usage emphasizes that this technical term was known to the scribes and administrators of the time, but that the Sacred Text mentions it in a punctual and precise manner.
H3734B.portee: The cor reminds the reader that divine Providence is also expressed through concrete and material means: the king's generosity towards the temple is not symbolic, but quantified, measurable, massive. This mention of abundant provisions shows God providing for the reconstruction of the temple and invites us to trust the Lord for our daily needs and to recognize His hand in the providential circumstances that bless us.

sens: to be troubled, agitated internally
to experience moral or spiritual distress
to be anxious in light of what one has just perceived or understood
H3735.detail:
1. The verb first describes an inner turmoil, an agitation of the mind or soul: the body and spirit are shaken by intense emotion. In Daniel 7:15, the prophet says: "The spirit that was in me was troubled" — he has the vision of the beasts rising from the sea, and this revelation plunges him into great internal distress.
2. This trouble is not mere surprise, but true moral distress: a deep fear, an anxiety in the face of the mystery or judgment revealed by what one has just seen. It is the natural reaction of the human heart in the face of God's mysteries.
H3735.origine: The word comes from a Semitic root that expresses the idea of trouble and agitation. In biblical Hebrew, this root is used to describe intense states of soul: the heart that stirs, the spirit that is troubled. The form used here (Ithpa'el) emphasizes that the subject passively undergoes this trouble — it is not he who causes the distress, but he is seized by it.
H3735.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 7:15. The prophet Daniel has a heavenly vision of terrifying beasts that prophesy future kingdoms — a revelation that completely shakes him. His spirit is "troubled" by what he has seen. This context shows that the word is used for the distress that seizes someone when God reveals mysteries or judgments to come.
H3735.portee: This verse teaches us that encountering God's mysteries, understanding His hidden and future designs, naturally provokes distress within us. Daniel is not weak for being afraid: it is the right human reaction in the face of the divine. For the reader, it is an encouragement to accept that our trust in God does not eliminate our troubled emotions, especially in the face of what surpasses us.

sens: To cover the body by putting on a garment
To wear a cloak or garment as a mark of function or honor
H3736.detail:
1. The word describes the action of putting on a garment, covering one's body with clothing. In 1 Chronicles 15:27, David is "clothed in a robe of fine linen": it is the image of the garment enveloping the body.
2. The cloak or garment becomes a sign of role and authority: when one puts on a cloak, one is not just dressing the body, but also taking on a function. David and the Levites wear their service garments in the context of the solemn procession of the ark.
H3736.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of wrapping or covering. There is a parallel form (kephat, "to bind") that emphasizes the sense of "to surround" or "to encircle." The primary image is that of fabric wrapping around the body.
H3736.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Chronicles 15:27. David and the Levites accompanying the ark of the covenant are "clothed" in their service garments during this solemn procession. The context is that of worship and respect for holy functions: the garment is not just an ordinary piece of clothing, but a visible mark of consecration to the work of God.
H3736.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, clothing is never trivial: it expresses who we are and the role we play before God and others. To be "clothed" in a service garment is also to be clothed in responsibility and respect for what is holy.

sens: loose-fitting garment worn over other clothes
outer covering or protection
H3737.detail:
1. The mantle is a loose-fitting garment made of fabric that is worn over other clothing to protect against cold or sun. In Daniel 3:21, the three young men thrown into the furnace keep their mantles along with their other garments — this highlights the importance of such clothing in daily and military life in Mesopotamia.
2. Figuratively, a mantle can refer to a covering, protection, or something that envelops: it wraps around and protects the one who wears it.
H3737.origine: The Hebrew word comes from an ancient Semitic root that denotes protective and enveloping garments. In Mesopotamia and the Middle East, the mantle was an essential element of official and warrior attire, worn by kings, leaders, and soldiers.
H3737.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 3:21. In this account, Nebuchadnezzar orders that Daniel's three companions be thrown alive into the blazing furnace with all their clothes, including their mantles. This mention shows that the mantle was an ordinary garment, even worn by captives in detention: it was part of the standard attire of the time.
H3737.portee: This detail about the mantles reminds the reader that even in extreme trials — facing imminent death in the flames — God does not let anything slip away. The three young men keep their garments, and God will protect them in the heart of the fire. It is an invitation to trust God in the most terrifying circumstances.

sens: Make a hole in the ground or rock by removing material
Prepare or dig a pit, a well, a grave
Pierce, open (a cavity, an ear)
Manufacture, prepare (especially misfortune, a trap)
H3738B.detail:
1. The primary and literal meaning: to dig means to make a hole by moving earth or rock. Isaac commands his servants to "dig" a well in the land of Canaan (Genesis 26:25), and a man who "digs" a pit must cover it so that no one falls into it (Exodus 21:33).
2. By extension, the verb refers to the intentional and careful digging of a burial place or a prepared space. King Asa "dug" a tomb in the city of David (2 Chronicles 16:14), an image of a grave carved into rock according to the customs of the time.
3. The word also takes on the meaning of "pierce" or "open": God "opened" the ears of the psalmist, meaning He gave him the ability to listen and understand His will (Psalms 40:7).
4. Figuratively and morally, to dig can mean to "manufacture" or "prepare" a trap or misfortune. The wicked man "prepares" misfortune with his actions (Proverbs 16:27), and those who dig a pit for others fall into it themselves (Psalms 7:16; Proverbs 26:27).
H3738B.origine: The Hebrew verb קָרָה (karah) expresses the idea of making an opening by digging or piercing. The root evokes the action of "carding" or traversing a material. It is linked to the concrete image of the craftsman or digger who, through manual work, creates a cavity or transforms the terrain. This verb is used for both practical actions (digging a well, a water well) and metaphorical acts (preparing a moral trap).
H3738B.emploi: The verb appears 14 times in the Bible, mainly in the Psalms and Proverbs, as well as in the narratives of the Pentateuch and Chronicles. In the Psalms and Proverbs, it acquires a strong spiritual charge: digging a pit becomes an image of sin that turns against the one who prepares it (Psalms 7:16; Proverbs 26:27). In legal and practical contexts (Exodus 21:33), it is an ordinary action. The figurative use dominates: digging misfortune, traps, or evil symbolizes the culpable elaboration of a wicked intention. God can also "dig" or "open" in a positive sense (Psalms 40:7: opening ears to obedience).
H3738B.portee: This word teaches the believer a spiritual law: the act of evil that one secretly prepares returns to the one who dug it. It is an invitation to watch over one's hidden intentions and actions, knowing that God sees what is being prepared. Conversely, it reminds us that God "opens the ears" of the humble heart to make it obedient to His word and will.

sens: Acquire something by paying money
Obtain through negotiation and exchange
Persecute, overwhelm someone (figurative sense)
Engage in commerce, trade
H3739A.detail:
1. The primary and most common meaning is to buy in the literal sense: to give money to obtain what one needs. In Deuteronomy 2:6, Moses commands the people of Israel to buy food and water from the Edomites for money, rather than seizing it by force — it is an ordinary purchase, a commercial exchange.
2. The word can more broadly refer to the act of negotiating, bargaining, or concluding a deal. It conveys the idea of a transaction where each party gives something to receive something in return.
3. Figuratively and surprisingly, the word takes on the meaning of "persecute" or "overwhelm": in Job 6:27, Job reproaches his friends for overwhelming him as one might do to an orphan. This shift in meaning may stem from the idea of "mistreating someone like a commodity." 
4. The word can also evoke the profession of one who buys and sells, the trader or merchant: in Job 40:25, it refers to fishermen who trade fish, selling or exchanging them among merchants.
H3739A.origine: The Hebrew root כָּרָה expresses the idea of buying and exchanging, of engaging in commerce. It is related to the realm of commercial transactions. The figurative sense of "persecute" developed from the image of being "mistreated" or "harshly treated" like a commodity. The word appears mainly in the wisdom and historical texts of the Old Testament.
H3739A.emploi: The verb כָּרָה appears 4 times in the Hebrew Old Testament according to these usages. Its primary use is commercial and concrete: buying consumer goods (food, water) for daily needs, as shown in Deuteronomy 2:6 in the context of the exodus. In the book of Job, the word takes on a different hue: in 6:27, it takes on a figurative and bitter meaning, signifying "persecute" or "overwhelm" — Job complains that his friends mistreat him. In 40:25, the same verb denotes the commerce or trade exercised by fishermen. This variation in meaning shows that the word can shift from the concrete (buying from the grocer) to the figurative (being overwhelmed) depending on the context.
H3739A.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that everything we need to live — food, water — has a price and must be acquired justly, without wronging others. It may also resonate with the teaching on persecution: being "bought" or "treated harshly" evokes the condition of the weak in the face of the powerful, which invites mercy towards those who suffer.

sens: give a feast, a banquet
H3739B.detail: 1. The word literally means to provide food during a grand festive occasion. It is to offer a rich and plentiful meal in honor of someone. In 2 Kings 6:23, the king of Israel prepares a great feast for the Syrian soldiers, which shows how this word describes a generous act of hospitality and reconciliation.
H3739B.origine: The Hebrew word kârah comes from a root that evokes the idea of preparing, arranging, or setting something up. It is related to other Hebrew terms concerning the preparation of food and the setting of a meal. The basic image is that of food carefully prepared for a special occasion.
H3739B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Kings 6:23, where the context is one of attempted reconciliation: after capturing an enemy army, the king of Israel orders that a feast be prepared for them instead of executing them. This unique usage shows how the word serves to describe a gesture of political generosity and peace, transforming captivity into welcome.
H3739B.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, sharing a meal is an act of peace and reconciliation, much more than mere sustenance. Feasting together can be a powerful means of transforming a hostile relationship into one of brotherhood and trust.

sens: gathering of people around a table to eat and drink together
occasion for sharing and conviviality
H3740.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a meal: a moment when people come together to eat and drink. In 2 Kings 6:23, the king of Israel serves a great meal to the Syrian soldiers he has miraculously captured, creating a moment of humanity and relaxation between enemies.
2. More broadly, this meal is an occasion for conviviality and sharing. By offering this meal, the king establishes a bond of peace with his adversaries: after eating and drinking together, the Syrian troops renounce their incursions into Israel's territory. The sharing of bread and wine thus seals a moment of reconciliation.
H3740.origine: The Hebrew word כֵּרָה (kérah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of digging or preparing a space. The initial image is that of a meal carefully prepared, set to receive guests. This word is rare in the Old Testament and belongs to the vocabulary of daily life and hospitality.
H3740.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Kings 6:23, in a narrative where the prophet Elisha helps the king of Israel capture a Syrian army. After this miraculous capture, rather than massacring the prisoners, the king of Israel treats them generously by serving a great meal. This unique usage shows how a simple meal can become an instrument of peace and transform enemies into grateful men, capable of renouncing violence.
H3740.portee: This passage teaches a profound lesson about the power of hospitality and kindness toward those who are hostile to us. The shared meal not only resolves an immediate political tension: it illustrates how treating one's enemy with dignity and generosity can accomplish more than violence or vengeance. For the Christian, it is a call to see in every moment of sharing an opportunity for reconciliation and peace.

sens: Hollow or dug-out place serving as a dwelling
Natural refuge or shelter in rock or terrain
Designed pasture where shepherds and their flocks can stay
H3741.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a cavity or hollow dug into the ground or rock. It is an emptied space, shaped by water, time, or human work. This can be a cistern (for water), a cave, or a prepared area.
2. It is a place of refuge and rest, where people and animals can find protection. In Zephaniah 2:6, the abandoned coastal areas become "dwellings for shepherds" — hollow and shaped spaces that offer shelter and protection.
3. In the same verse, the word describes a designed pasture, a place where shepherds can rest their flocks, finding water, grass, and a natural shelter dug into the terrain.
H3741.origine: The Hebrew word כָּרָה (karah) comes from a root meaning "to dig" or "to excavate." The same root produces other forms denoting actions of excavation. The basic image is that of a hollow, a shaped cavity, hence the meaning of hollow dwelling — a habitable place because it is protected, dug out, offering a natural or designed refuge.
H3741.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Zephaniah 2:6. In this prophetic verse, the prophet announces that the once-populated and rich coastal area will be transformed into pastures and hollow dwellings for shepherds. The context is that of divine judgment upon the nations: these lands will be abandoned to nomads and their flocks, who will find refuge in the caves and hollows of the terrain.
H3741.portee: This word reminds us that God can transform prosperous places into deserts, and conversely, that even in apparent abandonment, there are refuges and resources for those seeking shelter. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize divine providence in all places and situations, and to understand that God orders the history of nations according to His judgment and mercy.

sens: celestial creature with wings, guardian of God's sanctuary
sculpted or embroidered figure representing a cherub
invisible seat or support of the divine presence
mount or chariot of the Lord
H3742.detail: 1. The cherub is an angelic creature, a celestial being belonging to God's court. It is equipped with wings and serves a function as a guardian or protector: the cherubim guarded the entrance to the Garden of Eden after Adam's fall (Genesis 3:24), waving a flaming sword to forbid access to the tree of life. 2. The cherub also refers to the sculpted or embroidered image of this creature, particularly on the mercy seat (the cover of the Ark of the Covenant): two golden cherubim were placed there, facing each other, their wings covering the mercy seat (Exodus 37:9). These representations also adorned the temple (1 Kings 6:29) and were embroidered on the veil of the sanctuary (Exodus 26:31). 3. The cherub symbolizes the invisible throne or pedestal of God's glory: "You sit upon the cherubim" signifies that God reigns in majesty above celestial beings. 4. The cherub can also represent the chariot or means of transport of God: "He mounted on a cherub and flew" (2 Samuel 22:11) depicts God moving with power and speed.
H3742.origine: The Hebrew word כְּרוּב (kerouv) likely has a Mesopotamian origin, linked to Akkadian and Babylonian mythology that described hybrid guardian creatures of temples. It is found in Ezekiel 10, where the cherubim are described as complex beings with multiple faces and wings, reflecting the theology of Israel's neighboring kingdoms. The Hebrew plural "cherubim" (כְּרוּבִים) is very common in the Bible to designate these creatures.
H3742.emploi: The word "cherub" appears 66 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical and prophetic books. In Genesis, the cherubim guard the tree of life after the fall. In Exodus and Kings, they are artistically represented: two golden cherubim on the mercy seat (Exodus 37:9), sculpted cherubim in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:29), and embroidered on the veil of the sanctuary (Exodus 26:31). Ezekiel extensively and complexly describes the cherubim of the divine throne (Ezekiel 10), blending celestial vision and theatrical representation. The Psalms speak of God sitting upon the cherubim (Psalms 80:2; 99:1). The word designates either the celestial creature itself or its material image in Israelite worship.
H3742.portee: For the Christian, the cherub reminds us that God's presence is both hidden and visible: invisible as divine essence, but signified by images and symbols. The cherubim planted at the entrance of Eden illustrate that sin separates man from the presence of God, but also that this separation is not definitive — it can be crossed through redemption. The central place of the cherubim above the Ark of the Covenant reminds us that God reigns in mercy: they are not terrifying creatures, but guardians of grace. Understanding the role of the cherub helps to grasp how God, though infinitely holy and distinct from the world, makes Himself present to His people.

sens: Location in Babylon from which some exiles returned with Zerubbabel
H3743.detail: Thel-Harscha is a place in Babylon (modern-day Iraq) from which men departed who accompanied Zerubbabel during the return from exile. These individuals could not prove their Israelite ancestry (Ezra 2:59).
H3743.origine: The Hebrew word כְּרוּב (Kerub) literally means "blessing." This place name appears in the list of Babylonian locations mentioned in the records of the return from exile, alongside other names like Thel-Melach and Kerub-Addan.
H3743.emploi: Thel-Harscha appears only twice in the Bible, in the two parallel lists of the return from exile: Ezra 2:59 and Nehemiah 7:61. It is among the three Babylonian locations (along with Thel-Melach and Kerub-Addan) from which some repatriates came whose Israelite genealogy could not be verified. These places served as markers to identify the origin of families returning from captivity.

sens: official messenger who proclaims public orders
one who announces an authoritative news
spokesperson for a king or power
H3744.detail:
1. A herald is an official messenger tasked with loudly proclaiming the orders and decisions of the king or government. He stands in public and cries out so that all can hear him: this is his special function, as seen in Daniel 3:4, where the herald of the king of Babylon "cried out loudly" to command the peoples to bow down before the golden statue.
2. More broadly, the herald is one who solemnly announces an important news, vested with the authority of the one who sends him. He does not speak in his own name, but in the name of the king or established power, and people must listen to him as they would listen to the king himself.
3. This is why a herald is also a spokesperson, a representative of authority. His word carries weight because it comes from above and must be obeyed.
H3744.origine: The Hebrew word כָּרוֹז (karoz) likely borrows from the Persian word "*keroz" (كارز). It is a term from the official vocabulary of ancient Near Eastern empires, especially used in Babylonian narratives. The root carries the idea of crying out, making one's voice heard with authority to disseminate an order or announcement.
H3744.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 3:4. In this passage of the story of Nebuchadnezzar and the golden statue, a royal herald cries out the king's decree to the peoples, nations, and men of all languages. This context clearly shows the function of the herald: he is an officer who solemnly proclaims public orders with the authority of the central power. The Babylonian setting explains the use of this Persian-origin word, attested in the administrations of the empire.
H3744.portee: The herald reminds us that God Himself uses messengers to announce His will to men: prophets, apostles, and preachers are God's heralds, tasked with proclaiming His message to the world. Understanding this word helps grasp the solemn and official importance of biblical proclamation: it is not a private opinion, but an authorized message that demands a response.

sens: To make known publicly through an official proclamation
To solemnly announce to the entire population
H3745.detail:
1. To publish means to make known a decree, message, or promotion in an official and public manner. It is to proclaim something with authority so that all the people learn it. In Daniel 5:29, King Belshazzar "publishes" (proclaims) that Daniel will have the third place in the government: it is an official act by which the news is announced to the entire kingdom.
2. This verb emphasizes the idea of making something public and solemn, as when a news is cried out in the streets or disseminated by a herald. It gives a word the authority and scope of an official announcement that no one can ignore.
H3745.origine: The word comes from an Aramaic root that evokes the action of crying out or announcing loudly. It is formed with the Aphel prefix, which in Aramaic reinforces the meaning of the verb and makes it causative: these are not just words, but an action of making something proclaimed, initiating an official act of dissemination.
H3745.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 5:29. It is part of the story of Belshazzar's feast, where the king, after Daniel interprets the mysterious writing on the wall, rewards him by granting honors and a position of power. The royal proclamation is the act that makes this decision public and irrevocable. The context shows that it is a verb of official and solemn action.
H3745.portee: This word reminds us that decisions and honors granted by authorities need to be publicly proclaimed to have full force. For the believer, it also evokes how God makes His will and word known to men: not in secret, but in clear and official proclamation.

sens: Group of foreign mercenary soldiers
Bodyguards of King David
Executors of royal sentences
H3746.detail:
1. The Cherethites are a body of foreign soldiers that King David hired as professional mercenaries. They formed an elite military unit.
2. They primarily served as personal bodyguards for King David, tasked with protecting his life and that of his family. In 2 Kings 11:4, the priest Jehoiada mobilizes them to defend the young king Joash and to overthrow Queen Athaliah, who had usurped the throne.
3. These soldiers also served as royal executioners, carrying out death sentences ordered by the king. Their military competence and loyalty to the crown made them reliable for these delicate tasks.
H3746.origine: The name "Cherethites" comes from a root that likely refers to the island of Crete (Kéreth in Hebrew), from where these mercenaries originated. These soldiers were foreigners, recruited for their military expertise and their detachment from internal rivalries in Israel, which made them particularly loyal to the king who employed them.
H3746.emploi: The Cherethites appear twice in 2 Kings chapter 11, during the coup led by the priest Jehoiada. In verse 4, he contacts them to prepare the action: he gathers them with the captains of hundreds and the runners, making them swear to ensure the protection of the young king Joash. In verse 19, they actively participate in bringing the king down from the temple and installing him on the royal throne. These two passages show their crucial role as a loyal military force capable of overthrowing a usurper and restoring dynastic order.
H3746.portee: The Cherethites illustrate the recourse of Israelite kings to loyal troops without local ties to consolidate their power against internal threats. Their mobilization by Jehoiada shows how the legitimacy of the king depends on the support of armed forces. For the believer, this narrative reminds us that maintaining just order in the kingdom requires courageous men ready to act, and that God can use these human instruments to rectify what is corrupt.

sens: Brook on the eastern Jordan where God hid the prophet Elijah
H3747.detail: 1. Kerith is a brook located east of the Jordan, in the Holy Land. Its name means "cut" or "separation" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking a watercourse that carves and divides the terrain. It is here that the prophet Elijah hid at God's command during the great drought he had caused (1 Kings 17:3).
H3747.origine: The name Kerith comes from the Hebrew root that means "to cut" or "to slice," evoking the image of a brook that carves and slices through the landscape. This word designates an intermittent watercourse or ravine, a common characteristic of the arid lands of Jordan. The name reflects the physical geography of the place: a cut in the terrain.
H3747.emploi: Kerith appears only twice in the Bible, both in the first chapter of the account of Elijah (1 Kings 17). After Elijah announced a drought to Ahab, king of Israel, God commands him to hide near this brook, east of the Jordan. It is a place of refuge and divine protection: God feeds Elijah there by ravens and the brook provides him with water to drink. This brook thus becomes the site of a manifestation of divine providence toward His prophet.
H3747.portee: Kerith reminds us that God provides for the needs of those He calls to serve Him, even in the most difficult circumstances. This brook symbolizes a place of retreat and trust, where the believer can experience God's faithfulness. It is an invitation to believe that divine protection is more secure than any human security.

sens: Legal act of marriage dissolution
Written document confirming separation
Repudiation of a wife by her husband
Figurative rejection or abandonment
H3748.detail:
1. Divorce is the official dissolution of marriage: a man who "finds something indecent about her" writes a certificate of divorce and sends her away from his house (Deuteronomy 24:1). It is a legal act regulated by the Law.
2. This word refers to the document itself, the "certificate of divorce" that the husband gives to his wife to mark the separation (Deuteronomy 24:3). This letter is the official proof of the dissolution of the marriage.
3. By extension, it means repudiation — the rejection of a wife: the Lord figuratively says, "I have divorced your mother" when speaking of unfaithful Israel, just as a husband sends away his wife (Isaiah 50:1; Jeremiah 3:8).
4. The word can evoke any abandonment or definitive separation, especially when God uses this image to describe His punishment of Israel: she received her certificate of divorce because of unfaithfulness (Jeremiah 3:8).
H3748.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to cut" or "to sever." Divorce is a cutting, a definitive separation of the marital bond. The form of the word (the suffix -ut) creates an abstract noun that designates the act or state of rupture rather than the simple action. This vocabulary is part of Israel's matrimonial law, where divorce was a recognized reality governed by the Law of Moses.
H3748.emploi: The word appears only four times in the Old Testament, always to denote divorce in the strict sense. Three occurrences are found in the Law (Deuteronomy 24:1 and 24:3), where Moses regulates divorce: a husband may write a certificate of divorce and send away his wife. The other two usages are prophetic (Isaiah 50:1 and Jeremiah 3:8): God uses the image of divorce to express how He rejected Israel because of her unfaithfulness, just as a husband repudiates his wife. The word retains its sense of rupture but shifts from the legal domain to the spiritual and metaphorical domain.
H3748.portee: This word invites the reader to see that while the Law of Moses tolerated divorce, it strictly regulated it — it was not a private gesture but an official act with a written document. The prophetic use of this term also shows the gravity of Israel's sin: her unfaithfulness made her unworthy of the covenant, just as an unfaithful wife loses her marriage. For the Christian, this word reminds us that God takes the covenant seriously and that breaking with Him is the consequence of sin.

sens: Protruding edge of an object, ledge or cornice
Protruding part of an architectural structure
H3749.detail: 1. A ledge is an edge that extends or protrudes from a surface — an edge that projects outward. In descriptions of the altar of burnt offerings, the ledge is that projection that runs around the middle of the altar and serves as a support or structural limit: this is where the bronze grating is placed (Exodus 27:5). 2. More broadly, it refers to any cornice or raised border of a construction. The ledge of the altar divides it into two functional levels — the lower part where the ashes rest, and the upper part where the sacrifices burn (Exodus 38:4).
H3749.origine: The Hebrew word karkov comes from a root evoking protrusion or projection. It literally designates what advances, what makes an angle. This type of architectural vocabulary is found in descriptions of the tabernacle and the temple, where every detail is given with precision.
H3749.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the Torah, to describe the furnishings of worship. Exodus 27:5 and Exodus 38:4 speak of the same ledge of the altar of burnt offerings — the first time at the moment of the divine prescription for its construction, the second during its actual realization by Bezalel. In both cases, it indicates where to place the grating of the combustion chamber, showing that the ledge is a precise constructive marker.
H3749.portee: This word reminds us that in ancient worship, every detail of the sacred furniture had its place and function, reflecting the order and holiness of God. The ledge, though simple, embodies this divine rigor in the establishment of worship.

sens: Orange and yellow flower of the crocus, used as a spice and fragrance
Characteristic flavor or aroma of saffron
Figuratively, beauty and richness in romantic language
H3750.detail:
1. Saffron is a flower from the crocus family, orange and yellow in color, from which a precious spice and dye are derived. In Song of Solomon 4:14, it is listed among the most refined aromatic plants — spikenard, calamus, cinnamon, myrrh, aloes — that adorn the beloved and symbolize her exquisite beauty.

2. Saffron is used to flavor drinks and dishes and was renowned in the East for its healing properties, particularly for promoting sweating and cooling the body. In biblical and ancient usage, it is a luxury spice, reserved for the wealthy and solemn occasions.

3. In the context of the Song, saffron becomes a poetic image of refinement and seduction: the beloved is compared to a garden where all the most precious aromatics grow, thus expressing her incomparable grace and allure.
H3750.origine: The Hebrew word כַּרְכֹּם (karkom) designates saffron, this precious flower known to Eastern cultures since antiquity. Its etymology remains uncertain, but the word is rooted in the knowledge of cultivated plants in the Middle East. Saffron was imported from Asia and was very expensive, which explains its mention alongside other high-priced spices.
H3750.emploi: The word saffron appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 4:14, in the poetic description of the beloved. It is part of a list of perfumes and aromatics — a typical enumeration of luxurious Eastern gardens. This unique mention underscores the importance of saffron as a symbol of wealth, refinement, and timeless beauty in biblical literature. The romantic context makes it an image of seduction and splendor.
H3750.portee: Saffron reminds us that the Bible does not disdain the sensible beauty and delicate pleasures of creation. In the Song, this enumeration of perfumes invites us to celebrate love in its aesthetic and generous dimension, without guilt. It is also a lesson in humility: the most beautiful and precious things on earth remain fragile and temporary, which turns us toward the true riches of the Kingdom.

sens: Fortified city of Upper Asia, on the Euphrates, formerly the Hittite capital
Strategic stake in the wars between Egypt and Babylon at the end of the kingdom of Judah
H3751.detail:
1. Carkemisch is a fortified city located in northern Mesopotamia, on the Euphrates River, beyond the lands of Israel. It was once an important center of Hittite power. It is here that a decisive event takes place during the reign of King Josiah: Necho, Pharaoh of Egypt, goes there "to fight" (2 Chronicles 35:20), which shows the military significance of this city.
2. Carkemisch embodies the power of the great nations that dominate the region. The prophet Isaiah mentions it alongside other famous cities — Calno, Hamath, Arpad, Samaria, Damascus — to show that all fortresses, no matter how powerful, are vulnerable to the judgment of God. In Jeremiah 46:2, we learn that it is at Carkemisch that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, achieves a decisive victory over the Egyptian army, marking a shift in power in the East and foreshadowing the fate awaiting Judah.
H3751.origine: The Hebrew name "Karkemish" literally means "fortress of Chemosh" (or possibly of Kemosh, a Moabite deity), reflecting its military role and roots in the world of ancient Levantine kingdoms. It is an urban center whose historical importance spans empires: Hittite first, then a contested stake between Egypt and Babylon in the final days of the kingdom of Judah.
H3751.emploi: Carkemisch appears three times in the Bible: in 2 Chronicles 35:20, where Pharaoh Necho goes there to fight, leading to the dramatic end of King Josiah; in Isaiah 10:9, where it is listed among the conquered cities to illustrate the false sense of security of nations that ignore God; and in Jeremiah 46:2, where it marks the site of the Egyptian defeat by Nebuchadnezzar in 605 B.C., a major geopolitical turning point. Each time, Carkemisch symbolizes the power struggles between empires and God's judgment on nations.
H3751.portee: Carkemisch reminds us that the great fortresses of the world, even those reputed to be impregnable, cannot withstand God's plans. It illustrates how external empires — Egypt, Babylon — dominate and determine the fate of peoples when they stray from God. For the reader in Jeremiah's time and beyond, this city becomes a symbol of the turning point in history: it is where Babylon seals its hegemony, which also seals the fate of Judah.

sens: eunuch in the service of King Ahasuerus
H3752.detail: Carcas is the seventh of the seven eunuchs who served King Ahasuerus (Xerxes I) at the court of Susa. These eunuchs were high-ranking officials tasked with important functions at the Persian monarch's court. Nothing else is known about him other than what is mentioned in Esther 1:10, where he is listed among the seven servants whom the king ordered to summon to his queen Ahasuerus during a royal banquet.
H3752.origine: The name Carcas, probably of Persian origin meaning "severe" or "harsh," reflects the typical names and titles of court officials in the Persian court of the 5th century B.C.
H3752.emploi: Carcas appears only once in the Bible, in Esther 1:10. He is included in the list of the seven eunuchs of King Ahasuerus named during the grand royal banquet, prior to the deposition of Queen Vashti. His inclusion in this specific enumeration indicates that he held an important rank at the Persian court, although his exact role is not detailed.

sens: Mounting and pack animal of the desert, one-humped camel
Fast and heat-resistant means of transport
H3753.detail:
1. The dromedary is a one-humped camel, well adapted to life in the desert and arid regions. It is a robust animal, capable of carrying heavy loads and traveling long distances without needing to drink. In Isaiah 66:20, dromedaries are among the prestigious mounts that nations will use to bring back the scattered children of Israel: they symbolize the transport of treasures and honor, as in the processions of princes or commercial expeditions along caravan routes.
2. More broadly, the dromedary represents a reliable and efficient means of transport, particularly in the desert lands of the East where the animal was common and valuable. Its mention alongside horses and chariots underscores that it is a prestigious animal, worthy of accompanying a triumphant return.
H3753.origine: The Hebrew word כִּרְכָּרָה (karkarah) belongs to the family of terms designating the camel and its variants. Its etymology may suggest a root evoking movement or circulation (the idea of travel), which perfectly suits a caravan animal. The word appears in biblical Hebrew as a specific term for the dromedary, distinct from the ordinary camel.
H3753.emploi: The word כִּרְכָּרָה (karkarah) appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 66:20. In this prophetic passage of the end times, it evokes the glorious return of the scattered children of Israel to Jerusalem. Dromedaries are listed among the exotic and prestigious mounts — horses, chariots, litters, mules — that the nations will use for this triumphant procession. The context suggests a solemn and honorable procession, where each animal represents a form of respect towards the people of God being brought back to Zion. It is less a technical term than a poetic image of restoration and glory.
H3753.portee: This verse invites the reader to envision the final restoration of Israel in terms of total restoration and restored honor: the nations themselves will participate in this return. The mention of the dromedary, a noble and rare animal in the biblical context, emphasizes the wealth, dignity, and extraordinary nature of this return. It is a call to trust in God's faithfulness to His people, even in dispersion.

sens: Field planted with vines, intended for the production of grapes
Valuable property and economic asset
Image of prosperity and divine blessing
Figure of the people of Israel in their relationship with God
H3754.detail:
1. A vine is a plot of land planted with vine stocks, cultivated to produce grapes and wine. It is a demanding crop that requires constant care: pruning, enclosing the land, and protecting the harvests. Noah "planted a vine" after the Flood (Genesis 9:20), marking the resumption of agricultural life.

2. In the ancient Near East, owning a vine is a sign of wealth and stability. A well-maintained vine can be passed down from generation to generation and sustain a family. This is why coveting it is serious: Naboth refuses to sell his vine to Ahab (1 Kings 21), even under pressure from the king.

3. A vine produces its fruit after years of patient work. It thus symbolizes a happy and established life, blessing: God promises that His people "will plant vines, and you will eat their fruit" (Isaiah 37:30). Stripping someone of their vine is to take away their joy and future.

4. The prophet Isaiah uses the vine as an image of Israel: God "planted a vine" (Isaiah 5:1-7), surrounded it with care, but it bears bad fruit. This comparison expresses both God's love and His disappointment with the sin of His people.
H3754.origine: The Hebrew word "kèrem" primarily means a planted and cultivated field. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of delimitation and intentional cultivation. In biblical Hebrew, the vine is never wild: it is always a space that is arranged, enclosed, and monitored. This word is common throughout the Bible to designate this economic and spiritual reality central to the life of Israel.
H3754.emploi: The word "vine" appears 81 times in the Old Testament, in almost all historical, poetic, and prophetic books. It always designates a concrete earthly possession: a field one owns (1 Kings 21:1-2), that one cultivates (Isaiah 37:30), from which one harvests fruit (Judges 9:27), or that one can lose through war or injustice (Nehemiah 5:5, Amos 5:11). The laws of Moses regulate respect for others' vines (Deuteronomy 23:24, Leviticus 19:10). From Isaiah (Isaiah 5) onward, the word takes on a prophetic dimension: the vine becomes the image of the relationship between God and Israel. This metaphor is enriched in the Song of Songs, where the vine also evokes love and beauty.
H3754.portee: The vine reminds the Christian reader that God blesses honest and patient work, cares about our material sustenance, and values those who protect the property of others. The prophetic image of the vine invites reflection on our own response to God's love: do we produce good fruit, or do we disappoint the Lord's expectations? It is a word of tenderness and a call to repentance.

sens: one who cultivates the vine and makes wine
agricultural worker specialized in vineyard work
one who takes care of a vineyard
H3755.detail: 1. The vineyard keeper is a man who cultivates the vine, that is, he plants, maintains, and harvests the grapevines to make wine. It is a well-defined agricultural profession: in 2 Kings 25:12, after the fall of Jerusalem, the chief of the guards leaves "as vineyard keepers" some of the poor of the land to cultivate the fields. 2. The word also describes the agricultural worker who specifically masters the tasks of the vineyard: pruning, hoeing, harvesting. In 2 Chronicles 26:10, King Uzziah "had many herds" and "vineyard keepers in the mountains and in Carmel, for he loved agriculture" — this is a specialized and valuable workforce. 3. The vineyard keeper can be both the owner of vineyards and a worker hired to cultivate them: in Isaiah 61:5, in the vision of the coming salvation, "strangers will be your farmers and your vineyard keepers," which shows that the vineyard keeper holds an important and necessary role in the economic life of Israel.
H3755.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of cultivating, keeping, caring for. The vineyard keeper is literally one who "keeps" or "cares for" the vine, as one cares for something precious. The vine, very important in rural life in Israel, requires continuous and skilled work, hence this specialized term to designate the man in charge of it.
H3755.emploi: The word appears only five times in biblical Hebrew, always to designate the character of the vineyard keeper. It mainly appears in historical or prophetic contexts: during the destruction of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:12 and Jeremiah 52:16), the king leaves the poor to cultivate the vines; under King Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:10), the vineyard keepers are part of his rural administration; in Isaiah 61:5 and Joel 1:11, the word designates either a future hope (strangers will cultivate your vines) or a present catastrophe (the vineyard keepers groan because of the drought). The context is always concrete and rural.
H3755.portee: The vineyard keeper reminds us that the work of the land and agricultural know-how are gifts from God. The vine being a symbol of Israel in Scripture, the vineyard keeper represents one who takes care of God's people or cultivates his own faith with fidelity. It is a beautiful image of dedication and patience: just as the vineyard keeper cares for his vine year after year, the believer nurtures his relationship with God.

sens: Son of Reuben and ancestor of the Carmites
Father of Achan, the disruptor of Israel
H3756G.detail:
1. Carmi is the fourth son of Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, mentioned during the descent into Egypt (Genesis 46:9). He becomes the founder of a family, the Carmites, which bears his name and whose generations are listed at the time of the census in the wilderness (Numbers 26:6).
2. Carmi is also the name of another man, the father of Achan. This Achan is famous for having transgressed the divine prohibition by taking consecrated objects during the conquest of Jericho, which caused trouble throughout Israel at the time of Joshua.
H3756G.origine: The name Carmi means "my vine" in Hebrew (from kèrem, "vine"). This name evokes the image of a vine, a symbol of fertility and blessing. It is a patriarchal family whose name recalls the divine promise of multiplication and prosperity in fertile land.
H3756G.emploi: Carmi appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. Three occurrences concern the son of Reuben: two in the genealogical lists of Genesis and Exodus (during the migration to Egypt), and one in the wilderness census (Numbers 26:6), where his descendants are officially recorded as a family. A fourth mention in 1 Chronicles 5:3 resumes the genealogy of Reuben. The only Carmi directly named in an active narrative is the father of Achan, although this passage is not provided here; the context shows that the name primarily designates the Reubenite patriarch.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, father of Achan
Son of Zabdi and grandson of Zerah
H3756H.detail: Carmi is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned for the first time during the conquest of the land under Joshua. He is the father of Achan, the man who committed a grave sin by taking sacred objects dedicated to the Lord during the capture of Jericho (Joshua 7:1). His name primarily appears in the account of Achan's punishment, where the complete genealogy is given: Achan, son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah (Joshua 7:18). The account in 1 Chronicles 2:7 also mentions him, referring to Achan by the alternative name "Achar," which literally means "to trouble" — for Achan "troubled Israel" when he committed his unfaithfulness.
H3756H.origine: The name Carmi literally means "my vine" or "my vineyard" in Hebrew, composed of two elements: "karm" (vineyard) and the possessive suffix "i" (my). It is a name that evokes the abundance and fertility of the soil of Canaan. Several men bear this name in the Old Testament: a son of Reuben is also called Carmi, and this name appears in various genealogies of Israel.
H3756H.emploi: Carmi is mentioned three times in the Bible, all during the conquest of Canaan under Joshua. His name first appears in Joshua 7:1, where it is learned that his son Achan violated the divine prohibition by taking things devoted to the Lord. In Joshua 7:18, during the casting of lots to identify the guilty party, Carmi is named again, as it is through his house and family that Achan was designated. Finally, 1 Chronicles 2:7 records this same genealogy in a chronological recap, confirming Carmi's place as the father of Achan "who troubled Israel." His name remains attached to the infraction committed by his son.
H3756H.portee: The story of Carmi and especially that of his son Achan reminds the biblical reader that individual sins have communal consequences. Although Carmi himself is not presented as a sinner, his name is forever linked to Achan's transgression, showing how a single act of disobedience can affect an entire family and a whole nation. It is a humble lesson on the seriousness of disobeying God and the seriousness with which God ensures that His people adhere to His commandments.

sens: Son of Judah, ancestor of a lineage in the tribe of Judah
H3756I.detail: 1. Carmi is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Judah. He is presented in 1 Chronicles 4:1 as one of the sons of Judah, alongside Perez, Hezron, Hur, and Shobal. His name appears among the direct ancestors of Israel and marks a particular branch of the Judean lineage.
H3756I.origine: The name Carmi literally means "my vine" or "my vineyard" in Hebrew, composed of "kar" (vine) and the suffix "mi" (my). This image evokes fertility and fruitfulness, important values in the genealogy of Israel.
H3756I.emploi: Carmi is mentioned only once in the Bible in 1 Chronicles 4:1, where he is cited among the direct sons of Judah. He represents an important genealogical branch of the tribe of Judah, although few additional details are provided about his personal life or direct descendants in the biblical passage that has been transmitted to us.

sens: Descendant of Carmi, son of Reuben
H3757.detail: 1. The Carmites are the descendants of Carmi, who was one of the four sons of Reuben (the first son of Jacob and Leah). Carmi lived during the time of the Exodus from Egypt and the wilderness. In Numbers 26:6, during the census of the Israelite tribes in the wilderness, the families descended from Reuben are listed, including that of the Carmites, who bore the name of their ancestor.
H3757.origine: The name Carmite comes from Carmi, whose name means "my vine" in Hebrew — an image of fertility and blessing. Carmi is first mentioned in Genesis 46:9 among the sons of Reuben who went down to Egypt with Jacob. The Carmites thus form one of the branches of the tribe of Reuben.
H3757.emploi: The term "Carmites" appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:6, during the census of the Israelites at the end of the wilderness. At that time, Moses orders the counting of men by family, and it is recorded that Carmi fathered the family of the Carmites. It is a simple act of genealogical enumeration without a particular narrative attached to this clan.

sens: Bright red or dark purple color obtained by dyeing
Fabric or garment dyed this color
Symbol of wealth and royal or sacred splendor
H3758.detail:
1. Crimson is a bright red color, sometimes leaning towards purple, obtained by dyeing with precious dyes — notably cochineal or purple. It is a brilliant and durable hue, very difficult to produce. In 2 Chronicles 2:7, King Solomon requests fabric "dyed in purple, crimson, and blue" for the temple work, which shows that it is a color of choice, costly and prestigious.
2. The word refers not only to the color itself but also to the fabrics or garments dyed crimson. In 2 Chronicles 2:14, the skill of the master craftsman Huram-Abi is mentioned "in fine linen and crimson fabrics" — the fabric itself, worked by high-level artisans.
3. In the context of the temple and its sacred ornaments, crimson symbolizes wealth, majesty, and holiness. In 2 Chronicles 3:14, the temple veil is made "of blue, purple, and crimson, and fine linen," royal colors that reflect the glory of God.
