H3758.origine: The Hebrew word כַּרְמִיל (karmil) likely designates a shade obtained from an insect or a dye plant (probably a kermes worm or a Mediterranean cochineal). Its origin may be linked to the Hebrew כֶּרֶם (kerem, "vine"), as some dyes came from grapevines, or it reflects a borrowing from a neighboring language associated with the regions where this dye was produced and traded, such as Phoenicia.
H3758.emploi: The word crimson appears three times in the Bible, all in the accounts of the temple works of Solomon (2 Chronicles 2 and 3). It is associated with precious fabrics, ordered for the decoration and equipment of the sanctuary. Each occurrence underscores the luxurious and refined nature of the materials used: in 2 Chronicles 2:7, Solomon requests artisans capable of working with crimson fabrics; in 2 Chronicles 2:14, Huram-Abi is presented as a master in this technique; in 2 Chronicles 3:14, the temple veil itself is combined with blue and purple. Crimson always appears alongside other precious dyes (blue, purple) and noble materials (fine linen, gold), never alone.
H3758.portee: For the Christian reader, crimson in these passages reveals the importance that God placed on the beauty and splendor of the temple, the earthly house of His presence. The bright colors and refined materials are not vanity, but a concrete expression of the honor given to God. This detail reminds us that the excellent quality of things that serve God is not contrary to piety: it manifests it.

sens: Land planted with fruit trees and productive crops
Fruit or harvest from the orchard
Fertility and abundance of the land
Beauty and richness of a region
Image of prosperity and divine blessing
H3759.detail: 1. An orchard is a cultivated area where fruit trees and various crops grow — olive trees, fig trees, pomegranate trees. It is a fertile land, carefully tended, that produces its fruits (Jeremiah 2:7: "I brought you into a land like an orchard"). 2. The word also refers to the fruit itself or the harvest: the "new ears" and sheaves from the orchard that were offered to the Lord (Leviticus 2:14; 2 Kings 4:42). 3. The orchard represents the fertility of the soil, its ability to nourish — often contrasted with the desert or barrenness. Isaiah 32:16 places righteousness and justice "in the orchard," symbolizing a land that lives and prospers. 4. By extension, an orchard can describe the beauty and richness of an entire region: Isaiah 29:17 imagines Lebanon transforming into an "orchard," expressing its future beautification. 5. In biblical language, the orchard becomes the image of divine blessing — God's promise to His people of a fertile and generous land to dwell in.
H3759.origine: The Hebrew word karmel comes from a root meaning "high, fertile" or "prosperous": the orchard is not just any field, but a rich and well-cultivated land. This same root appears in the proper name "Mount Carmel" (the Mountain of the Orchard), a symbol of fertility. The paronymy with the fruit of carme — or rather the idea of generous production — emphasizes that the orchard is primarily a land that bears, that gives, that nourishes.
H3759.emploi: The word karmel appears fifteen times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the prophets. It primarily designates the concrete orchard: royal estates (2 Chronicles 26:10), plantations that are cultivated and harvested (2 Kings 4:42, Leviticus 2:14). But the Bible often uses it figuratively to speak of the land of Israel as an orchard — a pledge of the covenant and blessing. Isaiah and Jeremiah use it this way: "I brought you into a land like an orchard" (Jeremiah 2:7), or: "Lebanon will become an orchard" (Isaiah 29:17). When the Lord threatens to devastate the land, it is precisely this orchard that He consumes: "The splendor of its forest and its fields" (Isaiah 10:18). The orchard thus becomes both a material reality and a symbol of the covenant — what God promises His people when they obey Him.
H3759.portee: For the believer, the orchard reminds us that God does not only promise spiritual salvation: He also promises an abundant life, a fertile land, concrete abundance. The orchard invites us to see God's blessing in simple things — the fruit, the harvest, the nourishing land. But it is also a warning: whoever defiles this orchard, who transforms it into an abomination, loses the blessing. The orchard speaks of responsibility — God entrusts us with a land to cultivate, not to ravage.

sens: Mountain town in the southwest of the Promised Land
Fertile region known for its beauty and greenery
H3760G.detail:
1. Carmel is a fortified town in the mountains of Judah, located south of Hebron and overlooking the region of Maon. It is where Nabal, a wealthy owner of flocks, lived, and David came there during the sheep shearing (1 Samuel 25:2).
2. Figuratively, Carmel symbolizes the beauty and splendor of nature. The Bible invokes it as an image of magnificence: the head of the beloved in the Song of Songs is compared to Carmel for its grace (Song of Songs 7:6), and the prophet Isaiah speaks of the glory of Carmel alongside that of Lebanon to describe future restoration (Isaiah 35:2).
H3760G.origine: The name means "fertile garden" or "cultivated land" in Hebrew, evoking the abundance of this mountainous region. Carmel was known for its vineyards, olive groves, and rich pastures, which is why it is used by poets and prophets as a symbol of fertility and natural beauty.
H3760G.emploi: Carmel appears seventeen times in the Hebrew Bible. It is primarily a real town, an economic center for the flocks of King Saul and the wealthy Nabal (1 Samuel 15:12; 25:2-7, 40). Within the boundaries of the tribes (Joshua 12:22; 19:26), it marks the geography of Judah. But it becomes especially a poetic image: the prophets invoke it to evoke the splendor of divine creation (Isaiah 33:9; 35:2; Jeremiah 46:18; 50:19) or to symbolize what can be dried up or restored (Amos 1:2; Nahum 1:4). It thus embodies both a concrete place and a figure of divine magnificence.

sens: mountain on the Mediterranean coast of northern Israel, near Haifa
residence of the prophet Elisha
site of the great confrontation between Elijah and the prophets of Baal
H3760H.detail: Carmel is a mountain that rises on the northern coast of Israel, overlooking the Mediterranean. Its name means "land of garden" or "fertile land," as this region was lush and productive. It is in this major natural setting that the most spectacular spiritual events of the New Testament take place: in 1 Kings 18, the prophet Elijah gathers all Israel with the four hundred fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of Asherah for a decisive prophetic duel. After this confrontation where God consumes Elijah's sacrifice by fire from heaven, the prophet goes up to the top of Carmel to pray and fast, with his face between his knees (1 Kings 18:42). Carmel also becomes the dwelling place of the prophet Elisha: the Shunammite woman goes there to meet him when her son dies (2 Kings 4:25), and the prophet regularly stays there before heading to Samaria (2 Kings 2:25).
H3760H.origine: The Hebrew name קַרְמֶל literally means "garden" or "orchard" (karmel comes from a root that evokes the idea of cultivating, of fertility). The mountain bears this name due to its lush vegetation and agricultural richness, which distinguished it from the surrounding drier regions. It is a real biblical geography, well attested in the history of ancient Palestine.
H3760H.emploi: Carmel appears five times in the books of Kings, exclusively in chapters 18-19 and 2-4 of 1 and 2 Kings. These uses focus around two major prophetic figures: first Elijah, who summons all Israel there for divine judgment against the idolatrous prophets (1 Kings 18:19-20), then remains there to intercede after the victory (1 Kings 18:42); and then Elisha, who lives there and receives the visit of the Shunammite woman (2 Kings 2:25; 4:25). Carmel is thus the scene of the greatest acts of divine power and prophetic intercession of that time.
H3760H.portee: Carmel reminds us that God reveals Himself in concrete and visible places. It is a mountain where heaven descends to earth: the fire of the Lord consumes the sacrifice when the whole sky seemed closed. For the believer, this place teaches that God answers authentic prayers and delivers those who seek Him from the idols that distract them. It is also a refuge where the prophet can withdraw to intercede, a space where the word of God is visibly fulfilled.

sens: inhabitant de Carmel, ville du territoire de Juda
H3761.detail: Carmel was a city in the territory of Judah, located in the hill country of Judea. The word refers to a person from this city. In the Bible, it is best known through Nabal, a wealthy owner from Carmel, and his wife Abigail, whom David will marry after Nabal's death (1 Samuel 27:3). Abigail, referred to as "Abigail of Carmel," also appears among the mothers of David's sons born in Hebron (1 Chronicles 3:1), and a warrior named Hetsraï is also from Carmel (2 Samuel 23:35).
H3761.origine: The word comes from Carmel, whose Hebrew name literally means "garden" or "fertile land" (from kar, "garden"). This etymology evokes the cultivated and fertile lands of this region of Judea. The adjective "Carmelite" (or "Carmeli") simply designates someone from or a resident of this place, according to common usage in the Bible to form names of peoples or people from a region.
H3761.emploi: Carmel appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate someone from the city of Carmel. The most important references concern Abigail: wife of Nabal from Carmel, she later becomes one of David's wives and mother of several of his sons (1 Samuel 27:3; 30:5; 2 Samuel 2:2; 2 Samuel 3:3; 1 Chronicles 3:1). She illustrates the life of a well-to-do woman from this region. The word also appears for a warrior of David named Hetsraï (2 Samuel 23:35), confirming that Carmel was a place of some importance. All uses locate Carmel in Judea, in a royal context.

sens: Fils de Dischon, personnage de l'époque patriarcale
H3763.detail: Kéran is a man living in the time of the Patriarchs, son of Dishon and brother of Hemdan, Eschban, and Jithran. He was a Horite Edomite, meaning a member of a population that lived in the region of Edom before the Edomites themselves. He is mentioned in two genealogical lists: that of Genesis 36:26 and that of 1 Chronicles 1:41, which correspond almost word for word.
H3763.origine: The name Kéran (Hebrew כְּרָן) means "lyre" in Hebrew. It was a musical instrument known in the ancient Near East. The name likely reflects a characteristic or skill of this ancestor, although specific details elude us.
H3763.emploi: Kéran appears only twice in the Bible, both in genealogical lists: in Genesis 36:26, where he is listed among the sons of Dishon, and in 1 Chronicles 1:41, where the same genealogy is repeated with a slight spelling variation (Hamran instead of Hemdan). These genealogies of the Horite Edomites place Kéran among the ancestors of the pre-Edomite population, with no particular narrative concerning him.

sens: Siège royal où s'assoit le roi ou un souverain
Pouvoir royal, autorité souveraine
Demeure céleste ou divine
H3764.detail: 1. The throne is primarily the physical seat, the royal furniture where the king sits to exercise his power: it is a seat of honor and majesty. In Daniel 5:20, Nebuchadnezzar is "cast down from his royal throne," which means he loses not only his seat but his position as king. 2. The throne also represents royal power and authority themselves: to possess a throne is to reign. When it is said that one is "sitting on a throne," it refers to governing with power. 3. In a heavenly vision, the throne symbolizes the seat of God or a divine being: in Daniel 7:9, the throne of the Ancient of Days is described with flames of fire and burning wheels, showing divine majesty and power rather than just a piece of furniture.
H3764.origine: The Aramaic word "korsa" (כׇּרְסֵא) comes from the Hebrew "kissi" (כִּסֵּא), both meaning literally the seat or royal chair. It is an ancient word from the Semitic world, used throughout the Middle East to denote the symbol of royal power. The root evokes the idea of sitting, being established in a position of authority.
H3764.emploi: This Aramaic word appears twice in the Book of Daniel, in chapters 5 and 7, two key passages of prophecy. In Daniel 5:20, it refers to the royal throne of Nebuchadnezzar, which the king loses due to his pride: it is the throne of an earthly king. In Daniel 7:9, the word appears twice: first in the plural (“thrones”), then it designates the majestic throne of the Ancient of Days, clothed in white and seated in a heavenly vision. This passage elevates the word from the political and human realm to the divine and eternal realm.
H3764.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that all human power, even the greatest, is fragile and subject to God's judgment. But it also announces that God alone possesses the true and eternal throne, majestic and unshakeable. The vision in Daniel 7 prepares the way for the coming of the Son of Man and His eternal reign.

sens: To bend the knees, to kneel down
To lie down, to collapse, to fall
To yield, to be defeated or dominated
To bow in respect or worship
H3766.detail:
1. To kneel literally means to bend one's knees to kneel down: it is the physical gesture of one who lowers the body. In Judges 7:6, the warriors "kneeled down to drink" at the spring, their bodies bent. In 2 Chronicles 29:29, after the sacrifice, "the king and all those who were with him knelt down and worshiped."
2. The word also describes the collapse or weakening of the body. In Job 4:4, it speaks of "knees that were bending," an image of weakness and failure. It is the state of one who is losing strength.
3. To kneel expresses defeat or submission: being forced to bend the knee is to acknowledge a domination. In Psalms 18:40, the psalmist sings that God "makes my adversaries kneel before me," forcing them to submit.
4. Finally, it is the gesture of reverence and worship towards God or a king. In Isaiah 45:23, God says: "Every knee shall bow before me," expressing the universal homage rendered to Him.
H3766.origine: The Hebrew root כָּרַע (karaʿ) fundamentally means "to bend, to bow." It is related to the image of the body bending, the knees bowing under weight or emotion. The word belongs to a family of expressions of movement and posture: to bend, to bow, to collapse. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this verb is always used to describe an action of the body changing position, from the simplest (to kneel) to the most significant (to submit or worship).
H3766.emploi: The verb "to kneel" appears 32 times in the Old Testament. It is found mainly in the Psalms and the Kings, as well as in historical accounts (Judges, Samuel) and the prophets (Isaiah). It first describes everyday gestures: kneeling to drink, to rest. Then it takes on a military sense: to be defeated, to be forced to submit under an enemy (Psalms 18:40; Isaiah 46:1-2). Finally, it expresses worship and obedience towards God: bending the knee in prayer or respect (1 Kings 8:54; Isaiah 45:23). The context transforms the physical gesture into a spiritual act.
H3766.portee: This word teaches that true strength consists in willingly bowing before God. To kneel is not primarily a humiliation: it is the proper gesture of the believer who recognizes that God is Lord. God Himself calls all nations to bow the knee before Him (Isaiah 45:23). It is also an invitation to prayer: to kneel is to physically and spiritually place oneself in the attitude of one who depends on God and seeks His help.

sens: The part of the animal's body from the knee to the foot
Part of the sacrificial victim intended to be burned on the altar
H3767.detail:
1. The word refers to the leg of an animal, that is, the part of its limb that goes from the knee to the foot. In sacrificial texts, the legs are mentioned alongside the head, the entrails, and the other parts of the offered animal. In Exodus 12:9, during the Passover, the lamb must be eaten whole "with the head, the legs, and the inner parts," which shows that the legs are a distinct and important part of the animal.
2. In worship, the legs of the sacrificed animal are part of what is presented to God. In Leviticus 1:9, the priest "washes the entrails and the legs" before burning them all on the altar as a burnt offering. This law applies to burnt offerings of cattle and birds: this part of the body is purified before being consumed, as with the other parts. It is an act of respect towards what is offered to the Lord.
H3767.origine: The Hebrew word כֶּרַע (kéra') comes from a root that fundamentally means "the leg" or "the limb" — the part that carries and makes the animal walk. It primarily designates the physical organ, and it is in this simple sense that it appears in the sacrificial codes of the Torah. It is a word from the everyday vocabulary of herders and butchers, without hidden nuance.
H3767.emploi: The word appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the laws concerning sacrifices (Exodus, Leviticus). It appears each time there is a need to enumerate the parts of the animal to be offered or eaten: in Exodus 12:9 (Passover), in Exodus 29:17 (consecration of the priests), and especially in the descriptions of burnt offerings in Leviticus 1, 4, 8, and 9, where the legs must be washed before burning. It is also found in Leviticus 11:21 (clean animals to eat) and in Amos 3:12 (poetic image). Each time, it refers to a specific and material part of the animal, never in a figurative sense.
H3767.portee: For the believer reading the Torah, this word reminds that God does not accept sacrifices lightly or in any manner: each part of the victim must be treated with respect, washed, and prepared according to His prescriptions. It is a detail that speaks of order, holiness, and obedience in worship. It taught Israel that serving God requires careful attention, from the heart to concrete actions.

sens: white or dyed fabric, very fine and soft, imported or made in the East
curtain or drapery of this fabric, in delicate colors
H3768.detail:
1. Karpas refers to a precious, very fine and delicate fabric, probably high-quality cotton or linen. It is a rare and expensive cloth, coming from afar — from the Eastern world — and symbolizes luxury. In Esther 1:6, King Ahasuerus adorns the palace of Susa with curtains of white, green, and blue karpas, attached to purple cords: it is a mark of his power and immense wealth.
2. By extension, the word also refers to the curtains or draperies themselves, which hang gracefully and create the beauty of royal rooms. This fine drapery creates an atmosphere of luxury and delicacy, contrasting with massive materials like marble and gold: it soothes the whole, making it livable and harmonious.
H3768.origine: The word karpas likely comes from a root related to fabrics or textiles. Its use in Esther, unique in the Hebrew Bible, shows that it is a specialized term, perhaps borrowed from Persian or other Near Eastern languages, which well reflects the context of the narrative — the royal Persia, far from Israel. It is a word that evokes a refined and foreign world.
H3768.emploi: Karpas appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Esther 1:6. It describes the draperies that adorn the palace of King Ahasuerus in Susa during the great banquet held in the sixth year of his reign. These draperies of various colors (white, green, blue) are associated with other signs of extreme wealth: purple cords, silver rings, marble columns, gold and silver beds. The context emphasizes the unimaginable splendor of the Persian court, and karpas plays the role of a noble fabric that adds to this unparalleled magnificence.
H3768.portee: This word invites the reader to contemplate the beauty and refinement of this royal world, while placing it in perspective: this magnificence of the palace of Susa, with its delicate draperies, is the backdrop of the story where God acts hidden to save His people. It is a subtle reminder that even in the courts of foreign kings, divine providence is at work.

sens: To move with jumps and spins, rhythmically or freely, under the influence of joy or to honor a deity.
To express joy and gladness through bodily movements.
H3769.detail:
1. To dance is to execute movements of the body, jumps, and spins, generally in rhythm. It is a visible and spectacular physical action. David danced "with all his might" before the Lord (2 Samuel 6:14), which shows that he put all his energy and body into this gesture.
2. In the Bible, dancing expresses overflowing joy and gladness in response to God's actions. It is also an act of worship and honor towards the Lord. When David danced upon seeing the Ark of the Lord enter Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:16), he was manifesting his religious exultation and devotion to the God of Israel.
H3769.origine: The Hebrew verb kârar belongs to a family of words evoking the idea of spinning and whirling. The form used here (Pilpel) intensifies the action: it describes not just a simple movement, but repeated, swirling, and energetic movements. It is the image of a person turning around and jumping vigorously.
H3769.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both occurrences in the same passage: David's dance during the ascent of the Ark to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:14 and 6:16). These two verses show that David did not dance discreetly, but with such strength and exuberance that it became a public spectacle, visible from afar. Michal, David's wife, saw him dancing from the window and despised him. This act of dancing, although extraordinary, reveals David's joyful and worshipful heart in the presence of God.
H3769.portee: This dance reminds us that the joy in the believer's heart can and should be expressed freely before God. David was not afraid to make a spectacle of himself to honor the Lord; it is a call to abandon false dignity and pride to rejoice freely in the divine presence and action. Michal's contemptuous reaction shows that the world may criticize those who openly express their faith, but that should not deter us.

sens: The inner part of the body, between the chest and the thighs
(figurative) The capacity to contain, to devour
(figurative) The seat of desires and covetousness
H3770.detail:
1. The belly is the cavity of the body that contains the organs and digests food. It is the physical seat of appetite and hunger. In Jeremiah 51:34, the king of Babylon, compared to a dragon, fills his belly with all that he has plundered — the image evokes an insatiable predator that devours its prey.
2. By extension, the belly represents a capacity to engulf, absorb, devour. The dragon fills its belly as one fills a container: it is the idea of swallowing, engulfing, devouring conquest.
3. Spiritually, the belly symbolizes carnal desires, the appetite for power and wealth. The text illustrates this well: Babylon, personified as a woman, sees the king fill his belly with her precious treasures — it is the expression of limitless covetousness.
H3770.origine: The Hebrew word כְּרֵשׂ (kérès) literally means "belly." It comes from a root that expresses the idea of hollow, cavity. The word belongs to the lexical field of the human body. In Jeremiah 51:34, it is used figuratively to describe the dragon (Babylon) that devours without limit.
H3770.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible at this lemma. It is found in Jeremiah 51:34, where Jeremiah depicts the Lord speaking to oppressed Jerusalem. The king of Babylon (Nebuchadnezzar) is compared to a dragon that devours the city and empties it of its riches by filling his belly. The image is that of a wild and insatiable beast, which intensifies the horror of conquest and foreign domination.
H3770.portee: This word reminds us that covetousness, symbolized by a belly to fill without limit, is a destructive force. It devours peoples and strips them bare. For the believer, it warns against greed and pride: filling one's belly with ill-gotten wealth is an act of violent injustice that attracts God's judgment.

sens: one of the seven princes of Persia and Media serving King Ahasuerus
H3771.detail: Carchena is one of the seven great princes of the kingdom of Persia and Media under the reign of King Ahasuerus. These seven men had the privilege of seeing the king face to face and held the highest offices in the kingdom (Esther 1:14). His name, in the Persian language, means "illustrious" or "distinguished."
H3771.origine: The name Carchena is of Persian origin. Its etymology suggests the root kara-, meaning "eminent" or "illustrious," which reflects the high rank and distinction of the bearer in the Persian royal hierarchy.
H3771.emploi: Carchena appears only once in the Bible, in Esther 1:14. He is listed among the seven most important princes of Persia and Media, those who had direct access to King Ahasuerus and played influential advisory roles within the empire. His name is mentioned alongside Shethar, Admatha, Tarsus, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan.

sens: To slice, separate with a sharp instrument
To fell a tree
To remove a part of the body
To destroy, annihilate
To make a covenant
H3772G.detail:
1. To slice, separate with a sharp instrument: this is the most basic meaning. One cuts wood, one cuts a rope, one divides something in two (Jeremiah 10:3: "They cut wood in the forest").
2. To fell a tree: a concrete application of the previous meaning, but significant enough in the Bible to deserve its place. Deuteronomy 20:20 speaks of the permission to "cut down" non-fruit trees to build siege machines.
3. To remove a part of the body: to cut also means to mutilate or amputate. Exodus 4:25 describes Zipporah who "cuts" her son's foreskin with a stone; 2 Kings 18:4 speaks of statues that were "cut down" (to cut them is also to destroy idols).
4. To destroy, annihilate: the meaning extends to the total destruction of something or someone. When God threatens to "cut off" a people or a generation, He means to exterminate them.
5. To make a covenant: a figurative meaning specific to the Hebrew Bible. "To cut a covenant" means to make it, to conclude it — probably because in ancient rites, an animal was cut in two and one passed between the two halves (Jeremiah 34:18).
H3772G.origine: The Hebrew verb כָּרַת comes from a root that expresses the action of cutting, dividing. It is found in both main forms of the Hebrew Bible: the simple form (Qal) for "to cut," and derived forms for "to have someone cut" (Hiphil) or "to be cut" (Niphal). The starting image is purely mechanical: the blade that slices. The figurative meaning of "covenant" developed by association with ancient Near Eastern rites.
H3772G.emploi: The verb כָּרַת appears about 50 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives and the prophets. It first denotes concrete and violent acts: Zipporah cuts her son's foreskin (Exodus 4:25), kings have trees felled (Deuteronomy 20:20) or idols cut down (2 Kings 18:4). In religious contexts, it takes on the meaning of "to make a covenant" with God or with a king, which was a solemn and irrevocable act (Jeremiah 34:18). The Niphal (passive form) means "to be cut off," particularly in divine threats of destruction. The word always carries an idea of separation, rupture, or definitive end.
H3772G.portee: For the believer, this verb reminds us that God acts with power and decisiveness: His covenants are unshakeable, His threats of judgment are real. The idea of "cutting a covenant" shows that God commits irrevocably to His people, which is both reassuring and demanding. It is strong language that invites us to take God's word seriously.

sens: To cut, to sever, to section a body or an object
To kill, to cause to perish, to destroy
To annihilate, to erase, to make disappear
To conclude a pact or a covenant (the dominant meaning in biblical usage)
To negotiate, to agree with someone on a deal
H3772H.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to cut, to sever. For example, in Job 40:23, the Leviathan "cuts" the reeds, meaning it removes them from the ground.

2. The verb also denotes the action of killing or destroying someone: "you shall utterly destroy them" in Deuteronomy 7:2 means to eliminate them completely.

3. It expresses annihilation, the total erasure of something: to be "cut off" from the people (Exodus 12:15) means to disappear, to be eliminated.

4. The most important meaning in the Bible is "to conclude a covenant." This expression comes from an ancient practice: to confirm a pact, an animal was cut in two and the parties would walk between the two halves. Genesis 15:18: "The Lord made a covenant with Abram," and in 2 Kings 11:4: Jehoiada "made a covenant with them."

5. More broadly, "to negotiate" a covenant means to establish it, to formally conclude it with someone. In 1 Samuel 11:1, the inhabitants of Jabesh ask Nahash: "Make a covenant with us"—that is, conclude an agreement.
H3772H.origine: The root denotes the action of cutting. The connection with "covenant" comes from an ancient gesture well attested in the Near East: to validate a solemn contract, an animal was cut, and the parties would commit their word by passing between the pieces. This is why "to cut a covenant" means to conclude it irrevocably: one "cuts" to establish something lasting. The secondary forms of the verb (passive, causative) express the result: to be cut off, to cause to be cut off.
H3772H.emploi: This verb appears 87 times in biblical Hebrew, very often with the meaning of "covenant." In the Pentateuch and the historical books, the expression "to make a covenant" or "to negotiate a covenant" predominates: God "makes" a covenant with Abram (Genesis 15:18), Moses reminds of the covenant "made" at Sinai (Deuteronomy 5:2), the people "make a covenant" with their kings (2 Samuel 5:3, 1 Chronicles 11:3). In Deuteronomy 7:2, the people must not "make a covenant" with the pagan nations. The prophetic books also use this language: Jeremiah recalls that God had "made a covenant" with the fathers (Jeremiah 31:31-33). The usage regularly retains the meaning of "to cut, to sever, to destroy" when the context requires it (Job 40:23, Isaiah 28:15).
H3772H.portee: This word reveals that the covenant is not a mere verbal agreement, but a solemn, almost sacramental commitment. God "cuts a covenant" with Abraham, not lightly, but by irrevocably committing Himself. For the believer, this emphasizes that God's relationship with His people is based on a definitive word and gesture. It is also a call to faithfulness: if God "cuts" a covenant, His commitment is firm; the one who "negotiates" it binds themselves seriously.

sens: To cut, to sever, to make a clean cut
To cut someone off from their people, to eliminate them from the community
To completely destroy a people, a nation
To conclude a covenant by cutting an animal in two
H3772I.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very concrete: to cut with a sharp object. Literally, this can mean to cut a part of the body or to slice something into pieces (like David who cuts off Goliath's head in 1 Samuel 17:51).
2. In religious and legal contexts, "to cut off" means to exclude someone from the community of Israel or from their people—a serious penalty that God inflicts on those who violate the commandments (Leviticus 20:17: the offenders will be "cut off").
3. On a larger scale, the word denotes the complete elimination of a nation or people through war or by the hand of God (Amos 1:5: "I will exterminate the inhabitants of Bikath-Aven").
4. The word is also used for "to conclude a covenant": an animal is cut in two and the contracting parties pass between the pieces, as a symbol of solemn commitment (Genesis 15 and similar passages evoke this practice).
H3772I.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to cut, to sever." The same root produces words that denote a knife or a sharp object. The basic image—separating by cutting—extends into all usages: cutting off a limb, severing a life (to kill), cutting off from the social group, or even "to cut" a covenant by solemnly contracting it. It is a common word in the Old Testament, used in various contexts.
H3772I.emploi: The verb appears 134 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the Law, the Psalms, and the prophets. The Segond translates it as "exterminate" (60 times), "cut off" (41 times), or "destroy" depending on the context. In the laws of Moses, "to be cut off" (passive form) is the penalty for various transgressions: eating without ritual purity, violating holy days, eating blood, or committing serious sins (Leviticus 7, 20, 23). In historical narratives and the Psalms, the word describes the destruction of enemies or the elimination of the wicked: God "cuts off" the rebels (Psalms 37:38), or the king overturns the houses of the wicked (Psalms 101:8). The word is also used for solemn covenants: "to cut a covenant" means to formally conclude it.
H3772I.portee: This word reminds us that breaking with God has serious and visible consequences: to be cut off from the people is to lose one's connection with the community and divine blessings. For the reader, this serves as a warning: disobedience is not merely a matter of feelings, but of actions that separate from God and His people. Conversely, when God "cuts off" the enemy or the wicked, it is because He protects His covenant and His people. Finally, "to cut a covenant" shows that commitments before God are solid and definitive—a picture of the firmness of the divine pact.

sens: To be cut off, removed, eliminated
To be absent, not exist, be missing
To cease to exist, disappear completely
H3772J.detail:
1. The primary and concrete meaning of the word is that of a cut, a separation: something or someone is cut off, eliminated. It is the image of what is severed and cannot return. In 2 Samuel 3:29, the curse wishes that someone in the house of Joab "lacks" bread, meaning they do not have it — the bread is absent from them.

2. By extension, the word means "to be absent" or "to be missing": a thing or a person is lacking when it is not where it should be. When King David receives the promise "You will never lack a successor on the throne of Israel" (1 Kings 2:4, 8:25, 9:5), it means that a son will always continue to reign: there will never be a break, never a void on the throne.

3. The word also expresses the idea of disappearance or definitive interruption: what is lacking will not reappear. In 1 Kings 18:5, during the drought, the king fears he will have to "slaughter livestock" due to lack of grass — in the absence of food, he will have to resort to extremes. It is the total absence that forces one to act differently.
H3772J.origine: The Hebrew word כָּרַת (karath) comes from a very ancient root meaning "to cut, to sever." This image of cutting has expanded to denote everything that is removed, cut off, or lacking. The word has several verbal forms depending on the meaning: the simple form (Qal) expresses the action of cutting, while the passive form (Niphal) designates the one who is cut off or who disappears. It is a concrete word at first — one cuts a branch, one severs a rope — which gradually becomes more abstract: one "cuts" a covenant (that is, one concludes it by sacrificing), one "cuts" a life (one ends it), or simply something "is lacking."
H3772J.emploi: This verb appears about ten times in the provided passages, mainly in the royal and prophetic books. The most recurring context is the dynastic promise: God promises David and his descendants that they will "never lack" a successor on the throne (1 Kings 2:4, 8:25, 9:5; 2 Chronicles 6:16, 7:18; Jeremiah 33:17, 33:18, 35:19). This repeated promise shows that the word here carries major theological significance: it guarantees the continuity of the dynasty. In other cases, such as in 1 Kings 18:5, the word has a simpler meaning: to have a "need" for something means that this thing is lacking and that one must do without it. In 2 Samuel 3:29, the curse pronounced on the house of Joab wishes that bread "lacks," meaning there is famine.
H3772J.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reveals two important truths. First, the promise that God never "fails" to keep His word: His commitment holds, even over several generations. Second, the word invites trust: when God promises that something will not be lacking, it is an absolute guarantee. This certainty strengthens faith in God's faithfulness. It is a word of stability and assurance in an unstable world.

sens: Large piece of wood, long and thick, used as support in construction
Structural element resting on columns or walls
H3773.detail: 1. A beam is a large piece of worked wood (shaped, squared) used as a load-bearing element in buildings. In the three instances where this word appears, the image is clear: cedar beams laid out in regular rows in the monumental structures of King Solomon, forming an impressive decor due to their precious material and size. In 1 Kings 7:2, the cedar beams rest directly on the cedar columns, showing their structural role: they span the space and bear the weight of the building. 2. The word also describes the orderly arrangement of these beams in regular rows. Three times, there is mention of a "row of beams" integrated into a construction sequence (cut stones + beams), creating an alternating and architecturally significant effect. It is the image of a carefully and majestically constructed building, worthy of the royal palace and the wealth of the Kingdom.
H3773.origine: The Hebrew word כָּרֻתָה (karutah) comes from a root meaning "to cut" or "to square." It thus designates a piece of worked wood, prepared by the hand of the craftsman. The cedar of Lebanon, a precious and durable wood, was the material of choice for royal and sacred constructions in Israel. The form of the word indicates a shaped piece, not raw wood.
H3773.emploi: This word appears three times in the First Book of Kings, all in the context of Solomon's constructions (6:36; 7:2; 7:12). It specifically designates the cedar beams that structure the royal buildings: the inner courtyard of the Temple, the House of the Forest of Lebanon, and the portico of the Temple. In each context, the beams form a regular "row," placed between cut stone bases, creating an architectural effect that alternates mineral material and plant material. The word never varies in meaning: it is always a load-bearing piece of wood, never a simple accessory.
H3773.portee: This word reminds the reader of the splendor of Solomon's constructions and the abundance of resources that God had granted to the Kingdom of Israel. The cedar beams symbolize stability, wealth, and the care given to important edifices. For the Christian, it is an invitation to recognize how God concretely blesses His people, not only through spiritual realities but also through durable and magnificent material realities.

sens: Foreign mercenaries serving as bodyguards for King David
Group of foreign warriors executing royal sentences
Coastal people of the region, identified with the Cretans or proto-Philistines
H3774G.detail:
1. The Cherethites formed an elite corps of mercenary soldiers in the service of King David, tasked with personally protecting him (they are also called "executioners" because they carried out royal sentences). This term primarily designates these professional palace warriors.
2. The word can also more broadly refer to foreign warriors who lived as mercenaries or professional soldiers in the region.
3. Some identify them as a coastal people established along the shores of the Mediterranean Sea, either as Cretans (inhabitants of Crete) or as a proto-Philistine group — which would explain why the prophets Ezekiel and Zephaniah mention them alongside the Philistines or the land of Canaan (Ezekiel 25:16, Zephaniah 2:5).
H3774G.origine: The Hebrew word likely comes from an ancient geographical name: the people or region of Chereth, whose exact identity remains debated. The meaning "executioners" is secondary and descriptive of their military function alongside the king. These mercenary soldiers were common in the ancient Near East, hired by kings for their martial loyalty.
H3774G.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In 1 Samuel 30:14, it is encountered in the context of a military incursion in the south of Judah. The other two occurrences (Ezekiel 25:16 and Zephaniah 2:5) show that the prophets rank them among the peoples destined for divine judgment, alongside the Philistines and the coastal inhabitants. This confirms that they are a distinct coastal people, not merely a local military caste.
H3774G.portee: Understanding who the Cherethites are helps to grasp the geopolitical stakes of David's time and the prophets, as well as the mercenary system of royal protection in Israel. This detail also shows how foreign powers and coastal peoples played a strategic role in the history of Israel.

sens: Foreign soldiers forming the personal guard of King David
Elite mercenary warriors in the service of the crown
Group of executioners or shock warriors
Loyal men-at-arms tasked with protecting the king and executing his orders
H3774H.detail:
1. The Kéréthiens are primarily a group of foreign soldiers that David recruits as royal bodyguards. Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, is their chief; along with the Péléthiens (a similar group), they form an elite unit close to the king (2 Samuel 8:18). They accompany him in his movements and military endeavors: when David flees from Absalom, all the Kéréthiens follow him (2 Samuel 15:18).
2. These men are also executors of royal will: during Solomon's succession, the Kéréthiens and the Péléthiens bring him up on the royal mule to lead him to the throne, thus fulfilling King David's order (1 Kings 1:38). They act with the direct authority of the crown.
3. Their very name, which means "executors" or "cutters," evokes their role as determined warriors, ready to strike and fight without hesitation for the king.
H3774H.origine: The Hebrew word kéréthî likely derives from a root meaning "to cut" or "to execute." Some have identified them as Cretans or proto-Philistines recruited by David, which would explain their status as foreign mercenaries. The name reflects their direct and straightforward warrior function before the monarch.
H3774H.emploi: The Kéréthiens appear 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the books of Kings and Samuel, covering the reign of David and the beginning of Solomon's. They form an inseparable pair with the Péléthiens, another elite guard. Benaiah is their responsible officer during the reigns of David and Solomon. They are seen in action during the king's movements (2 Samuel 15:18, 20:7), during official appointments (1 Kings 1:38, 1:44), and they are always mentioned as the most reliable men close to the crown. Their presence underscores the organized military power of the Davidic kingdom.
H3774H.portee: The Kéréthiens remind us that the political power of the king, even a king after God's own heart, relies on concrete military structures and loyal men. They embody loyalty to established authority and the readiness to execute the king's orders. For the reader, they illustrate how God organizes governance through determined men and that the stability of a kingdom depends on reliable leaders and steadfast warriors.

sens: Young sheep, lamb
Animal offered as a sacrifice to the God of Israel
Group of lambs, flock of young sheep
H3775.detail:
1. The lamb is the young of the sheep, a valuable young animal. It is a domesticated creature, easy to raise in the flocks of Israel. Jacob separates his lambs to distinguish them in his flocks (Genesis 30:40).
2. The word also refers to the animal offered as a sacrifice to the Lord. It was a major victim of the Mosaic law: the lamb is presented before the Lord for peace offerings (Leviticus 3:7) or sin offerings (Leviticus 4:35). The law prohibited eating its fat, just like that of the ox or goat (Leviticus 7:23).
3. By extension, the word can also refer to a flock of lambs or the entirety of the young animals in the flock, as when counting livestock (Leviticus 22:19).
H3775.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of riding or mounting — the lamb is the animal that can be easily handled and directed. In the family of Hebrew words, there are related terms for domestic livestock and pastoral life, a central universe of biblical life in the Old Testament.
H3775.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the laws of Moses and the patriarchal narratives. It is primarily used in Leviticus and Numbers to describe the victims of sacrificial worship — always unblemished lambs, often males. It is also found in the pages of worship: the firstborn of the lambs belonged to the Lord and had to be consecrated (Numbers 18:17). In Jacob's narrative (Genesis 30), the lamb is the animal of the small shepherd, the one that is sorted and separated from the flock to follow its genealogy.
H3775.portee: The lamb reminds believers how Israel approached God: through the shed blood of an innocent and unblemished creature. This image of the gentle animal offered in sacrifice anticipates the meaning of Christ's sacrifice, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. It teaches that salvation costs, and that an innocent life is required for atonement.

sens: female animal of the sheep species
passive and vulnerable creature, easy to dominate
sacrificial victim offered for atonement
H3776.detail:
1. The ewe is a female sheep, a domesticated animal raised for its wool and meat. It is among the "small livestock" that could be offered as a sacrifice at the Sanctuary, alongside the goat (Leviticus 5:6).
2. In the Bible, the ewe embodies vulnerability and dependence: it cannot defend itself and needs a shepherd to guide and protect it. This is why it becomes the image of one who submits to the Lord.
3. The ewe is also the quintessential sacrificial animal for atonement of sin. When a man acknowledges his guilt and wants to make peace with God, he brings a ewe to the priest, who offers this victim in his place for his sins to be forgiven (Leviticus 5:6).
H3776.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that designates the ewe, distinct from the ram (male) and the young lambs. In the Old Testament, several terms designate sheep according to age and sex: this specific term applies to the adult female, commonly used for offerings at the Sanctuary.
H3776.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 5:6, in the context of guilt sacrifices. This rarity underscores that biblical Hebrew prefers more general terms to speak of sheep and lambs. The context is one of repentance: the faithful who has committed an offense may present a ewe or a goat at the Sanctuary to obtain atonement.
H3776.portee: This word reminds the believer that the forgiveness of sin comes through sacrifice and that God has provided ways to reconcile with Him. The ewe, a weak and innocent creature offered in place of the guilty, prepares the way to understand Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world.

sens: son of Nahor and Milcah, nephew of Abraham
H3777.detail: Késed is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 22:22. He is the fourth son of Nahor (Abraham's brother) and his wife Milcah. He belongs to the patriarchal generation and represents one of the branches of Abraham's descendants through his uncle.
H3777.origine: The name means "growth" or "increase" in Hebrew. It evokes the idea of growth or multiplication, which corresponds to one of God's great promises to Abraham: that of a numerous offspring. This name reflects the abundance and prosperity promised to the patriarchs.
H3777.emploi: Késed appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 22:22, where he is listed among the sons of Nahor. This enumeration occurs after the sacrifice of Isaac, when Abraham learns of his brother's descendants through a messenger. Like many of the names listed in the patriarchal genealogies, Késed represents an important link in the genealogical chain that connects Abraham to his cousins and the peoples of the ancient Near East.

sens: region of lower Mesopotamia, around Babylon and the Persian Gulf
people living in Chaldea, along the lower Euphrates and Tigris rivers
wise men and diviners renowned for their wisdom and occult arts
H3778.detail:
1. Chaldea is primarily a geographical territory located in lower Mesopotamia, bordering the Persian Gulf. Abraham is originally from there, according to Genesis 11:28: "Haran died in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans." It is the fertile region of the Euphrates and Tigris rivers, where Babylon developed.

2. The Chaldeans are the inhabitants of this territory. From the 7th century BC, they formed a powerful empire that conquered Jerusalem. Jeremiah constantly describes the army of the Chaldeans besieging the city: "Zedekiah, king of Judah, will not escape the Chaldeans" (Jeremiah 32:4). They are the soldiers and generals of the king of Babylon.

3. By extension, the Chaldeans become synonymous with magicians, scholars, and diviners. In Daniel 2:2, the king summons "the magicians, the astrologers, the enchanters, and the Chaldeans" — here the term refers to those who claim to know hidden secrets and interpret dreams. This is the sense of the renowned "wise men," experts in astrology and divination.
H3778.origine: The name comes from a Semitic root meaning "one who cultivates the land" or "one who works the land in clods" — the image of farmers tilling the soil. Historically, the Chaldeans were a semi-nomadic people who gradually settled in southern Mesopotamia. Subsequently, the name designated both the region and its inhabitants, and then, by reputation, the scholars and magicians of these lands. The Hebrew word וַי כַּשְׁדִּים appears in the Old Testament to translate this historical and cultural reality.
H3778.emploi: The word is used 80 times in the Old Testament. Genesis and Job mention it regarding Ur of the Chaldeans, the birthplace of Abraham. From 2 Kings and especially in Jeremiah, the term designates the conquering army that besieges and destroys Jerusalem in 587 BC: it then becomes a political and military term denoting the enemy. The prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel use "Chaldeans" or "Chaldea" to speak of Babylon and its tyrannical power. In the book of Daniel, the Chaldeans are specifically the scholars of the court, the experts in divination and dream interpretation: "the magicians, the astrologers, the enchanters, and the Chaldeans" (Daniel 2:2).
H3778.portee: For the biblical reader, Chaldea embodies both the cradle of faith (Abraham comes out of it at God's call) and the center of earthly power hostile to God (the Babylonian empire that enslaves Judah). The word reminds us that no human wisdom, even that of the greatest scholars, can escape God's judgment. The Chaldeans represent false confidence in worldly knowledge and strength.

sens: Inhabitant of Chaldea, region of southern Mesopotamia
Learned person versed in occult sciences and dream interpretation
H3779.detail:
1. The Chaldeans are the inhabitants of Chaldea, a fertile region located in southern present-day Mesopotamia, between the Euphrates and Tigris rivers, near the Persian Gulf. This people dominated Babylon and constituted a great political and cultural power during the time of the book of Daniel (Daniel 2:5, 2:10).
2. By extension, the term refers to the wise men and scholars of Babylon renowned for their knowledge in astrology, magic, and dream interpretation. King Nebuchadnezzar consults them to explain his dreams: "The Chaldeans answered the king: There is no one on earth who can tell what the king asks" (Daniel 2:10). These men are ranked alongside the magicians and astrologers, as a class of intellectuals and advisors to royal power (Daniel 5:11).
H3779.origine: The Hebrew word כַּשְׁדַּי comes from the name of the region כַּשְׁדִּים (Chaldea), itself derived from a root that evokes the work of the land ("clod-breakers"). This geographical name extended to the inhabitants of the land, and then by metonymy to the wise men and scholars that this renowned civilization produced.
H3779.emploi: The word appears seven times in the book of Daniel, notably in chapters 2, 3, 4, and 5. All occurrences concern the environment of King Nebuchadnezzar's court in Babylon. The Chaldeans hold a position of advisors and interpreters: they are consulted to explain the king's dreams (Daniel 2:5), they are accused if they fail in their task (Daniel 3:8), and they are ranked among the wise men of the kingdom alongside the magicians and astrologers (Daniel 4:7; Daniel 5:7; Daniel 5:11). The biblical context emphasizes their reputation as scholars rather than their simple geographical origin.
H3779.portee: For the reader, the Chaldeans embody the wisdom of the world without God, rich in techniques and appearances of knowledge, but incapable of penetrating the mysteries that only the God of Israel can reveal. Daniel distinguishes himself from these "wise men" by drawing his understanding from prayer and the Spirit of God. This contrast invites the believer to place their trust in divine wisdom rather than in human resources alone.

sens: To reach satiety by eating
To be filled, stuffed to excess with food
H3780.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of eating until completely satisfied, filled. It is the state where the stomach is full and one can eat no more. In Deuteronomy 32:15, Israel became "fat, thick, and sleek": the people, nourished abundantly by God, reached a satiety that made them proud and turned them away from their Creator.
2. Figuratively, the word also evokes a moral satiety: to be filled, gorged to the point of forgetting where this wealth comes from. The image of the animal becoming fat from abundance symbolizes here the forgetfulness of God and ingratitude.
H3780.origine: The Hebrew verb כָּשַׂה comes from a root expressing the idea of growing fat, of becoming plump. The word literally denotes the physical result of abundant eating: the body thickening. This root evokes the herd animal that becomes fat in pasture, a common image in the Bible to describe prosperity and sometimes the pride it can engender.
H3780.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 32:15, in the song of Moses. There, Moses reproaches Israel for having forgotten God precisely at the time of their abundance: nourished and enriched by the Lord, the people became "fat" and rebelled. This context underscores how material satiety can lead to pride and distance from the Creator. The unique usage gives this word a strong symbolic significance in this warning song.
H3780.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the spiritual danger of prosperity. When God fulfills our needs and enriches us, it is easy to forget that these goods come from Him and to fall into pride. The text calls us to remain humble and faithful to God, even —especially— in abundance, and to recognize that true blessing depends on our obedience and gratitude.

sens: cutting tool with a wide blade and a handle, used for splitting wood or striking
H3781.detail: 1. The axe is a tool for work or combat, consisting of a sharp and wide blade fixed to a handle. In Psalm 74:6, it is among the instruments of destruction used to break the sculptures of the temple: the enemies "have broken all the carved work with axes and hammers," which shows the brute force and violence of the desecration.
H3781.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the action of cutting or splitting. The axe is an ancient tool, a symbol of power and destruction in biblical texts, used both by lumberjacks and warriors.
H3781.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 74, in a context of sacrilegious destruction. The psalmist describes the invasion of the temple of Jerusalem by enemies who demolish the sacred artwork, highlighting the gravity of the desecration: the axe, a tool of ordinary violence, becomes the symbol of the outrage done to God.
H3781.portee: This passage reminds us that the enemies of God's people do not respect His sanctuaries or His spiritual treasures. The mention of the axe invites the reader to see in the material destruction of the temple a wound inflicted on the communion with God Himself.

sens: To trip, lose balance while walking
To fall, be overturned
To be weak, weakened, to wither
To be defeated, succumb
To cause someone to stumble, ruin or thwart them
H3782.detail:
1. To stumble or lose footing while walking: this is the basic physical image of a person whose legs give way (Leviticus 26:37, where the Israelites "will stumble over one another").
2. To actually fall, be overturned: the transition from stumbling to actual falling, as in Jeremiah 46:6, where soldiers "stumble" and then "fall."
3. To be weakened, exhausted, without strength: when speaking of a person who is withering or losing strength, their life is draining away (Psalms 31:11, "my strength is gone").
4. To succumb, be defeated, not resist: this is the moral or warrior image, that of an opponent who cannot stand firm (Proverbs 24:17, the enemy "stumbles," meaning they falter).
5. To cause to stumble, bring someone down, ruin them: when God or an enemy overturns someone, puts them to flight (Isaiah 59:14, truth "stumbles," meaning it is brought down).
H3782.origine: The Hebrew verb kashál comes from a root that depicts the movement of a body losing balance and falling. The word first evokes the physical image of a step that slips or breaks. The same root produces "kashol," which means a stumbling stone or obstacle. In the context of the Hebrew Bible, the verb is used for both a man who stumbles and a defeated nation, or for a cause that collapses — always this notion of losing balance, the solid becoming unstable.
H3782.emploi: The verb to stumble appears 58 times in biblical Hebrew, primarily in Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Proverbs. It primarily describes military defeat: warriors falling in battle (Jeremiah 46:6). It also denotes physical exhaustion and weakening: one whose strength is wearing out, who withers from iniquity (Psalms 31:11). In Proverbs, it represents moral testing: the righteous may stumble but rise again, while the wicked fall (Proverbs 24:16). Isaiah uses it figuratively: it is truth that stumbles when injustice reigns (Isaiah 59:14). The verb can also express the action of God who causes His adversaries to fall or who strengthens the weak (Job 4:4).
H3782.portee: To stumble reminds the believer that earthly life is fragile, that one can fall or be defeated — but not permanently. Proverbs comforts by saying that the righteous fall and rise again, while the Bible invites one to seek God's support to not stumble in faith. It is also a warning: those who reject God can only stumble and collapse.

sens: The act of falling, losing balance
Ruin, destruction, collapse
Moral or spiritual debacle
H3783.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the act of physically falling, losing footing — the concrete image of a body collapsing.
2. It extends to ruin or collapse: not only of the body that falls, but of everything that crashes or is destroyed. In Proverbs 16:18, it describes the fall of a man into misfortune: after pride comes the fall, meaning the collapse of his prosperity and position.
3. On a moral and spiritual level, the fall signifies the collapse of one who has risen through arrogance: it is the punishment for presumption.
H3783.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that expresses the idea of stumbling, losing balance, and collapsing. It paints the image of a person or structure tipping downward. The family of this word always evokes the movement of falling, from high to low, with a sense of collapse or destruction.
H3783.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible. It is found in Proverbs 16:18, where wisdom teaches an immutable moral law: arrogance and pride carry within them the seeds of ruin. The fall is not an accident, but the natural consequence of presumption. This sapiential context makes the word a teaching on God's ways toward the proud.
H3783.portee: This word reminds the believer of a fundamental truth of biblical wisdom: pride always precedes the fall. It invites humility as an antidote to ruin, and to recognize that it is God who lifts up and brings down. For those who wish to walk in wisdom, this word is a salutary warning.

sens: One who practices magic or sorcery
One who claims to know the future through occult arts
One who deceives through tricks or illusions
H3784.detail:
1. An enchanter is a man or woman who practices magic and sorcery. In Egypt, at the time of Moses, Pharaoh summons his enchanters to compete with God's miracles through their own tricks (Exodus 7:11). It is a profession practiced publicly, recognized in royal courts as a particular skill.

2. An enchanter claims to access hidden knowledge: they observe omens, interpret signs to predict the future. King Nebuchadnezzar gathers magicians, astrologers, and enchanters to interpret his dream (Daniel 2:2) — he consults them as experts in divination and secrets.

3. The enchanter deceives through tricks and illusions: their practices rely more on artifice than on true power. The Law of Israel absolutely forbids the profession of magician (Deuteronomy 18:10) and Malachi 3:5 classifies the enchanter among the sinners whom God will judge, alongside perjurers and those who oppress the weak.
H3784.origine: The Hebrew verb literally means "to bind" or "to tie" — the idea is to tie magical formulas or to master through occult ties. The root evokes the use of ritual words, incantations, and gestures to claim to act upon the supernatural reality. The word designates one who professes this art: the enchanter or enchantress.
H3784.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate practitioners of magic. In Egypt, Pharaoh's enchanters represent human wisdom in opposition to God's miracles. In Israel, the enchanter is strictly forbidden by the Law (Deuteronomy 18:10) and no legitimate enchanter exists among God's people. In Babylon, enchanters are among the king's courtiers, consulted for their supposed powers. God, through Malachi, announces that He will judge enchanters as transgressors, alongside other injustices.
H3784.portee: The enchanter reminds the believer of the radical difference between human (even purported) powers and the real power of God. These figures of occult deception invite rejection of all forms of divination or magical practice, and to trust solely in God's revelation. The judgment announced on enchanters in Malachi 3:5 shows that God takes seriously the turning toward these false powers.

sens: magical practice intended to cast a spell, to enchant
evil charm believed to produce supernatural effects
set of occult practices and secret formulas
deceptive and seductive influence exerted by magic
H3785.detail:
1. Sorcery is an ancient magical practice: formulas, gestures, and objects intended to produce supernatural effects and cast spells. Jezebel uses it to dominate and seduce (2 Kings 9:22), and Babylon boasts of its multitude of sorceries as a formidable weapon (Isaiah 47:9, 47:12).
2. It is an act of seduction and deception: sorcery attracts, fascinates, charms. Nahum describes a sorceress who sells nations through her sorceries (Nahum 3:4), showing how magic serves as an instrument of manipulation and domination.
3. It is a practice strictly forbidden to the Israelites, as it implies an alliance with powers other than God. Micah 5:11 shows God exterminating the enchantments of Israel, symbolizing the elimination of anything that claims to rival His power.
H3785.origine: The Hebrew word kesheph comes from a root that evokes binding, magical chaining: sorcery is that which binds, that which enchants. It is related to verbs and nouns that express the idea of tying, constraining. In Hebrew, it specifically denotes witchcraft, unlike other divinatory practices: it is active magic, that which claims to produce real effects through occult means.
H3785.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in a context of criticism or condemnation. It is associated with Jezebel (2 Kings 9:22), an idolatrous queen whose sorceries are among the abominations; with Babylon (Isaiah 47:9, 47:12), which is mocked by saying that its sorceries will not save it; with a sorceress of Nineveh (Nahum 3:4), who uses magic to dominate nations; and finally, with Micah 5:11, where God promises to exterminate the enchantments of the people. The word always carries a negative connotation: it is a practice that God condemns.
H3785.portee: For the believer, sorcery represents the temptation to seek power and protection outside of God, through hidden and deceptive means. The Bible portrays it to show that these practices cannot rival God's sovereignty: they may seduce for a moment, but they do not save and will perish. Recognizing that God alone controls the future invites the Christian to place their trust in Him rather than being seduced by illusory promises.

sens: One who practices magic, who claims to produce extraordinary effects through supernatural powers
Specialist in occult practices and spells, classified among false prophets
H3786.detail:
1. The magician is one who claims to accomplish impossible acts through supernatural powers — by reciting mysterious words, manipulating objects, or invoking spirits. He is a figure who fascinates through mystery, promising hidden revelations or power. In Jeremiah 27:9, the magician appears alongside the diviner and the astrologer: together, they advise the Judeans not to submit to the king of Babylon, while God commands this very submission.
2. In biblical thought, the magician is a false prophet, an impostor who deceives the people. He does not act by the power of God, but claims to master hidden forces outside of himself. The Bible thus classifies him among those who lead the people away from the truth and obedience to God.
H3786.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that designates murmurs, whispers, mysterious words — like those a magician utters in secret for his enchantments. This image of whispered, obscure, and supposedly powerful words is at the heart of the word: the magician speaks softly, enigmatically, to impress and deceive. It is a practice strictly forbidden in Israel.
H3786.emploi: The word appears only once in Jeremiah 27:9. In this passage, Jeremiah reports God's command to the exiles: they must not listen to the prophets, diviners, astrologers, or magicians who urge them to rebel against the king of Babylon. The context shows that the magician is equated with other false religious advisors: together, they contradict the authentic word of the Lord and lead the people toward lies and ruin. The magician thus represents a form of dangerous spiritual seduction.
H3786.portee: This word reminds the Christian that promises of supernatural power or hidden revelations, coming from human sources not recognized by God, are traps. Like the exiles of Judah, we are called to listen to the truth of God rather than the deceptive words of those who claim to dominate the invisible. It is a warning against the temptation to seek spiritual answers outside of God and His Word.

sens: To have a happy result, to achieve one's goal
To be suitable, appropriate, pleasing to someone
To give success to something, to ensure its prosperity
H3787.detail:
1. The word describes an action that comes to fruition, that bears fruit, that is successful. It is the idea of a venture carried out successfully. In Ecclesiastes 11:6, the sower does not know whether his morning or evening seed will succeed — this indicates that to succeed is to bear fruit, to produce a good result.

2. The word also means to be adapted to the situation, to suit, to please. It is a judgment on the relevance of an action or a word. When Esther asks the king that her request be deemed suitable (Esther 8:5), she is asking that her appeal be judged just, appropriate to his ears, worthy of being heard.

3. Less frequently, the word means "to give success to," "to make prosper." Wisdom, says Ecclesiastes 10:10, has the advantage of success: it leads ventures to a good port where pure brute force would fail.
H3787.origine: The Hebrew verb כָּשֵׁר (kasher) comes from a root that evokes the idea of success and suitability. The word is related to the adjective "kasher" (pure, legitimate, suitable), which has given the term "kosher" in modern languages for foods compliant with Jewish law. The underlying image is that of correctness: what succeeds is what is right, appropriate, in accordance with the order of things.
H3787.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in the wisdom books (Ecclesiastes and Esther). In Ecclesiastes, it describes the success of human endeavors: the seed succeeds or not, wisdom brings success. It carries here a meaning close to "prosper," "to be crowned with effect." In Esther 8:5, it has a meaning closer to "to suit," "to please" — must Esther's request appear suitable to the king? This shift from the concrete (succeeding in an action) to the judgment of value (finding appropriate) shows how the word oscillates between effectiveness and suitability.
H3787.portee: This word reminds us that success does not depend solely on our efforts, but on an alignment between our actions and reality. The sower in Ecclesiastes does not know what will succeed, for success partly eludes our control. Wisdom, however, brings success: not through brute force, but through the right adjustment to circumstances. For the believer, this invites seeking less success at all costs than a just action, entrusted to God for its outcome.

sens: The ability to succeed at a task, to accomplish work with competence
The positive result, the success or profit derived from it
What remains for the one who uses it when circumstances allow
H3788.detail: 1. Skill is the competence and know-how brought to a task: in Ecclesiastes 2:21, it is the fruit of labor "with wisdom and knowledge and with success," referring to the concrete result of intelligent effort. 2. It is also the success itself, what works: in Ecclesiastes 4:4, "all toil and skill in work" refers to what functions, what prospers. 3. Finally, it is the advantage gained, the personal benefit: in Ecclesiastes 5:10, the author asks what "advantage" comes to the possessor of wealth, meaning what real profit can be kept for oneself. In all cases, Ecclesiastes raises a bitter question: even with skill and success, what really remains for the one who acts?
H3788.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to be in good condition, to succeed" and expresses the idea of know-how and what works well. It describes both the ability (the skill you bring) and the result (what follows). It is a characteristic word of the wise reflection of Ecclesiastes on earthly goods and what they are truly worth.
H3788.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, all in Ecclesiastes, this book of meditation on the meaning of life. In 2:21, it qualifies the product of wise work. In 4:4, it describes what provokes jealousy among men. In 5:10, it questions the real profit of the possessor of riches. Each time, Ecclesiastes uses this word to show the irony of the human condition: even what succeeds, even what brings profit, remains empty if one does not know to whom it will serve or what will be done with it.
H3788.portee: This word invites the Christian to ask the real question: not "Will I succeed?" or "Will I gain an advantage?" but rather "What will it serve me?" and "What will remain of it?" It challenges a blind ambition for success and profit, reminding us that without an eternal perspective, all human effort, even that of the wise, leads nowhere.

sens: To trace characters on a surface to form words or signs
To compose a text and put it in writing
To officially record, inscribe in a register or document
To command or prescribe in writing
To be put in writing, to be recorded
H3789.detail:
1. To trace characters on a surface to form words or signs: this is the material act of writing, the gesture of the hand marking ink, brush, or chisel on parchment, papyrus, or stone. Moses writes the words of the law in a book (Deuteronomy 31:24), or the ten commandments are written on stone tablets (Exodus 32:15).
2. To compose a text and put it in writing: beyond the gesture, it is to create a written work, to shape and articulate a thought, a law, or a narrative. Moses must write the words of this law (Deuteronomy 31:24) and Joshua writes all the words of the law on the stones of Mount Ebal (Joshua 8:32).
3. To officially record, inscribe in a register or document: it is to entrust to writing what must be preserved and recalled, like the records of kings (2 Chronicles 13:22) or the ordinances of worship (Nehemiah 10:34). What is written becomes official and binding.
4. To command or prescribe in writing: to send orders by mail, in written form that binds the one giving them. Jehu writes letters to the leaders of Samaria to convey his instructions (2 Kings 10:1).
5. To be put in writing, to be recorded (passive sense): what is written becomes durable, memorable, and accessible. The number of trees can be written, meaning counted and recorded (Isaiah 10:19).
H3789.origine: The Hebrew verb katav comes from an ancient root that evokes the gesture of tracing, marking a surface. The family of the word includes ketav (the writing itself, the document), ketib (what is written), and many words related to the act of documenting and memorizing. The fundamental image is that of a hand engraving or inscribing, making permanent what was fleeting. This verb is fundamental in any biblical culture where writing, especially the written Law, holds absolute value.
H3789.emploi: The verb katav appears more than 200 times in the Hebrew Bible, particularly in the Pentateuch, historical books, and the prophets. Its most solemn use concerns the writing of the Law: Moses writes the commandments (Exodus 24:4, Deuteronomy 31:24), the ten words are written by the finger of God on the tablets (Exodus 31:18). In the books of Kings and Chronicles, katav serves to record the actions of sovereigns in the royal annals (2 Kings 10:34). The sense of prescribing or ordering in writing also appears (2 Kings 10:1, where Jehu writes letters). The passive sense (to be written, to be recorded) frequently appears to signify that something is established definitively and immutably.
H3789.portee: This word reminds the believer of the decisive role of writing in the divine covenant: God gives His Law not by word alone, but engraved and written, so that it may be fixed, transmissible, and irrevocable. Biblical writing is not a mere recording; it is an act of creation and stabilization: what is written endures. For today's reader, this establishes the authority of Scripture itself.

sens: To trace characters, letters, or words on a surface
To compose a text, a document, a letter
To put in writing, to record, to document
To be written, engraved (passive form)
H3790.detail:
1. To write is to trace letters and form words on a material: stone, parchment, papyrus. When King Darius writes to the peoples (Daniel 6:25), he orders that words be traced and sent. It is the material action of the hand marking a surface.
2. To write is also to compose a text with intention: to draft an official letter, a report, a decree. Rehum and Shimshai write to King Artaxerxes a letter concerning Jerusalem (Ezra 4:8): they compose a structured message, they think, then they trace.
3. To put in writing is to record, document, keep a trace. When names of the men who are in charge of the work are put in writing (Ezra 5:10), they are fixed durably in an official register.
4. To be written is to receive the action of writing: the record found at Achmetha was written, engraved (Ezra 6:2). Mysterious fingers wrote on the wall of the palace (Daniel 5:5) — what was written remained marked, visible.
H3790.origine: The Aramaic word ketav (כְּתַב) comes from an ancient Semitic root that designates the action of tracing, marking, engraving. A similar root is found in Hebrew (katav, כתב). The basic idea is that of a hand marking a surface durably. The root is also related to the concept of "what is written," "the writing," "the document."
H3790.emploi: This verb appears 7 times in the Aramaic portions of the Book of Ezra and the Book of Daniel — texts that report official correspondences, royal decrees, administrative records. All uses refer to formal, public, official writing: kings, governors, scribes drafting letters, reports, decrees intended to be read and known. The context is always that of important documents, words fixed in writing to last. Here, the idea of simple scribbling is not found, but of writing that engages, orders, testifies.
H3790.portee: To write is to give a durable form to the word, to preserve and disseminate it. For the reader, this word reminds us that the Word of God, like the decrees of kings, needs writing to traverse time and reach peoples. The texts of Ezra and Daniel, themselves "written" and preserved, testify that God acts through human written words, and that what is written carries the weight of eternity.

sens: A written text, placed on paper or parchment
An official document, a decree or an edict
The collection of letters and characters that make up a writing
The specific way a region or people writes
H3791.detail:
1. A written document is primarily the result of the action of inscribing words onto a medium: it is a text fixed by writing. David receives from the Lord a "written" document that gives him the understanding of the temple to be built (1 Chronicles 28:19); it is a detailed plan, an instruction put in writing.
2. A written document gains its full force when it comes from royal authority: it then becomes a decree, a command that must be obeyed. Artaxerxes sends "letters" to all provinces, and these letters contain edicts that all must follow (Esther 1:22, 3:14, 8:9).
3. The term also refers to the writing itself, the visible characters: each province receives the order according to its own "writing" (Esther 1:22), meaning its own letters, its writing system.
4. It can finally signify the style or distinctive character of the writing of a region: in Persia, writing varies according to peoples and languages, and this diversity must be respected in official documentation.
H3791.origine: The word comes from the root "ktb" which means "to write," to inscribe something with visible signs. This verb "ktb" is known throughout the Semitic languages, from Phoenician to Aramaic. The noun "ktav" (written) is its fruit: what has been written and remains written. The Bible uses the verb and the noun side by side: one "writes" (verb) a "written" document (noun). The Hebrew verb "ktb" expresses the fundamental action of fixing the word in a material and lasting form.
H3791.emploi: This word appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the accounts of Chronicles, the book of Esther, and Ezra — books full of official correspondence, decrees, and records. In 1 Chronicles 28:19 and 2 Chronicles 35:4, the "written" document is a prescription that the king transmits or has received from God: it is a documented and authentic act.
