In Esther, the word constantly arises to speak of royal letters that are disseminated: the stakes are high, for a document signed by the king cannot be revoked (Esther 8:8). Ezra 4:7 shows that the "letter" transcribed in Aramaic characters is an official administrative document. The word can also simply refer to the style of writing specific to a region (Esther 1:22, 8:9), emphasizing that each people recognizes its own writing system.
H3791.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us of the importance of fixing the word, not leaving it solely to the whims of memory. What David receives in writing is a stable and transmissible revelation. The Bible itself is a "written" document — the Word of God put into written form, which can be read, verified, and passed on to generations. It is also an invitation to respect the authority of official texts: a written document engages, it creates a lasting obligation.

sens: Marks drawn to represent words and convey a message
Document or written text, official inscription
Decree or written order
H3792.detail:
1. Writing is primarily the collection of graphic signs drawn to express speech and fix it — the act of marking characters on a surface. In Daniel 5:25, the phrase "This is the writing that was inscribed" shows these mysterious words marked in ink on the wall of the palace.
2. By extension, the word designates the document itself, the written text that must be read and interpreted. In Daniel 5:7-8, the king asks who can "read this writing and give its interpretation" — he seeks someone to decipher and understand the inscribed message.
3. Finally, a writing can be an official act, a decree or an ordinance promulgated by authority. In Daniel 6:9, King Darius "wrote the decree and the prohibition," meaning he established a law in writing that would apply to all.
H3792.origine: The Hebrew word ketav comes from a root meaning "to trace" or "to engrave." It designates the action of marking and the object that results from it — what is written. The same root appears in other Hebrew words related to writing and engraving. It is a practical and everyday term in the ancient Near East, where writing was the means of transmitting the king's orders and fixing sacred texts.
H3792.emploi: The word ketav appears twelve times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the later books of Ezra and Daniel. These books, which recount the lives of the Hebrews in Babylonian captivity or under Persian domination, feature kings who communicate through official writings (Daniel 6:9-10 with the decrees of Darius). The most vivid passage remains Daniel 5, where the mysterious writing on the palace wall becomes the dramatic crux of the entire plot: no one can read it until Daniel deciphers it. The word is also used to refer to a prior text, as in Ezra 6:18 which cites "the book of Moses." Thus, ketav covers both the material object (the marks) and the document with its content.
H3792.portee: The importance of writing in these passages emphasizes that God speaks and acts through fixed words — engraved, written, transmitted. The king's decree, the inscription on the wall are real forces that change the course of human history. For the Christian, this reinforces the idea that the Word of God, recorded in Holy Scripture, is reliable and executable: it accomplishes what it says.

sens: To make an imprint, a mark engraved or inscribed on something, especially on the skin
H3793.detail: 1. To imprint a mark means to trace, engrave, or inscribe an imprint on a surface, particularly on the flesh of the body. It is the action of leaving a lasting trace, like a seal that sinks into wax or an inscription carved in stone. In Leviticus 19:28, God commands the people of Israel: "You shall not make any cuts on your body" — it refers to intentionally marking the body with incisions or tattoos, a practice forbidden in idol worship or in honor of the dead.
H3793.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the action of engraving, of tracing deeply. The fundamental meaning is that of a lasting imprint, a trace that sinks in and persists — like an engraving that cannot be easily erased. The starting image is very concrete: that of a punch that digs, of a chisel that splits the material to leave its mark.
H3793.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 19:28. The context is legislative and cultic: God enumerates prohibitions intended to preserve the holiness of Israel and to distinguish it from the idolatrous practices of neighboring peoples. The prohibition against imprinting figures on the body is part of a series of rules that touch on the integrity of the body and the separation between the living and the dead, between the sacred and the profane. It is an act of devotion that violated divine ethics.
H3793.portee: This word reminds Christians that the body is not a blank canvas to be covered with signs according to our desires: it is the temple of the Holy Spirit and belongs to God. The biblical prohibition invites us to examine what drives us to mark our bodies — the search for identity, belonging to a group, mourning — and to recognize that our true identity comes from our relationship with the Lord, not from external signs. It also sheds light on the danger of spiritual practices that seek to merge the body with the worship of contrary powers.

sens: vertical surface built of stone or brick that encloses or delineates a space
fortified structure that protects a city or building
interior wall of a building, plastered and whitewashed
H3797.detail:
1. The primary and most concrete meaning: a vertical structure built of cut stones or bricks, which serves to enclose a space or delineate a plot of land. The text in Ezra 5:8 describes the walls of the temple being rebuilt, assembled stone by stone, with wood placed between the courses.
2. A fortified wall, built to protect a city or palace from attacks. In Daniel 5:5, the wall of the royal palace of Babylon is coated with white lime, making it visible and impressive.
3. The interior wall of a building, particularly when it is whitewashed or painted. The same passage in Daniel describes this smooth surface where mysterious fingers write words of warning.
H3797.origine: The Aramaic word כְּתַל (ketal) is the constructed form of כֹּתֶל (kotel), which literally means "wall" in Hebrew. This root refers to the image of an erected partition, and it is attested in both Semitic languages (Hebrew and Aramaic) with the same concrete and concise meaning: that which surrounds, that which supports, that which separates. Aramaic, a language spoken in Syria and Mesopotamia, borrows here from Hebrew or shares with it a very ancient common root.
H3797.emploi: The word appears only twice in biblical Aramaic, both in the historical books of Ezra and Daniel. In Ezra 5:8, it refers to the walls of the Jerusalem temple that the Jews are rebuilding after the exile, emphasizing the raw material (stones) and the progress of the work. In Daniel 5:5, it evokes the wall of the royal palace of Babylon, specifically its lime coating, which becomes the backdrop for a supernatural and terrifying sign. In both cases, the word emphasizes the solidity and visibility of these structures.
H3797.portee: These two occurrences of the word "wall" frame a striking contrast: on one side, the patient and laborious reconstruction of the temple by the exiled people (the wall is built stone by stone); on the other, the sudden ruin of a powerful empire signified by the supernatural appearance on its royal wall. The wall thus becomes a symbol of the contrast between the fragility of human kingdoms and the constancy of God's plan for His people.

sens: City of Lower Judah
H3798.detail: Kithlisch is a small city in the low region of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible as one of the localities allocated to the tribe of Judah.
H3798.origine: The name Kithlisch is of Semitic origin. Its exact meaning eludes us today, as it is an ancient Palestinian toponym whose etymology has been lost. Like many place names in Canaan, it likely reflects a geographical feature or the name of an ancient founder.
H3798.emploi: Kithlisch appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:40, in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the Promised Land. This list enumerates the localities of Lower Judah, a region of hills that are lower than the central plateau. Kithlisch is listed among other small towns like Cabbon and Lachmas, reflecting the administrative organization of the Judean territory at the time of the conquest.

sens: To leave a trace, a stain that does not fade
To remain engraved, impregnated despite all cleaning efforts
To visibly persist in a state of guilt
H3799.detail:
1. The word evokes a stain or impurity that deeply ingrains itself in a material and cannot be removed by simple washing. Even with the best detergents (niter and potash), a deeply rooted stain remains visible — this is the image in Jeremiah 2:22.

2. Figuratively, this means that Israel's sin will not simply disappear because one pretends to change: it remains engraved, inscribed before God, impossible to hide. The word emphasizes the permanence and depth of the mark.
H3799.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of dyeing, impregnating, leaving a lasting color or mark. The basic meaning is very concrete: a dye that penetrates the fabric and does not wash out. Used in a spiritual sense, it denotes guilt that has taken root and that nothing can erase, except divine intervention.
H3799.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 2:22, where the prophet denounces Israel's illusion: believing that its sins could be erased by its own efforts or purification rituals. The Lord affirms that iniquity remains marked, visible, persistent in His eyes. The context is that of divine judgment in the face of unfaithfulness.
H3799.portee: This word teaches the believer a humbling and salutary truth: our sins do not disappear through our personal efforts or good works. Only God, through His grace and forgiveness in Christ, can truly cleanse us. It urges us to renounce self-justification and turn towards divine mercy.

sens: Wild animal resembling a pig, with tusks, that lives in forests
(Figuratively) Destructive force, enemy that ravages
H3765.detail:
1. The wild boar is a robust and aggressive wild animal, known for its sharp tusks and strength. In Psalms 80:14, the psalmist uses the image of the wild boar that gnaws and ravages the Lord's vineyard to evoke a destructive enemy that devastates the people of Israel.
2. Figuratively, the wild boar represents a hostile and devastating force — the image of brutal destruction reminds us how a powerful enemy can destroy what has been carefully planted and cultivated, just as wine represents God's blessing.
H3765.origine: The Hebrew word כִּרְסֵם (kirsem) comes from a root that literally means "to tear" or "to lacerate." The wild boar embodies this notion of destructive tearing: it is the animal that tears and ravages with its brute strength. This image was familiar to the Israelites who lived close to nature and were well aware of the damage that wild animals caused to crops and vineyards.
H3765.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 80:14, where the poet-priest cries out to God, pleading for Him to protect His vineyard (an image of the people of Israel or the kingdom). The wild boar symbolizes an invader, likely the Assyrian empire or another external enemy. The image is striking: just as the wild boar brutally destroys a cultivated vineyard, so the enemy has devastated God's people. It is a call for divine deliverance in the face of the threat of devastation.
H3765.portee: This image reminds us that hostile powers can seem invincible and destructive — like a wild boar ruthlessly ravaging a vineyard. But the psalm teaches us that we must cry out to God to come and defend what belongs to Him. For the believer, it is an invitation to place trust in divine protection against the forces of evil that threaten His people.

sens: Descendants of Javan, son of Noah
The peoples of the Mediterranean islands and coasts
H3794G.detail:
1. Kittim primarily refers to a person: one of the sons of Javan, who is himself a son of Noah (Genesis 10:4). He is an ancestor from whom entire peoples descend, as seen in the biblical genealogies that trace all humanity back to Noah.
2. The name later becomes the general term for all the peoples inhabiting the islands and shores of the Mediterranean. Rather than a unique ethnicity, it is a geographical and cultural category: all those who live on the water and engage in maritime trade.
H3794G.origine: The name comes from Hebrew and literally means "crusher" or "striker," an image perhaps related to the waves crashing against the rocky shores of the Mediterranean islands. Kittim appears in the genealogical list of Genesis alongside Tarshish and Elishah, other names associated with the maritime peoples of the Mediterranean basin. This name primarily applies to the Greeks and Phoenicians in historical understanding.
H3794G.emploi: Kittim appears only twice in the Bible, in the two parallel genealogies of humanity after the Flood: in Genesis 10:4 and 1 Chronicles 1:7. In both cases, it is listed among the four sons of Javan. The Bible uses it as a geographical and genealogical marker to designate the distant populations of the Mediterranean shores, those that the Israelites primarily knew through trade and maritime contact.
H3794G.portee: Kittim reminds us that the table of nations in Genesis 10 classifies all the known peoples of the ancient world according to their common genealogy: all descend from Noah and receive their place in God's plan. It is an invitation to see all humanity as a dispersed family, not as enemies or strangers unrelated to us.

sens: The Mediterranean islands, particularly Cyprus and its coasts
The maritime and trading peoples of the Mediterranean
The naval powers that threaten land empires
H3794H.detail:
1. Kittim primarily refers to the islands and coastal regions of the Mediterranean basin, particularly Cyprus and its surroundings. In prophetic visions, these islands represent distant territories known through maritime trade: Isaiah 23:1 reports that the news of the destruction of Tyre "comes from the land of Kittim," emphasizing that even the most distant traders hear the news.
2. Kittim later becomes a generic term for all the maritime and trading peoples of the Mediterranean: Jeremiah 2:10 urges to "pass over to the isles of Kittim" to seek a people who have changed their god, as if Kittim represented the entirety of the known maritime world.
3. Finally, in ultimate prophecies, Kittim symbolizes the naval powers that rise to strike down continental empires: Numbers 24:24 announces that "ships will come from Kittim" to humble the Assyrian, and Daniel 11:30 describes "ships of Kittim" advancing against the king of the North, embodying a threat from the sea against land dominance.
H3794H.origine: Kittim comes from the Phoenician Kittim, which designated the island of Cyprus (the ancient Kition or Citium). This name extended to all the Mediterranean islands and coasts known and frequented by the Phoenicians. In the Hebrew Bible, Kittim gradually takes on a symbolic meaning: from a geographical territory, it becomes the expression of a distant, rich, powerful world, and inaccessible to the domination of continental empires.
H3794H.emploi: Kittim appears six times in the Hebrew Bible (Numbers, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel). In earlier periods (Numbers, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel), it refers to the Mediterranean maritime world, often in contrast to land peoples: Jeremiah 2:10 contrasts it with Kedar (the desert peoples). In the later prophecies of Daniel, written after the exile, Kittim acquires an eschatological significance: the ships of Kittim represent a military power that will emerge to transform the world order (Daniel 11:30). Ezekiel 27:6 mentions the islands of Kittim as a source of precious wood and ivory for the ships of Tyre, recalling their legendary wealth.
H3794H.portee: Kittim teaches the biblical reader that the boundaries of the world are not limited to what terrestrial empires control. It affirms that the God of Israel also reigns over distant and maritime peoples, and that His providence transcends seemingly invincible empires. In the visions of the end times, Kittim becomes a sign that no human power can escape God's will: even the powerful ships that come from afar will be instruments of His judgment.

sens: Crushed or ground olive to extract oil
Oil obtained in this way, of pure and fine quality
Figuratively: something precious, obtained through meticulous work
H3795.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to the olive itself after it has been crushed in a mortar or under a stone to extract the oil. This process produces a very pure oil, free from impurities, ideal for sacred uses: this is what is commanded to the Israelites in Exodus 27:20, for the oil of the lampstand of the tabernacle. 2. By extension, the word refers to the oil itself, obtained through this meticulous and delicate method. This crushed olive oil is included in the grain offerings (Exodus 29:40, Numbers 28:5) and becomes a commercial commodity: Solomon provides it to Hiram each year, as noted in 1 Kings 5:11. 3. The term finally evokes the idea of something precious and refined, obtained not through violence but through slow and careful work: to crush means to finely grind, which is not coarse manufacturing.
H3795.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning 'to crush, grind, or mash.' The image is that of the mortar and pestle: the olive is not torn apart, but gently crushed to extract its essence. This finesse of work justifies that the resulting oil is called 'pure' and is reserved for the most noble uses of worship.
H3795.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in passages that describe the worship of the tabernacle and the temple, and the official offerings. In Exodus 27:20 and Leviticus 24:2, the crushed olive oil must fuel the sacred lampstand. In Exodus 29:40 and Numbers 28:5, it accompanies the grain offerings. Only once, in 1 Kings 5:11, does it come out of the religious context: Solomon pays tribute with it to the king of Tyre. In all cases, it is a choice product, intended for the most important uses.
H3795.portee: This word reminds Christians that quality and care are offered to God. Crushed oil—obtained through slow and meticulous work, not through brutality—symbolizes how our offerings, even humble ones, become precious when given with attention and delicacy. It is a lesson on the value of work done with heart and the beauty of what has cost effort.

sens: vertical wall that closes or surrounds a space
barrier, limit that separates
H3796.detail:
1. The wall is the vertical side of a house or construction: it is what encloses the sides of a dwelling. In the Song of Solomon, the beloved sees her lover behind the wall of the house, which partially hides him from her view (Song of Solomon 2:9).
2. By extension, the wall represents a separation, a limit between the one who is outside and the one who is inside: it creates a distance, a barrier that must be crossed to come together.
H3796.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of closing or enclosing. In Aramaic, the very similar form ketalь (כְּתַל) carries the same meaning. The word reflects a simple and universal image: in biblical times, as today, the wall was the essential structure for building and protecting a habitat.
H3796.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Song of Solomon 2:9. It refers to the wall of an ordinary house, one that is part of daily life. This context of romantic poetry transforms the wall into an element of the scene: it is not a fortress or a city wall, but simply the side of a dwelling, which partially hides the beloved from her lover.
H3796.portee: This passage speaks to us of separation and desire: the wall that separates two people in love reminds us of the obstacles that life often places between us and those we cherish. It is a poetic image of waiting and tender gazes across barriers.
